Predictions we got right (or wrong)

Programming note: We’ll be off starting next week for the holidays but will be back to our normal schedule on Monday, Jan. 5.

PAGING MISS CLEO — Around this time last year, we gazed into the crystal ball and made a series of big predictions about California politics in the year ahead — from the tenor of Trump resistance 2.0 to major policy fights on AI safety and housing.

How did our prognostications fare in the roller coaster ride that was 2025? What did we get right and what missed the mark?

Our POLITICO California team huddled to revisit our biggest predictions — and what the outcomes say about how those political and policy fights could evolve in the year to come:

CALIFORNIA RESISTANCE, PART 2: Some argue Democrats are too tired or bloodied to resist Trump, but those fights will begin immediately once he takes office.

Gov. Gavin Newsom and other prominent Democrats did initially downplay the idea of resistance 2.0, but that lasted about five minutes. California filed dozens of lawsuits challenging Trump’s executive orders within his first few months in office, aiming to protect the state’s policies on everything from immigration to the environment. And by the early summer, Newsom’s office embraced a more combative tone and trolling social media persona. The pivot came as Trump stretched political norms and sent the National Guard into Los Angeles and a host of other blue cities. Heading into 2026, Newsom and other prominent pols have a strong political incentive to keep the resistance alive and well in the Golden State.

AFFORDABILITY IS THE WORD: 2025 will be the year of the “affordability” buzzword.

Nailed it (forgive the brag). Democrats so relentlessly leaned into the affordability messaging that the word itself seemed to get under Trump’s skin, prompting him to dismiss it as a “con job.” But California’s ruling Democrats, who vowed to make affordability a centerpiece of their focus in 2025, learned that actually tackling the high cost of living is a lot harder than just identifying the problem. Democrats passed measures to address the state’s housing (more on that below) and energy prices, but California is still one of the most expensive states to live in. Nationally, we can expect Democrats to continue to hang the affordability albatross around the GOP’s neck in the midterms. But the issue will undoubtedly be a theme in next year’s governor’s race too, and the many Democrats hoping to succeed Newsom will need to walk a tightrope, acknowledging voters’ worries about high costs without laying the blame on the incumbent governor and their own party.

OPINION SHIFT ON IMMIGRATION: California won’t take substantial action to impede ICE agents.

This prediction looked good at first. Some California House Democrats opened the year voting for the GOP’s Laken Riley Act, and Newsom for months barely spoke publicly about immigration.

But everything changed when Trump ramped up deportations and, in June, sent the National Guard and Marines to Los Angeles. Democrats at all levels of the state’s politics — especially Newsom — ripped the deployments and raids. By September, Newsom had signed legislation attempting to ban ICE agents from wearing masks used to conceal their identity, alongside laws meant to shield immigrants’ health care information and require families be notified of federal agents’ presence at schools.

We’ll take a shred of credit, though, for pointing out that the federal government’s sweeping immigration authority would limit the effectiveness of any California response. The mask ban is tied up in a court fight, and the Trump administration has vowed not to follow it, anyway.

HOUSING WILL BE KING: Democrats in the Legislature are expected to go BIG on housing this year.

On the money. There could hardly have been a bigger year for housing in Sacramento. Legislators and the governor, after a monthslong brawl with unions and environmentalists, enacted the most sweeping reforms to state housing law in decades. They took a major bite out of environmental reviews for urban infill housing. Another landmark measure, Senate Bill 79, will require large cities to allow taller apartment buildings near rail stations.

Now, the question remains: Will these big swings actually lead to more housing construction? Newsom and YIMBY-aligned state lawmakers are under pressure to show these laws can bear fruit. There’s also expected to be a host of “clean-up” bills on SB79, which could potentially remove its teeth and revive a heated debate over the state’s role in mandating housing. Don’t forget that these major housing laws narrowly passed. It’s not inconceivable that the Legislature could move the other direction next session.

REPRO FUNDING WANTED: Expect reproductive health care to be a major budget issue this year.

Last year we thought the reproductive health question was whether Newsom would reup the $200 million in new abortion funding he spent in response to 2022’s Dobbs decision. Turns out the issues were much more existential. Federal family planning grants have been pulled, Planned Parenthood clinics around the state have closed and Congressional Republicans are debating further restrictions. Instead of the expansive new programs from a few years ago, expect the repro world to be lobbying for money to keep clinic doors open.

TECH BATTLES INCOMING: The fight of artificial intelligence regulation is far from over.

If anything, we underestimated AI’s impact, judging by the amount of late nights our new California Decoded team pulled this year. Sen. Scott Wiener brought (most) tech giants together to pass his internationally-watched AI transparency bill. Washington was watching, too, and it helped spark Trump’s ongoing fight to preempt state AI rules. Back home, the political debate around AI chatbots exploded amid a series of high-profile wrongful death lawsuits implicating OpenAI’s flagship model ChatGPT. OpenAI and kids’ safety groups might even take chatbot controls to the ballot in 2026 — a mark of how quickly the issue went mainstream. Don’t even get us started on data centers, which are shaping up to be a serious issue in next year’s midterms.

EXPECT MORE RECALLS: After a series of successful recall campaigns, voters across the state will try to take their frustrations with elected officials to the ballot.

Although there were a handful of recalls across California last year (notably, successful efforts to remove San Francisco Supervisor Joel Engardio and the sheriff of San Mateo County, as well as a failed attempt in Fairfax), no serious statewide campaigns materialized. Instead, it was Proposition 50’s redistricting that ultimately gave voters the power to target politicians, installing new congressional maps that will leave Republican representatives fighting for their political lives.

— Dustin, Blake, Melanie Mason, Rachel Bluth, Tyler Katzenberger and Will McCarthy.

GOOD MORNING. Happy Friday. Thanks for waking up with Playbook.

WHERE’S GAVIN? Nothing official announced.

TOP READS

FROM MARIN TO MODOC COUNTY — We sent Will McCarthy to drive 15 hours across the state, traversing mountain ranges and rock slides, dirt roads and agricultural checkpoints, from Marin to Modoc County — a nearly 700-mile ramble through California’s most egregiously gerrymandered new district.

Perhaps the most extreme example of the newly enshrined gerrymander is CA-02, Will writes, a massive, hatchet or flag-shaped district that links Marin, one of the wealthiest counties in the country, with the remote, isolated high desert of northeastern California. It is million-dollar mansions in Tiburon, empty beaches in Sonoma, struggling lumber mills in Siskiyou, healing rocks in Mt. Shasta, and simply sand and sky and silence. There is little uniting these communities politically, economically, climactically, culturally, historically — or even symbolically. But as a result of Prop 50, they will all share the same representative in Congress. And that representative, in all likelihood, will be a Democrat.

While Prop 50 has been trumpeted as a victory for Democrats and democracy, it was also, fundamentally, a decision to further distance vast stretches of the state from political representation. Far-flung places that couldn’t feel more different from urban centers like Marin will now, at least geographically, make up the vast majority of the district.

So, Will decided to drive it. Read his story here.

CAMPAIGN YEAR(S)

FIRST IN PLAYBOOK: WAITING IN THE WINGS — Santa Clara County District Attorney Jeff Rosen is considering running for attorney general if incumbent Rob Bonta enters the governor’s race, according to an ally granted anonymity to discuss Rosen’s planning.

Rosen could fill a progressive lane, with his history criticizing the tough-on-crime Proposition 36 and working with Assembly Speaker Robert Rivas on competing retail theft proposals. Part of California’s criminal justice reform movement, Rosen has also sought resentencing for death row inmates and expungement of some low level drug crimes since he took office in 2011.

Rosen is one of more than a dozen Democrats who’ve been floated to replace Bonta, meaning a succession campaign would likely be crowded.

CAN HE SEE SOME I.D.? — Prominent conservative donor Richard Uihlein made a massive donation to a California voter I.D. ballot initiative, buoying the chances the measure makes the 2026 ballot and outlining the national stakes. Midwestern shipping supply magnate, Uihlein reported a $4 million donation, by far the campaign’s largest to date. Uihlein is a prolific donor to Trump and Republicans. — Jeremy B. White

FIRST IN PLAYBOOK: SPEAKER’S BLESSING — Former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi endorsed Lt. Gov. Eleni Kounalakis for state treasurer in a video released this morning. Pelosi’s nod comes as little surprise given she previously backed Kounalakis for governor (before she pivoted races) and the two are longtime friends from the well-heeled world of Pacific Heights. But it could help Kounalakis, who’s raised close to $9 million, solidify her dominance in the treasurer’s race.

“Eleni has really been a leader all her life,” Pelosi said in the video. “People know that when you hear the name ‘Eleni,’ it is synonymous with great values, vision and love of the people.”

FIRST IN PLAYBOOK: IN THE TRENCHES — Josh Fryday, a former Naval officer and Democrat running for lieutenant governor, is leaning into his military record in the race, arguing Democrats have a self-inflicted liability due to the party overlooking the needs of veterans and the military.

“Too often Democrats lack credibility on military and national security issues,” Fryday told Playbook. “As President Trump continues to abuse the military to intimidate the public and for political gain, we need to elect veterans with the authority to stand up and push back.”

Fryday — who served at Guantanamo Bay (and testified to the Senate about abuses there) and in Japan during the Fukushima nuclear accident — will today unveil the endorsement of VetVotes. The group one is one of the nation’s largest progressive PACs focused on the needs of veterans.

Fryday, who works as the chief service officer in Newsom’s administration, said he would leverage the lieutenant governor’s office to expand a state jobs corps program that helps veterans and military families find jobs when they return to civilian life. Another proposal would expand an initiative to help veterans get college credit for their service.

FIRST IN PLAYBOOK: EARLY MONEY — Meanwhile, a person familiar with Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel’s fundraising operation said he has raised almost $900,000 in the week since he opened a campaign finance account for an attorney general race that has not yet started.

Gabriel, chair of the Assembly Budget Committee, also has more than $2.9 million in his legislative campaign account, which he could tap into if he runs to be the state’s top cop. — Nicole Norman

GOVERNOR'S RACE

SWALWELL THE PRODUCER — Rep. Eric Swalwell is coming under fire from some labor unions over his connection to a film production where the crew has gone on strike over workplace conditions and compensation disputes.

Swalwell, a Democratic gubernatorial contender, is listed as the executive producer of the film, “The Gun on Second Street,” an independent crime drama filming in West Virginia. The crew went on strike Thursday, and the International Alliance of Theatrical Stage Employees called upon its union members not to cross the picket line.

The representative, in a statement, downplayed his involvement. He said he shared details of his “family’s law enforcement experiences with the writer” and was offered an executive producer credit in exchange.

“I never personally invested,” Swalwell said. “I have also been a lifelong supporter of labor. While I am prohibited by Congressional ethics rules from participating in the negotiations between production and labor, I joined the film expecting that labor standards would be adhered to and urge the production team to seek a fair outcome for the crew. Should that not be achieved, I will remove my name from the film’s screen credits.”

But Lindsay Dougherty, the head of Teamsters Local 399, which represents more than 6,000 workers in Hollywood, suggested Swalwell should pay a price. Teamsters California has endorsed former Rep. Katie Porter in the race.

“We want candidates that are going to protect working people, and this is not an example of that,” Dougherty told Playbook. “This is not helping our Hollywood industry in California, either. I don’t see how this is a positive for him at all.”

REPUBLICANLAND

TRUMP BUMP — Trump has intervened in Republicans’ bid to oust frontline Rep. Adam Gray, endorsing former Stockton Mayor Kevin Lincoln in a TruthSocial post.

“As your next Congressman, Kevin will work tirelessly to Grow our Economy, Cut Taxes and Regulations, Promote MADE IN THE U.S.A., Champion American Energy DOMINANCE, Keep our now very Secure Border, SECURE, Stop Migrant Crime, Strengthen our Great Military/Veterans, and Protect our always under siege Second Amendment,” Trump wrote on Thursday.

House Speaker Mike Johnson followed the president’s lead, endorsing Lincoln in a move poised to consolidate the Republican base in a GOP priority race. Gray won the current version of his district by fewer than 200 votes last cycle, and though it will swing from a district Trump carried to one Kamala Harris won under Democrats’ gerrymander, she carried it by less than a percentage point.

Both parties amplified the Trump endorsement. A spokesperson for the National Republican Campaign Committee celebrated the nod as evidence of Trump’s faith in Lincoln the “fighter who puts California families first,” while a Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee spokesperson accused Lincoln of “proving he answers to his Washington party bosses over the Central Valley.”

HEALTHCARE

FIRST IN PLAYBOOK: HOLDING THE LINE — A coalition of LGBTQ+ advocacy groups will send a letter to California hospitals and health care providers today, urging them to not comply with the Trump administration’s demands that they stop providing gender-affirming care to transgender minors or face massive funding cuts.

The groups argue that California law requires hospitals to provide health care access to transgender people, asserting that Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s proposed rules to ban such care cannot override the state’s policies.

“Even if the proposed … rules were finalized, medical care for transgender young people would remain legal and protected in California, and healthcare providers would continue to be bound by California’s nondiscrimination protections,” the letter states.

Signatories on the letter include Equality California, the Los Angeles LGBT Center, ACLU California Action and TransFamily Support Services.

CLIMATE AND ENERGY

THREADING THE NEEDLE — California energy regulators made an affordability case Thursday as they voted for a marginal cut to the profit rate of the state’s investor-owned utilities. Read last night’s California Climate to learn about the delicate balance the California Public Utilities Commission leadership tried to strike on profits — and why nobody, from utilities to investors to customers, is happy about it.

Mayor Karen Bass Launches Reelection Campaign with Broad Coalition Rally at LATTC

By Lila Brown

Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass officially launched her reelection campaign on December 13th with a rally that brought together Angelenos from across the city, alongside leaders from labor, business, faith, and government, signaling the breadth of her political coalition as she seeks a second term.

Held at Los Angeles Trade-Technical College's Culinary Arts Event Space, the rally drew hundreds of supporters. The atmosphere was celebratory but resolute, underscoring what speakers described as a pivotal moment for Los Angeles amid national political headwinds.

Mayor Bass framed her reelection bid around what she called tangible progress during her first term, emphasizing public safety, housing, affordability, climate action, and the protection of immigrant communities.

"We are told all the time that labor can't work with business, that community can't work with government," Bass said. "But what you see here today is Los Angeles. We come together because we believe in justice."

Central to the mayor's remarks was what her administration describes as the first sustained reduction in street homelessness in decades-an achievement that runs counter to national trends. Bass highlighted the city's emergency declaration on homelessness, the Inside Safe initiative, and the streamlining of more than 40,000 housing units to address affordability.

She also pointed to the creation of the Office of Community Safety, noting that homicide totals in 2025 are trending toward a decades-long low, and emphasized historic climate reforms, including the official elimination of coal usage in the City of Los Angeles.

"This city has had a tough year," Bass said. "But we stood together in tragedy, we stood together to protect our communities, and we are not done."

The rally featured a notable show of unity across sectors.

Los Angeles County Federation of Labor President Yvonne Wheeler formally announced the federation's endorsement of Mayor Bass, representing more than 800,000 union members across the county. Joined by SEIU 721 President David Green, labor leaders praised the mayor's efforts to protect city jobs, expand affordable housing, and champion living wages. "Karen Bass has always been a fierce advocate for working people," Wheeler said. "She understands a simple but powerful truth - that a job must be a good job, one that delivers wages and benefits so families don't just survive, but thrive. That's why the Los Angeles labor movement is proud to stand united in endorsing Mayor Karen Bass for reelection." "One layoff is one too many," Green said, crediting the mayor's hands-on leadership with reducing the threat of 1,600 layoffs to zero. "Now it's our turn to stand up for her."

From the business community, Stuart Waldman, President of the Valley Industry & Commerce Association (VICA), spoke alongside entrepreneur Karim Webb, CityView CEO Sean Burton, and business leaders George Pla, Annika Yeo, and Priscilla Chavez, highlighting the mayor's engagement with job creation and economic recovery across Los Angeles. Immigrant rights were front and center as Angelica Salas, President of CHIRLA Action Fund, addressed the crowd alongside leaders from diverse immigrant communities, commending Bass for what she described as decisive action in resisting federal policies that target immigrants.

Mayor Bass was joined on stage by a wide array of elected officials, including Congresswoman Sydney Kamlager-Dove, State Senators Maria Elena Durazo and Lola SmallwoodCuevas, Assemblymembers Jesse Gabriel, Mike Fong, and Isaac Bryan, and Los Angeles City Council President Marqueece Harris-Dawson, along with several councilmembers and school board leaders. Former state and city officials were also in attendance.

Councilmember Hugo Soto-Martinez pointed to Inside Safe operations in Hollywood, citing an independent RAND Corporation study that found homelessness reduced by 50% in the area. "That's leadership," he said. "That's the mayor's leadership."

Faith leaders representing multiple traditions led interfaith prayers, including Rev. Dr. Timothy Tyler of First AME Church and Rabbi Tamara Eskenazi of Hebrew Union College, reinforcing the moral framing of the mayor's campaign message. The program was moderated by Emmy-nominated actress, writer, and producer Yvette Nicole Brown, who described Mayor Bass as a "humble servant leader" whose career-from Speaker of the California Assembly to the U.S. Congress and now City Hall-has been defined by service.

"This 15 the kickoff of her campaign to serve a second term as Mayor of Los Angeles," Brown told the crowd. "And we're here at the very beginning."

Following the rally, SEIU organizer Maurice Littles shared his perspective on the mayor's leadership. "I've seen the difference," Littles said. "She's been on the front lines for years, even before she was mayor. Through all the attacks-from Washington, [D.C.] and elsewhere she's held her ground and delivered."

Littles also emphasized the significance of Bass's leadership as a Black woman. "She stands tall," he said. "People know her not just by her words, but by her deeds."

Jordan "TJ" Karter, a sound engineer who plans to enroll next semester in Los Angeles Trade-Technical College's Culinary Arts program, attended the rally at the invitation of his friend Rosco Hines, a colleague of Mayor Bass. Karter said he was encouraged by the mayor's remarks and her focus on the city's most pressing challenges.

"I really enjoyed the mayor's speech and think she's doing a great job overall," Karter said. "I'd love to see her continue working with Governor Gavin Newsom on immigration and homelessness."

In closing, Mayor Bass acknowledged the political fight ahead, characterizing the election as a choice between unity and division, and between working people and what she repeatedly referred to as the "billionaire class."

"Los Angeles is not for sale," she told supporters. "And I'm not finished."

As the 2026 mayoral race officially begins, Saturday's rally made clear that Mayor Karen Bass is entering the campaign with a coalition that spans labor halls, boardrooms, community organizations, and faith institutions-an alliance she will rely on as she seeks to extend her tenure at City Hall.

Meet the crypto billionaire hedging his bets for governor

FIRST IN PLAYBOOK: MATCHUP MAKER — Crypto billionaire and San Francisco megadonor Chris Larsen is spending heavily to back both a Democrat and Republican in the crowded race for governor.

Larsen told Playbook in an interview that he’s making a maximum $39,200 contribution to Republican Steve Hilton, a former Fox News host and author — matching his prior contribution to Democrat and former Rep. Katie Porter.

The Ripple co-founder, who’s worth an estimated $10.2 billion, said he wants Hilton and Porter to advance to the November election because they are both — despite their partisan disagreements — focused on “kitchen table issues” like California’s crushing affordability crisis.

Playbook spoke with Larsen about his unusual move, as well as his support for Porter despite her recent headwinds. Highlights from the interview, which has been condensed for clarity and space:

Why are you supporting both Hilton and Porter in this race?

I’m 100 percent behind Katie Porter, but I’ve met with Steve a couple of times, and I’d say they share something similar. They’re focused on really basic stuff. California’s problems are some pretty basic things around costs and getting rid of some of the overburdensome [rules] regulations that are holding us back on multiple fronts. Both of them come at that ‘back to basics, kitchen table’ thing. I know the affordability [mantra] is so popular everywhere. But I think both of them are coming at it genuinely, and have been for some time. It’s weird, they actually get along. I guess they’ve connected with each other. They both have the right temperaments for this divisive world we live in, and that’s also why I think it’d be good to have a Republican and a Dem in the final two — rather than having two Dems or two Republicans, which theoretically could happen.

Why would you prefer to have a Democrat and Republican in the runoff?

Things are just way, way too vilified, divided. We’ve got to start having conversations with the other side. So, having two Dems in there, you would lose that conversation, right? I don’t think that’s good for this state. We still have a lot of Republicans in the state. I know they’re in the minority, but they’re not represented at all. Generally, a one party supermajority is not really the best thing to have. You’re missing out on a lot of key debates that millions of people want to have. So I think it’s healthier to have one person from each party.

You’ve given heavily to Democrats in the past. What would you say to allies who might be surprised that you’re giving to a Republican and former Fox News host?

Well, I think we have to get away from those labels. You have to meet him. When you meet him, it’s like, he’s a reasonable guy and he’s focused on the right things and seems respectful. Everybody has to be judged by who they are. We got into problems with this kind of labeling people. The problems you have in this country, in this state, they’re coming from both extremes — the far left that’s done some wacky stuff and the far right that’s done some wacky stuff. There’s a huge range between those two points.

What if Porter and Hilton both advance from the June top-two primary — who would you support in November?

Well, I’m behind Katie Porter and have been for a long time. I still hope that she wins. But that’s a good matchup, and that brings out the best in her. And it brings out the best on the other side, too, with those two as the key voices in this contest. It’s a good thing for the debate.

What are those “kitchen table” issues they’re both talking about that you think need to be front of mind in the race?

It’s the big-cost things that are really holding people back: housing, obviously; education, that’s too expensive; energy costs. And then there’s just way over — and I’m not even going to say overregulation because regulation is important — it’s just burden, like this crazy number of burdensome [rules] that have obviously been put in there by special interests who control Sacramento. We’ve got to start hacking through that jungle because that’s a big part of what’s really hurting us.

Are you surprised that Porter doesn’t have more momentum? She’s been a front-runner, at least among Democrats, but her polling seems to have plateaued since her viral videos controversy.

Oh, not at all. I just did an event for her with a bunch of business folks and other leaders in San Francisco. I have to say, she just hit it out of the park, and that’s not necessarily an easy group to win over. You had people coming in curious, going out convinced. Also, the viral video thing, the fact that that’s an issue is the stupidest thing I’ve ever heard. I mean, she’s tough. She comes across as tough. And, you know what? Right on. We need somebody who’s tough to take on the folks that are driving Sacramento. She’s not a Sacramento person, she was in Congress. So she comes in not with a lot of IOUs, so to speak.

You emphasized your take on the viral videos controversy. Can you talk more about why you think that’s unimportant in the scope of the race?

It’s beyond unimportant. It actually is proof of how tough she is. Frankly, I don’t see it as an issue at all. Because she used the F word? Okay, fine. To handle this state, you know how complex it is, you’re gonna have to have some thick skin. And that’s what I take away.

GOOD MORNING. It’s Wednesday. Thanks for waking up with Playbook.

WHERE’S GAVIN? Nothing official announced.

GOVERNOR'S RACE

FIRST IN PLAYBOOK: MIDDLE MARCH — Rep. Eric Swalwell jumps out to a lead over longtime front-runner Katie Porter in a new governor’s race poll commissioned by California Issues Forum, a nonprofit tied to the moderate Democratic caucus that puts on trips and forums connecting lawmakers and interest group representatives.

The FM3 poll of likely voters finds Republicans Chad Bianco and Steve Hilton in an effective three-way tie with Swalwell for first place in the high teens, hinting at Democrats’ nightmare lockout scenario, followed by Porter at 13 percent, and then everyone else in single digits. Democratic voters prefer Swalwell (30 percent) to Porter (21 percent). But there’s still plenty of variability: One-fifth of voters remain undecided, and the poll doesn’t ask about Attorney General Rob Bonta, a heavyweight poised to leap in.

The survey also approximates what voters will actually see on the ballot by using likely designations, which means candidates’ current gigs rather than old ones — so ex-Representative Porter as a “law professor/community organizer” and former HHS Secretary Xavier Becerra as an “attorney,” for instance. — Jeremy B. White

CAMPAIGN YEAR(S)

FIRST IN PLAYBOOK: INSURE THING — State Sen. Ben Allen is rolling out endorsements from Reps. Julia Brownley, George Whitesides, Laura Friedman and Nanette Barragán, bringing his total congressional endorsements in the insurance commissioner’s race to 10.

He’s also ruling out switching to the attorney general’s race if Bonta runs for governor, according to a spokesperson for his campaign, waving away rumors that he might make a change. Two potential candidates to replace Bonta, Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel and state Sen. Tom Umberg, are among 21 of Allen’s colleagues in the state Legislature who are newly endorsing him. He has now locked up support from 40 state legislators, including the leaders of both chambers and former Senate President pro Tem Mike McGuire.

FIRST IN PLAYBOOK: TRADES PRAISE — The State Building & Construction Trades Council of California has endorsed former state Senate Education Committee Chair Josh Newman in the state superintendent’s race. Trades President Chris Hannan praised Newman’s resume on career training in offering the endorsement, which passed over labor-aligned Democrats including Al Muratsuchi, Nichelle Henderson and Anthony Rendon.

“Josh shares our belief that students should be informed about the full range of opportunities available to them after graduation — from traditional college pathways to state-approved apprenticeship programs that lead to high-quality union construction careers,” Hannan said in a statement.

FIRST IN PLAYBOOK: COURIC WADES IN — Brian Goldsmith, a Democrat running for the state Senate, has won the endorsement of journalist Katie Couric, as well as the support of two state lawmakers, Gabriel and state Sen. Henry Stern.

Goldsmith, a media consultant and former journalist, previously worked with Couric and produced her infamous interview with Sarah Palin during the 2008 presidential campaign. Couric, who lives in New York, offered this recommendation: “I’ve met a lot of smart people during the course of my career but, without question, Brian Goldsmith is one of the smartest.”

He is running in a crowded field of candidates vying for the open Senate seat in District 24 (Hollywood Hills, Santa Monica, Malibu). The district’s current senator, Allen, completes his final term next year.

FOR GOOD MEASURE

FIRST IN PLAYBOOK: HEALTH FISSURES — Some of the heaviest hitters in health policy have come out against an SEIU-UHW backed measure to put more restrictions on how community clinics can spend their money. California Medical Association, Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California, Black Women for Wellness Action Project and other groups have joined the clinics against the union. — Rachel Bluth

ON THE AIRWAVES

FIRST IN PLAYBOOK: CHASING LAWYERS, NOT LAWSUITS — A PAC pushing to reform tort law in California will today unveil a new TV ad targeting personal-injury attorneys. The spot comes as rival ballot initiatives sponsored by Uber and the Consumer Attorneys of California are proposed for the November 2026 ballot.

“Californians pay for ambulance lawyer schemes,” the ad states. “Lawsuit abuse makes greedy ambulance lawyers rich. We need reforms to end lawsuit abuse.”

The new ad, part of a six-figure buy to air during major sporting events like NBA and NFL games, was paid for by Protecting American Consumers Together, an advocacy group whose major donors include Uber and Waffle House Inc.

CLIMATE AND ENERGY

ALMONDS FOR SOLAR — California’s Trumpiest water district is making a very un-Trumpy pivot: Westlands Water District approved a master plan on Tuesday to convert more than a quarter of its increasingly parched farmland into solar panels, showing just how much Central Valley growers are looking for new business despite their recent water wins and the loss of federal solar tax credits. Read more about what’s next and who’s behind the plan in last night’s California Climate.

TOP TALKERS

SEASONALLY-APPROPRIATE SLIGHT — The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee is rolling mobile billboards through Rep. David Valadao’s district, depicting him as the Grinch. “The Congressman Who Stole Health Care,” reads a caption above a picture of a green-faced Valadao wearing a Santa hat.

The holiday-themed play echoes Democrats’ attempts to knock Valadao off by hitting for him his vote on Medicaid cuts in the “Big Beautiful Bill,” and as House leadership whips votes for a new legislative package that would allow Affordable Care Act extensions to expire.

GENDER-AFFIRMING CARE — Sutter Health has backtracked on a decision to stop providing gender-affirming care to patients under 19 years of age under public scrutiny, the San Francisco Standard reports. Northern California’s largest health care provider made the change abruptly and without a public announcement after several news outlets reported on the decision last week.

AROUND THE STATE

— Rob Reiner’s son Nick has been charged with first-degree murder in the deaths of his parents and, if convicted, faces life in prison or the death penalty. (Los Angeles Times)

— State legislators overseeing the project to renovate the state Capitol have provided an update on the project for the first time in years. (KCRA)

— San Francisco Mayor Daniel Lurie and much of the Board of Supervisors are opposing a plan to build a 25-story housing and mixed-use project on the site of the Marina Safeway. (Mission Local)

— The San Diego Unified Port District’s board has approved a plan to expand the agency’s authority to 7,900 more acres in the water. (The San Diego Union-Tribune)

PLAYBOOKERS

PEOPLE MOVES — AJ Mendiola is joining Lt. Gov. Eleni Kounalakis’ office as a policy analyst, handling the environmental portfolio.

— Brian Klein has joined Cooley as a partner in the firm’s Business Litigation and White Collar Defense and Investigations practice group in Los Angeles. He joins from Waymaker LLP.

— Carlos Gutierrez has been hired as legislative director in the office of Assemblymember Jessica Caloza. He has been in Legislature for 7.5 years and previously worked as an aide for Assemblymember Pilar Schiavo.

BIRTHDAYS — former Rep. Steve Knight … Alexa Cottrell of the Assembly Budget Committee … Airbnb’s Maria Manjarrez … actress Sarah Paulson … boxer Manny Pacquiao

<h4 class="wp-block-heading">By Vanguard Staff</h4>
<p class="wp-block-paragraph">SACRAMENTO, Calif. — Leaders of the California Legislative Jewish Caucus on Sunday condemned a deadly antisemitic attack in Australia that targeted Jews celebrating the first night of Hanukkah and announced a $36,000 contribution to support security at Jewish community events across California.</p>
<p class="wp-block-paragraph">According to media accounts, the shooting occurred during a Hanukkah celebration in Australia, where gunfire erupted at a community gathering marking the first night of the holiday. </p><div class="mmt-a9c22174-2d36-40ea-b2b4-d05c75d4e743 mmt-primary" id="mmt-a9c22174-2d36-40ea-b2b4-d05c75d4e743_1" style="display: block;"><div id="mmt-a9c22174-2d36-40ea-b2b4-d05c75d4e743_1_zone" style="visibility: visible !important;"><div class="videoMainContainer" id="mmt-a9c22174-2d36-40ea-b2b4-d05c75d4e743_1_1_ad" style="pointer-events: auto;"><div data-stn-player="rkmiwj3w"><stn-player data-stn-player="rkmiwj3w" style="display: block; <p class="wp-block-paragraph">Multiple outlets reported that at least 15 people were killed in the attack, which took place during a public Hanukkah event attended by families and community members. </p>
<p class="wp-block-paragraph">Authorities in Australia have described the shooting as a terrorist attack, and law enforcement officials said the incident prompted a major emergency response and a heightened security posture around Jewish institutions in the country.</p>
<p class="wp-block-paragraph">In a joint statement, Sen. Scott Wiener, D-San Francisco, and Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel, D-Encino, co-chairs of the caucus, and Vice Chairs Sen. Josh Becker, D-Menlo Park, and Assemblymember Dawn Addis, D-Morro Bay, said they were responding to what they described as a terrorist attack that killed at least 15 people at the community Hanukkah event.</p>
<div class="mmt-biacdsid-f2ic-jitb-kmil-ictoamttthtc mmt-primary mmt-flight mmt-repeatable mmt-r-first" id="mmt-biacdsid-f2ic-jitb-kmil-ictoamttthtc_1" style="display: block;"><div id="mmt-biacdsid-f2ic-jitb-kmil-ictoamttthtc_1_zone" style="display: flex; align-items: center; justify-content: center; gap: 10px; width: 100%; visibility: visible !important; box-sizing: content-box !important; min-height: 280px !important;"><div id="mmt-biacdsid-f2ic-jitb-kmil-ictoamttthtc_1_0_col" style="display: flex; align-items: center; justify-content: center; flex-direction: column; gap: 10px;"><div id="mmt-biacdsid-f2ic-jitb-kmil-ictoamttthtc_1_1_ad" style="pointer-events: auto;"></div></div></div></div><div class="mmt-5008259a-1823-45b6-a6cb-4adc770cc7f2 mmt-primary mmt-repeatable mmt-r-first mmt-monuad" id="mmt-5008259a-1823-45b6-a6cb-4adc770cc7f2_1" style="display: block;"><div id="mmt-5008259a-1823-45b6-a6cb-4adc770cc7f2_1_zone" style="display: flex; align-items: center; justify-content: center; gap: 10px; width: 100%; visibility: visible !important; box-sizing: content-box !important; min-height: 280px !important;"><div id="mmt-5008259a-1823-45b6-a6cb-4adc770cc7f2_1_0_col" style="display: flex; align-items: center; justify-content: center; flex-direction: column; gap: 10px;"><div id="mmt-5008259a-1823-45b6-a6cb-4adc770cc7f2_1_1_ad" style="pointer-events: auto;"></div></div></div></div><p class="wp-block-paragraph">“We are heartbroken and outraged by the deadly terrorist attack in Australia targeting the Jewish Community on the first night of Hanukkah,” the lawmakers said in the statement. “At least 15 individuals were murdered at a community Hanukkah event. Antisemitism, including violent attacks on Jews, is on the rise in the US and around the world. We must never allow this violence — or the rhetoric and targeting of Jews that gives rise to this violence — to be normalized.”</p>
<p class="wp-block-paragraph">The caucus said the attack comes amid growing concern within Jewish communities about rising antisemitic violence, including threats and attacks tied to religious and cultural gatherings.</p>
<p class="wp-block-paragraph">“As Hanukkah begins, Jews in our state are deeply concerned about this rise in antisemitic violence,” the statement said. “But Hanukkah is a celebration of resilience and our community will continue to stand proudly for our traditions and our values.”</p>
<p class="wp-block-paragraph">The lawmakers announced that the California Legislative Jewish Caucus, through its foundation, will donate $36,000 to help Jewish community organizations enhance security during Hanukkah and other community celebrations throughout the state.</p>
<p class="wp-block-paragraph">“The California Legislative Jewish Caucus, through our Foundation, is donating $36,000 to help Jewish community organizations enhance security during these celebrations,” the statement said.</p>
<p class="wp-block-paragraph">The caucus also offered a message of solidarity and resolve in closing the statement, emphasizing both remembrance and hope during the holiday.</p>

We are committed to our community’s future and safety, even in the face of so much hate.”</p>

La alcaldesa de Los Ángeles, Karen Bass, lanza su campaña de reelección

Tres personas han anunciado oficialmente sus campañas contra la actual alcaldesa, Karen Bass.

Publicado el 13 de diciembre del 2025 • Actualizado a las 7:37 pm del 13 de diciembre del 2025

La alcaldesa de Los Ángeles, Karen Bass, inició oficialmente su campaña para la reelección el sábado con un mitin en el centro de Los Ángeles, en el que prometió hacer que la ciudad sea más segura y asequible, al tiempo que se posicionó como una candidata que se enfrentará a la administración Trump.

Dos días después del tercer aniversario de su toma de posesión, Bass lanzó su campaña rodeada de familiares, amigos y aliados en el espacio para eventos del Los Angeles Trade-Technical College Culinary Arts.

"Esto es simplemente emocionante. Tengo que decirles que mi corazón está lleno", dijo. "Esto es muy poderoso y significa mucho para mí porque ha sido un año muy difícil."

"Dicen que no podemos unirnos. Los trabajadores no pueden unirse con las empresas, las empresas no pueden unirse con la comunidad y la comunidad religiosa no puede unirse. Pero todos nos unimos siempre", añadió Bass. "Y me enorgullece decir que las relaciones que hay en esta sala no son relaciones debido a la campaña... Son relaciones porque todos creemos en la justicia".

Aunque no mencionó directamente al presidente Donald Trump, el discurso de Bass se centró en su capacidad para plantar cara a la administración Trump, señalando: "¿Quién hubiera imaginado que tendríamos que defendernos de nuestro propio Gobierno?".

Bass relató los retos a los que sigue enfrentándose Los Ángeles: la recuperación del incendio de Palisades en enero, la actual crisis de la vivienda asequible y de las personas sin hogar, y la represión del Gobierno federal contra la inmigración ilegal en la ciudad.

La titular alabó lo que describió como sus logros en materia de asequibilidad a través de su orden ejecutiva n.º 1, que fue codificada en una ordenanza a principios de este mes por el Ayuntamiento para racionalizar de forma permanente los proyectos de vivienda asequible; la reducción en dos años del número de personas sin hogar en las calles, en parte gracias a su programa insignia Inside Safe, y la recuperación de la actividad comercial en el centro de la ciudad mediante una iniciativa permanente de terrazas al aire libre y el impulso de los puestos de trabajo sindicalizados.

Local

Los Ángeles 19 Oct Condado de Riverside 18 Oct

Bass también dijo que la ciudad había avanzado en la reducción de la delincuencia y en el trabajo para alcanzar su objetivo de cero emisiones.

"La ciudad en la que he vivido toda mi vida, la ciudad que amo, siento que hemos logrado mucho, pero aún no hemos terminado", dijo Bass. "Hasta que todos los palisadianos vuelvan a casa. No descansaré hasta que Los Ángeles sea asequible, hasta que un sueldo sea suficiente y las familias no tengan que compartir vivienda. Y no descansaré hasta que no haya angelinos en nuestras calles".

Entre los aliados presentes en el mitin de Bass se encontraban el presidente del Ayuntamiento, Marqueece Harris-Dawson, los concejales Hugo Soto-Martínez, Curren Price, Heather Hutt y Adrin Nazarian, así como los miembros de la Asamblea Sade Elhawary, demócrata por el sur de Los Ángeles, Isaac Bryan, demócrata por Los Ángeles, Jesse Gabriel, demócrata por Encino, Mike Fong, demócrata por Alhambra, la senadora estatal Lola Smallwood Cuevas, demócrata por el sur de Los Ángeles, y el exsenador estatal Steven Bradford, demócrata por Inglewood.

Roxanne Hoge, presidenta del Partido Republicano del condado de Los Ángeles, ofreció una visión diferente sobre la trayectoria de Bass hasta ahora.

"Karen Bass debería avergonzarse de pedir a los votantes que le den las llaves de un coche con el que se ha salido de la carretera repetidamente", afirmó Hoge en un comunicado. "Ya sea por ver cómo mueren en las calles pobres almas enfermas mentales y adictas a las drogas o por presidir la corrupción y la suciedad en la ciudad de Los Ángeles, nada de lo que ha hecho la actual alcaldesa sugiere que merezca un segundo mandato, especialmente con los próximos Juegos Olímpicos y la Copa del Mundo a punto de poner su disfunción en el escenario mundial".

Tres personas han anunciado oficialmente sus campañas contra Bass: Austin Beutner, antiguo superintendente del Distrito Escolar Unificado de Los Ángeles; Rae Huang, subdirectora de Housing Now California; y Asaad Alnajjar, miembro del Consejo Vecinal de Porter Ranch y empleado municipal desde hace mucho tiempo.

The shadow campaign for attorney general kicks into gear

California Playbook (with help from Tyler Katzenberger)

[Excerpt saved: the newsletter's lead item on the attorney general race, which profiles Gabriel among potential candidates. The rest of the California Playbook covers unrelated items.]

FLYING TO THE RACES — Rob Bonta is inching closer to running for governor, and the shadow campaign to succeed him as California attorney general is in full swing.

Bonta has told supporters in recent days he’s strongly considering entering the governor’s contest. If he pivots, it would create a highly-competitive race to become the state’s top prosecutor — a coveted role held previously by the likes of Kamala Harris and Jerry Brown, especially as California helps lead the blue-state resistance to President Donald Trump.

What to know about the potential contenders for attorney general, provided Bonta aims higher:

Rick Zbur: Out of the gate, the assemblymember has been among the most aggressive in forming his campaign-in-waiting. Zbur has called supporters in recent days, including labor unions and LGBTQ+ and Jewish leaders, to ask if he would have their support. An ally granted anonymity to discuss Zbur’s efforts said he is “actively planning” a potential campaign. Zbur would likely be the most progressive major contender in the race, at least among the current hypothetical field. Similar to Bonta, Zbur has close ties to unions and other progressive groups. He would, if elected, be California’s first openly LGBTQ+ attorney general — a factor that could help him tap into a national fundraising network. Before Zbur joined the Legislature, he led Equality California and worked as an environmental attorney.

Jesse Gabriel: The assemblymember’s name has been popping up increasingly in conversations about the race, and his entrance could make for an intrahouse fight with Zbur. Both are allies of Speaker Robert Rivas and Democrats from the Los Angeles area, so there’s a risk of splitting an overlapping base if both get in. Gabriel could benefit from his chairship of the Assembly Budget Committee, a powerful panel that is historically helpful for fundraising. An ally for the attorney said he has more than $2.9 million in his legislative campaign account, which is more than any other state legislator.

Brooke Jenkins: Another contender generating buzz is San Francisco’s district attorney. Jenkins, if she runs, would be one of the most moderate major Democrats in the race. She took the helm of the DA’s office after voters in the city ousted progressive Chesa Boudin in 2022, largely over frustrations with the city’s problems with drug addiction and property crime. Jenkins has charted a more pro-police direction and has aggressively targeted drug dealers. Like many cities, San Francisco has seen its crime rate plummet in recent years. That could offer Jenkins a compelling resume to run on, and wealthy tech donors from the Bay Area would likely spend heavily to advance her tougher approach to crime. At the same time, Jenkins has been outspoken in recent months about her support for San Francisco’s large immigrant communities and opposition to Trump’s immigration raids. An ally said Jenkins is looking at the potential race and receiving calls from supporters nudging her in that direction.

Tom Umberg: The term-limited state senator recently announced a run for the Board of Equalization, but a chance to be the state’s top cop could be too attractive to pass up. Umberg has focused much of his legislative career on criminal justice issues, and was earlier in his career a federal prosecutor. His moderate profile sets him up to run to the right of his fellow Democrats, and with three stints in the Legislature stretching back to the 1990s, he could tap into deep Sacramento roots.

Nathan Hochman: The Los Angeles district attorney came up short when he challenged Bonta as a Republican in 2022. But since then, he has shed his GOP affiliation and ousted progressive District Attorney George Gascón in a blue county. Hochman is probably the only would-be candidate on this list who could convincingly out-mod Umberg, and his running would provide a test of whether voters have moved ideologically since passing the tough-on-crime Prop 36.

Lorena Gonzalez: Her name has been in the rumor mill and Gonzalez, head of the state Labor Federation and a lawyer, would likely be a formidable contender. But Gonzalez told Playbook that she is “absolutely not” considering the AG’s race. Her not running would free up labor unions to gravitate toward another potential candidate, possibly Zbur or Gabriel.

Почему первый в США закон об ультраобработанной еде — это битва за будущее, а не за обеды?

Пока одни американские политики с пафосом рассуждают о «возрождении здоровья нации», Калифорния поступила по-своему — решительно и без лишней помпы. Губернатор Гэвин Ньюсом подписал исторический закон, который не просто вводит очередной запрет. Он делает нечто революционное: впервые в США даёт официальное определение «ультраобработанным продуктам» (UPF) и объявляет им поэтапную высылку из школьных столовых. В год, когда школьники штата съедят более миллиарда обедов, это — не регулирование, это объявление войны самой сути современной пищевой индустрии. Войны, в которой противник — не отдельные продукты, а целая философия питания.

Что такое UPF по-калифорнийски? Наука против «точки блаженства»

Закон «О настоящей еде и здоровых детях» — это не просто список плохих продуктов. Это — попытка научно и юридически описать целый класс пищевых объектов, которые доминируют в рационе американских детей (по данным CDC, почти две трети их калорий).

UPF — это то, что создано не на ферме и не на кухне, а в лаборатории и на конвейере. Продукт, который может содержать:

  • Коктейль из непитательных подсластителей, горы добавленного сахара, соли и насыщенных жиров.
  • Арсенал эмульгаторов, стабилизаторов, загустителей, усилителей вкуса и пищевых красителей.

Или быть специально сконструированным для достижения «точки блаженства» — того идеального соотношения соли, сахара и жира, которое заставляет мозг требовать добавки, минуя чувство сытости.

Закон не просто запрещает. Он поручает учёным и врачам выделить среди UPF самые вредные категории — «ультраобработанные продукты, вызывающие опасения». Те, что напрямую связаны с пищевой зависимостью, ожирением, диабетом, раком и жировой болезнью печени. Это переход от эмоциональных лозунгов к доказательной, точечной работе.

Почему это революция? Потому что до этого мир не мог даже договориться о терминах

До сих пор ни одна страна, включая США на федеральном уровне, не решалась на чёткое юридическое определение UPF. Европа ограничивала отдельные добавки, но не трогала саму концепцию «ультраобработанности». Калифорния сделала первый шаг, который остальной мир боялся сделать. И этим она бросила вызов не только индустрии, но и федеральной администрации.

Как заявил автор законопроекта Джесси Габриэль: «Пока жители Вашингтона заказывают отчёты и обсуждают гипотетические варианты, Калифорния лидирует с решительных действий». Он намекает на движение «Сделаем Америку снова здоровой» (MAHA) администрации Кеннеди-младшего, чей итоговый отчёт, по словам экспертов, свелся к «обещаниям и ничего по существу».

«Сопротивление было очень серьёзным». Как Калифорнии удалось пробить стену лоббирования

Бернадетт Дель Кьяро, соавтор законопроекта, не скрывает: «Пищевая промышленность всегда сопротивляется, кричит и бьётся изо всех сил, чтобы эти законопроекты не стали законом».

Почему же закон прошёл? Потому что проблема перестала быть идеологической. Она стала бытовой и медицинской. Родители, учителя, врачи — все видят последствия. Дети с ожирением, диабетом 2-го типа (который раньше называли «взрослым»), синдромом дефицита внимания. Закон получил широкую двухпартийную поддержку: против проголосовал только один республиканец из 120 законодателей. Это сигнал: когда вопрос касается здоровья детей, политические границы стираются.

Реализм против утопии: почему не запретят всё и не завтра

Законодатели проявили трезвый прагматизм. «Мы не можем исключить все ультрапереработанные продукты — они нам нужны, нам нужна стабильность полки, безопасность, удобство», — признаёт Габриэль.

Поэтому процесс растянется на десятилетие.

К 1 февраля 2028 поставщики должны будут начать отчитываться обо всех UPF в школах.

К 1 июля 2035 все «продукты, вызывающие опасения», должны быть полностью выведены.

Это не спецоперация, а стратегическая перезагрузка всей системы школьного питания, которая даст время на разработку альтернатив, переобучение персонала и адаптацию бюджета.

Главная битва впереди: Калифорния против Вашингтона

Самое большое препятствие — не пищепром, а федеральное правительство. Существуют реальные опасения, что Конгресс может попытаться принять слабый федеральный закон, который «предвосхитит» (и тем самым заблокирует) более жёсткие инициативы штатов. Это классический приём: создать иллюзию регулирования, лишив штаты права на собственные стандарты.

Но калифорнийцы надеются, что широкая общественная поддержка и двухпартийный консенсус в штате станут их козырем. «Мы все в одной команде. Мы входим в команду Public Health и Team Kids», — говорит Дель Кьяро.

Это не про еду. Это про будущее

Калифорнийский закон — это не просто диетическая директива. Это — акт культурного сопротивления. Попытка переломить парадигму, при которой самое дешёвое, доступное и агрессивно рекламируемое питание является одновременно и самым вредным. Это защита самой уязвимой аудитории — детей, чьи пищевые привычки формируются на десятилетия вперёд.

Если Калифорния устоит против давления и успешно реализует эту программу, она задаст новый стандарт для всей страны. Она докажет, что можно перестроить гигантскую систему, когда-то созданную для дешёвого насыщения, в систему, ориентированную на здоровье. Это долгая и дорогая война. Но она началась не с лозунга, а с определения в законе. А это, как известно, первый и самый важный шаг к любой реальной победе.

Возможно самый радикальный политический акт в современной Америке принят не в Вашингтоне, а в Сакраменто, и касается он не импичмента или бюджета, а содержимого школьного ланч-бокса. И в этой, казалось бы, малой детали — весь смысл большой битвы за будущее.

State budget hole deepens as costs rise Mandatory spending and greater safety-net outlays due to federal cutbacks erase gains. By KATIE KING SACRAMENTO -- Cali- fornia’s budgetary woes are worse than expected, forcing state lawmakers to grapple with a nearly $18-billion shortfall next year, accord- ing to a new report from the Legislative Analyst’s Office. This figure is $5 billion more than estimates in June. Frontline GOPers caught in health care jam

CONCEPTS OF A PLAN — Endangered House Republicans in California were forced back into health care limbo as the Trump administration on Monday delayed announcing a plan to extend Obamacare subsidies and started reworking the details amid backlash from hard-liners.

The whiplash was jarring — following reporting that the administration was planning to announce a health care framework including a two-year extension of the subsidies due to expire at the end of next month.

Republican Rep. Kevin Kiley expressed, before the delay, that he was “grateful that the President is endorsing the key components of our legislation,” referring to a bipartisan bill from him and Rep. Sam Liccardo geared at renewing the tax credits dividing the Republican conference.

Hours later, the White House’s support was in flux. It didn’t release specifics or hold an expected Monday afternoon announcement, limiting the political cover to vulnerable members absorbing attacks over the impending expiration.

Adding to the intraparty division: Conservatives were blindsided by President Donald Trump’s initial framework and were still evaluating Monday whether they would support it while waiting for information on whether it would expand restrictions on abortion-related funding, POLITICO reported.

It’s now unclear what exactly the president will propose, and more than that, what he’ll be able to get through the House as Speaker Mike Johnson labors to wrangle his members.

The purgatory state for the tax credits allowed opponents of frontline California Republicans, namely Kiley and Rep. David Valadao, to slam them over their party’s inability or unwillingness to extend the Affordable Care Act subsidies.

“Kevin Kiley and David Valadao can pretend they care about keeping health care affordable all they want – but when their party guts Medicaid and threatens ACA tax credits, they fall right in line every time,” Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee spokesperson Anna Elsasser said in a statement.

Democrats are prioritizing health care in their campaigns to oust both representatives. Though Kiley hasn’t declared which district he’s running in, Democrats are lining up in the open 6th, focusing their messaging heavily on his vote for Medicaid cuts earlier this year.

The Democratic challengers to Valadao, who lost a race in 2018 after voting to repeal the Affordable Care Act, have blasted him for the same thing.

Asked about extending Obamacare more broadly, he recently told POLITICO that, “obviously, there’s a lot of problems with the ACA and just extending it cleanly, I don’t think is a solution, but we’ll see how it plays out.”

The White House and vulnerable Republicans have little time to act before the midterms. With subsidies set to expire next month, constituents’ premiums could climb before Election Day. And health care groups aren’t optimistic that a broader restructuring of the signature health care law is possible before then.

“With just weeks until Californians must make their decisions about whether to keep their covered plans, there’s little time to thoughtfully implement sweeping financing or eligibility changes and high risk of unintended consequences that threaten health coverage and leave lives hanging in the balance,” California Pan-Ethnic Health Network Executive Director Kiran Savage-Sangwan said in a statement.

— Mia McCarthy contributed to this report

GOOD MORNING. Happy Tuesday. Thanks for waking up with Playbook.

WHERE’S GAVIN? Nothing official announced.

SACRAMENTO SCANDAL

‘COLLECTIVE OUTRAGE’ — Democratic consultant Steve Maviglio and other friends of Newsom’s indicted former chief of staff Dana Williamson have started fundraising for her legal defense. Facing Legal Pressure, Glock Revamps Pistols To Prevent Machine Gun Conversions

Champe Barton

The Business of Guns

Facing Legal Pressure, Glock Revamps Pistols To Prevent Machine Gun Conversions

The change comes after The Trace’s reporting informed California’s decision to ban the gunmaker’s products.

In September, two men outside a Walmart in Indianapolis allegedly shot three members of the same family with converted Glock pistols. A thumbnail-size device called a switch had effectively turned the weapons into machine guns, enabling them to fire as many as 20 bullets per second. One victim was hit in his hand, abdomen, legs, and chest. His brother suffered two gunshot wounds; his cousin, 11. All three survived.

Glocks outfitted with switches have turned up in crimes with devastating frequency across the country, prompting federal authorities to declare them a “serious threat to public safety.” 

Glock has for years dismissed the idea that it has any responsibility — or even the ability — to design handguns impervious to switches. But now, the gunmaker has abruptly reversed course, announcing that, come December, it will discontinue two of its signature pistols lines and replace them with a model apparently designed to resist the devices.

The about-face comes after California passed a first-of-its-kind ban on Glock handguns, a measure authored by Democratic State Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel. A spokesperson for Gabriel’s office said the ban was informed by reporting from The Trace, which last year detailed accounts from former Glock employees and firearm experts who argued Glock could alter its designs to build pistols more resistant to conversion.

Anthony Beverly, who runs Stop the Violence Indianapolis, a gun violence prevention group, said he was encouraged to hear that the gun industry had taken some accountability in the fight to combat machine gun shootings. “The industry is usually an uphill battle,” he said. “But this sounds like some good news.”

Glock did not respond to multiple requests for comment. 

The new line of pistols, known as Gen V, is virtually indistinguishable from its predecessors. But at the back of the gun, where switches are typically installed, the Gen V has a short steel rail to block switches from interfering with the weapon’s firing mechanism. Earlier Glock handguns relied only on a plastic nub, which could be easily shaved down with a file.

California’s law, passed in October, bans guns that can be converted to automatic fire with household tools. The law specifically singles out those with “cruciform trigger bars” — a reference to the construction of an internal component used in all Glocks. The Gen Vs also use a cruciform trigger bar, making it unlikely they will clear the state’s new standard. Images and videos have circulated online of Gen Vs modified to accept switches, though the changes were likely made using machining equipment, making them much harder for the average consumer to perform. 

New York, Illinois, and Maryland are mulling similar bans, though the bills will have to be considered or reintroduced in next year’s legislative session. New York State Senator Zellnor Myrie, who proposed New York’s bill, said he was confident of its chances after the Gen V announcement. “This confirms that state laws can drive changes that protect public safety — even when gun companies say it’s impossible,” he said. 

Most of the switches in the United States are illegal, and none are manufactured or sanctioned by Glock. They are mostly purchased online from China or 3D-printed at home. For years, state attorneys general and city mayors have demanded Glock overhaul its designs to more seriously address the crisis. In 2024, Chicago sued Glock, arguing that the company deceived consumers about the safety of its products and fueled the proliferation of machine gun fire on the city’s streets. Baltimore and Seattle subsequently filed similar suits, as did the attorneys general of New Jersey and Minnesota. Another 11 attorneys general signed a letter signaling their intention to sue, though no additional litigation has come. 

Glock sought to dismiss the lawsuits, but judges in state and federal court this year have allowed the Chicago, New Jersey, and Minnesota cases to proceed. (Judges have yet to rule on motions in Baltimore and Seattle.)

Chicago Mayor Brandon Johnson and New Jersey Attorney General Matthew Platkin linked Glock’s reversal to the company’s recent courtroom setbacks. Johnson told The Trace via email that Chicago “played a key role in pressuring Glock to make necessary changes.” Platkin noted that the Gen V was announced just weeks after a federal judge permitted New Jersey’s case to move forward. 

Both officials said they would press ahead with their lawsuits, which demand that Glock pay damages for the violence wrought with its products. “We will continue to fight to hold them accountable under the law,” Platkin said.

Champe Barton is a staff writer at The Trace covering the gun industry. His work has focused on the role of gun distribution in America’s gun violence epidemic, including lax enforcement of federal firearms laws by the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives, failure by California police departments to properly trace crime guns, and efforts by gun manufacturers to monitor how the guns they produce slip into the criminal black market. His work has appeared in USA TODAY, Rolling Stone, Slate, The Guardian, FiveThirtyEight, and The Daily Beast, among other publications.

Refugees from California like me wonder if the state can be saved from itself. Granting Medi-Cal benefits to illegal aliens is never-ending cash drain. When Governor Jerry Brown expanded Medi-Cal to cover illegal alien children in 2015, and Newsom followed up by extending the costly benefits to illegal alien seniors 50 and older in 2022, the cost to cover all illegal immigrants reached $9.5 billion last year. Roger Niello of Roseville, the Republican vice chair of the Senate Budget Committee, pinpointed the problem. Newsom’s White House ambitions may motivate him to make the “necessary corrections” that Niello encouraged. Yet other headaches remain. California will face another wildfire season before the Democratic primaries, and hard-hit neighborhoods like Altadena and the Pacific Palisades are built in high-risk fire zones. California Doubles Down in Legal Battle Over Nazi-Looted Pissarro Painting

Richard Whiddington

One of the longest running Nazi restitution cases has taken another turn. On November 17, California’s Attorney General, Rob Bonta, filed a motion to intervene in the Cassirer family’s 20-year pursuit of a Camille Pissarro painting that was stolen by the Nazis and is now owned by Spain’s Thyssen-Bornemisza Collection Foundation.

The family, the heirs of Jewish collector Lilly Cassirer Neubauer, have long been battling the Spanish museum for the return of Rue Saint Honore, Apres Midi, Effet De Pluie (1897), which was taken during World War II. Last year, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit ruled that the Madrid museum could keep the canvas, deciding that Spanish law applied over California law.

With his motion this week, Bonta said California will defend the validity of Assembly Bill 2867 in court, which protects the rights of victims of art theft and requires courts to apply California law to the claims of victims. The Thyssen-Bornemisza has previously claimed that the law is “constitutionally indefensible” and should be ignored. The measure was signed into law by California Governor Gavin Newson in September last year in response to the Ninth Circuit’s ruling.

Whereas California law would have protected the plaintiff as it holds that a thief cannot transfer the right to sell property, Spanish law states that an institution can retain an artwork as long as it has been held for three years in good faith and in the absence of ownership disputes. The Thyssen-Bornemisza Museum bought the painting from Baron Hans Heinrich Thyssen-Bornemisza in 1993; the first contact from the Cassirers came in the early 2000s.

The case received a new wind of life after the passage of Assembly Bill 2867, which prompted the U.S. Supreme Court to vacate the Ninth Circuit’s decision and ask for the case to be reconsidered. Since that decision in March, the case has rested with the U.S. District Court for the Central District of California.

“There is nothing that can undo the horrors and loss experienced by individuals during the Holocaust. But there is something we can do—that California has done—to return what was stolen back to survivors and their families,” Bonta said in a statement. “My office has supported the Cassirers’ quest for justice for two decades, and we will continue to fight.”

The Cassirers’ attorneys, Sam Dubbin and David Barrett, were pleased to see the Bonta’s office intervene. “It defends California’s interests in protecting the integrity of the art market and the rights of stolen-property victims,” they said over email. “California law has always provided strong protections for the victims of stolen property and stolen art in particular, which the Legislature has consistently reinforced.”

The Thyssen-Bornemisza Museum did not respond to a request for comment.

The Camille Pissarro painting hanging in the Berlin apartment of Lilly Cassirer (ca. 1930). Photo courtesy of David Cassirer.

The atmospheric Pissarro painting was sold in 1939 by Lilly Cassirer Neubauer and her husband Otto Neubauer in exchange for exit visas and $360 (roughly $8,000 today when adjusted for inflation), a sum she never received. After living out the war in England, Cassirer Neubauer sought the painting’s return. In 1958, the West German government paid her compensation of 120,000 Deutschmarks (more than $300,000 today), but the painting itself remained elusive.

According to records, the Pissarro was sold at a Nazi government auction in 1943 and then disappeared from view. It passed through the hands of art dealers in Beverly Hills and Missouri before being purchased by Baron Thyssen-Bornemisza in 1976, whose collection of more than 700 works was acquired by the Spanish government for $350 million in 1993.

California Attorney General Rob Bonta has stepped directly into a courtroom showdown over a Nazi-looted Camille Pissarro masterpiece, moving to intervene in a decades-long legal battle and throwing his weight behind a California law that widens the rights of art-theft victims. The move aligns the state firmly with the Cassirer family as they press to reclaim a treasured painting taken in 1939, and puts front and center a high-stakes question: should California rules or foreign law control who owns looted art?

Bonta's Filing And AB 2867

In a press release from the State of California - Department of Justice, Bonta’s office said it has moved to intervene in Cassirer v. Thyssen-Bornemisza Collection Foundation for the specific purpose of defending Assembly Bill 2867. The law, as described by the Attorney General’s Office, broadens protections for victims of art theft and instructs courts to apply California law when residents seek the return of property looted in the Holocaust or through political persecution. Bonta cast the intervention as part of the state’s effort to restore stolen property and offer survivors and their families at least a measure of justice.

The Painting’s History

The dispute centers on Camille Pissarro’s 1897 canvas Rue Saint-Honoré, après-midi, effet de pluie, which Lilly Cassirer was forced to hand over to a Nazi appraiser in 1939 as she fled Germany. After a series of private sales, the painting eventually surfaced at Madrid’s Museo Nacional Thyssen-Bornemisza. The Cassirer family filed suit in California in 2005 once they discovered the work was hanging in the museum’s galleries. Since then, the case has wound its way through the federal courts, including a remand and multiple rulings focused on which jurisdiction’s law should decide ownership, according to the Los Angeles Times.

Why AB 2867 Matters

Governor Gavin Newsom signed AB 2867 in September 2024, and the measure took effect immediately under an urgency clause. As outlined by the Governor of California, the law clarifies that California substantive law will govern disputes when a state resident seeks to recover property looted during genocide or political persecution. Legal observers say the statute was crafted in response to a Ninth Circuit ruling that had applied Spanish law in the Cassirer case, which was later vacated and remanded by the U.S. Supreme Court, allowing courts to factor in the new California law, as noted by JDSupra.

International Ripple Effects

Courts across Europe, major museums, and foreign governments are closely tracking the litigation. A decision that applies California law to this claim could echo across other restitution fights involving art seized in the Nazi era. Museums argue they acquired contested works in good faith, often decades ago, while heirs point to ongoing moral and legal duties to correct historical theft. The high-profile dispute has put cultural institutions on alert, according to The Art Newspaper.

Where The Cassirer Family Stands

The Cassirer lawsuit dates back to 2005, after Claude Cassirer learned in 2000 that the Pissarro was on display in Madrid. His son David now leads the case. Supporters and the family’s lawyers say AB 2867 offers California residents a clearer route to reclaim art and other property taken in periods of persecution. Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel has praised the state’s approach as an effort to stand on the right side of history, as reported by Politico. The Cassirers maintain that the painting is a priceless family heirloom and have repeatedly said they want it returned to their custody.

Legal Implications

Legal scholars say the case could explore the extent to which state statutes can reach in disputes involving foreign entities and highlight how the Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act interacts with state choice-of-law rules. By intervening, the Attorney General is asking the federal court in the Central District of California to uphold AB 2867 and to ensure that claims brought by California residents are resolved under state law. How California’s new ultra-processed foods law will transform school lunches

By Manola Secaira / Capradio

It’s lunch time at Lincoln Crossing Elementary. And today, they’re serving up burgers.

But this meal might be a little different than what you’d expect out of a school lunch.

“We have our grass-fed beef,” says Christina Lawson, the food service director for the Western Placer Unified School District. “We have our organic cheddar cheese from Rumiano, which is a producer up in Northern California. We have our local buns that are made by Dos Pisano’s, which is made out of the Bay Area.”

Lincoln Crossing Elementary has been working with the nonprofit Eat Real to phase out ultra-processed foods from school meals since 2023. Lawson says this school could offer an example of what school meals throughout the state could soon look like.

“We're looking at really kind of changing the stigma of what school meals are,” she says.

A new California law, kicking in next January, requires the phaseout of certain ultra-processed foods from school meals throughout the state. Some characteristics the law considers when targeting foods to remove or replace include high levels of saturated fat, sugar and sodium, alongside a host of other ingredients like non-nutritive sweeteners, color additives and thickeners.

These foods have attracted mainstream attention in recent years, especially as the federal administration’s Make America Healthy Again campaign has named eliminating them a key issue. U.S. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. went so far as to describe these foods as "poison."

But while federal officials have expressed interest in creating a standard definition for ultra-processed foods, it hasn’t happened yet. This law marks the first in the country to give that phrase a statutory definition.

“We felt a lot of pressure to get it right,” says Democratic Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel, who represents much of the western San Fernando Valley and authored the bill behind the new law. “It's basically what the advocates and scientists said to us — science has taken us as far as they can go when it comes to defining ultraprocessed foods, but to have a workable legal definition, this is where we need policymakers to step in.”

What is an “ultra-processed food”?

Eat Real’s CEO Nora LaTorre says ultra-processed foods — like soda, for example — have been linked to health issues like chronic kidney and liver disease. Her goal is to replace those ultra-processed foods with what she calls more nutrient-dense “real food.”

“Real food is the closest to how Mother Nature intended,” LaTorre says. “The longer the packaging ingredient list, the more processing it is.”

That’s a pretty typical way to guess if a food qualifies as ultra-processed or not. But the phrase doesn’t actually have one, concrete definition — at least, not one that’s universally accepted.

Charlotte Biltekoff, a food and culture expert with UC Davis, says there’s always going to be some disagreement about that.

“Disagreement happens for lots of reasons, but in part, it happens because people have different points of view, different assumptions, different world views and different vested interests,” Biltekoff says. “And so, the disagreement doesn't just happen because the facts are unclear. It happens because people have different motives and aims.”

She says the term “ultra-processed foods” originally comes from a 2009 Brazilian report that created a classification system called NOVA. The system organizes food into groups, from least to most processed.

Biltekoff says it offers a way to understand health and food beyond basic nutritional facts.

“NOVA classification is centrally focused on the amount and kind of processing that a food undergoes as a means of determining its quality,” she says. “So, this is actually a really revolutionary way of thinking about good food, and it really challenged the established paradigms.”

Facing a new choice

Biltekoff says NOVA was meant to be a tool for researching the connection between the degree of processing and health, which could ultimately lead to creating policy. But, despite the popularity of conversations around eliminating ultra-processed foods, actually creating laws around addressing them can be controversial.

“I think a real uptake of an ultra-processed food classification is very disruptive to business as usual,” Biltekoff says.

Gabriel says he knew the new law would have impacts beyond California schools. It’d also affect the companies producing food for students that don’t meet the law’s new guidelines. Inevitably, he says those businesses will have to face a choice.

Others worried it could inadvertently include foods that shouldn’t be banned — like foods that use natural additives like beet juice to enhance the color of a food, for example.

Gabriel says part of creating the law meant narrowing the definition enough to avoid unintended consequences.

“We took amendments, for example, to exempt natural seasonings and natural colorants,” he says. “So, just kind of working around the edges on some of the nuances there to make sure we had a really strong definition … but one that we also could implement and that would work for all of the diverse stakeholders.”
