California Glock Ban Explained: What AB 1127 Really Does

Casey Hartwell

The Bottom Line

California’s AB 1127, signed by Governor Gavin Newsom on October 10, 2025 and effective July 1, 2026, bars licensed firearm dealers from selling Glock-style “machinegun-convertible pistols.” It does not ban owning a Glock you already have, and it does not legalize the illegal switches it was written to fight. California’s own legislative analysis admitted the bill’s practical effect is to prohibit the sale of Glock handguns in the state.

AB 1127 — Key Facts at a Glance

LawAssembly Bill 1127 (Chapter 572, Statutes of 2025)
AuthorAssemblymember Jesse Gabriel
SignedOctober 10, 2025, by Gov. Gavin Newsom
EffectiveJuly 1, 2026 (dealer-sale ban)
Codified atCalifornia Penal Code § 27595
What it bansLicensed-dealer sale or transfer of “semiautomatic machinegun-convertible pistols,” meaning Glock-pattern pistols with a cruciform trigger bar
What it doesn’t banPossessing a Glock you already own; private-party transfers through a dealer
Roster impact54 Glock models then on California’s handgun roster lose civilian retail availability
Legal statusJaymes v. Bonta dismissed April 2026; U.S. DOJ threatened a federal lawsuit June 24, 2026

You won’t find the word “Glock” anywhere in AB 1127. The people who wrote it were careful about that. What they put in instead is a definition built so tightly around the Glock pistol that California’s own Senate analysts admitted, in writing, that the practical effect of the bill is to prohibit the sale of Glock handguns in California.

It didn’t come from a gun-lobby press release. It came from the Legislature’s own committee staff, describing what their bill would do, before they voted to pass it.

Gun owners just call it the Glock ban. Fair enough. But the nickname buries the part that should bother you, and it should bother you whether you carry a Glock or have never picked one up. California didn’t go after the illegal little gadget that turns a pistol into a machine gun. That gadget has been a felony for years. The state went after the ordinary, legal pistol underneath it.

That choice is the whole story. It’s also why this fight is nowhere near finished.

The Short Version

  • What passed: AB 1127, signed by Gov. Gavin Newsom on October 10, 2025 (Chapter 572 of the 2025 statutes). It cleared the Legislature on a party-line vote, every Republican against it.
  • When it bites: The dealer-sale ban kicks in July 1, 2026.
  • Who it hits: California gun dealers and anyone trying to buy a new affected pistol from one. It does not reach into your safe.
  • What it does not do: It doesn’t ban owning an unmodified Glock you already have, it doesn’t legalize switches, and it doesn’t make anybody surrender a gun.
  • Why it matters: California is restricting a common, legal pistol based on what a criminal might illegally bolt onto it. That logic is the real headline.
  • What’s in court: Gun-rights groups sued in Jaymes v. Bonta, then dropped the case in April 2026. Now the U.S. Department of Justice is threatening its own federal lawsuit.
  • Watch this: A June 30 federal deadline, a possible DOJ suit, dealer guidance from the state, and whether Glock ever redesigns for California.

What AB 1127 Actually Says

Starting July 1, 2026, a licensed California dealer cannot sell, trade, give, transfer, or hand over any “semiautomatic machinegun-convertible pistol.” That ban gets written into the Penal Code at section 27595, and breaking it costs dealers real money.

So what fits the phrase? The law says a semiautomatic pistol with a cruciform trigger bar that someone could turn into a machine gun by swapping a small converter onto the back of the slide, no gunsmithing required. In plain terms, it targets the internal part that a Glock switch happens to grab. We’re not going to walk anybody through how that conversion actually works, and you don’t need to know it to follow the law.

Definition

Cruciform trigger bar

The cross-shaped internal part inside Glock and Glock-pattern pistols that connects the trigger to the firing mechanism. AB 1127 uses the presence of this part as its legal trigger. Striker-fired pistols built without it, like the Sig P320 and Smith & Wesson M&P, are not covered.

The sleight of hand is in that definition. The state pinned the everyday pistol to an illegal part it could theoretically accept, then restricted the everyday pistol.

And the whole thing runs on dealers to enforce it. First slip, a fine. Second, your license can get suspended. Third, you’re looking at a misdemeanor and losing the license for good. For a small-shop FFL, the federally licensed dealer who runs your local gun store, that’s the difference between keeping the lights on and locking the doors.

Is This Really a Glock Ban?

Not by brand name, but in practice, yes. The bill never types out “Glock,” and on its face it covers any pistol that meets the cruciform definition. But the Senate’s own analysis didn’t bother dancing around it. Because the convertible pistols in question are Glocks, the staff wrote, the practical effect is to stop Glock sales in California.

They even did the math. 54 Glock models were sitting on the state’s approved handgun roster at the time, and every one of them would fall off the menu for regular buyers.

It catches the knockoffs too. Glock-pattern clones built on the same guts, like Shadow Systems pistols, get swept up right alongside the real thing.

What it does not touch is just as telling. Striker-fired pistols that skip the cruciform trigger bar are in the clear. Your Sig P320, your S&W M&P, at least the rostered versions, sail through untouched. So this isn’t “California banned plastic pistols,” and it isn’t “California banned one brand.” It’s a law written around a single internal part that just so happens to live inside the most popular handgun in the country.

What the Law Does NOT Do

Here’s the part the internet keeps butchering, so slow down. The quick version:

What AB 1127 Does

  • Bans dealer sale of “machinegun-convertible pistols” starting July 1, 2026
  • Targets pistols with a cruciform trigger bar (most Glocks and Glock clones)
  • Puts escalating penalties on dealers, up to losing the license
  • Stacks a new restriction on top of California’s handgun roster
  • Offers a redesign-and-recertify path back onto the roster

What It Does NOT Do

  • Ban possession of a Glock you already own
  • Legalize switches or converters (still illegal)
  • Force anybody to surrender a pistol
  • Stop private-party transfers through a dealer
  • Apply to non-cruciform striker pistols (Sig P320, S&W M&P)

A few of those deserve a sentence more. Switches were a serious crime before this bill and they’re a serious crime after it. AB 1127 stacked a restriction on the gun on top of that. It didn’t trade one for the other. And the exceptions list is long: private-party sales run through a dealer, repairs at a gunsmith, transfers to other dealers or out-of-state makers, guns coming back to you after storage or a temporary hold, forensic-lab transfers, police and military sales, peace-officer purchases, and a narrow allowance for inventory a dealer already had before January 1, 2026. For a normal person walking up to a counter, the only date that matters is July 1, 2026.

Definition

California handgun roster

The state’s list of handguns approved for new commercial sale. If a pistol isn’t on the roster, dealers can’t sell it new. AB 1127 strikes affected Glock-pattern models off that roster, which is why the practical effect lands on dealer sales rather than on ownership.

Who Actually Gets Hit

If you already own one, your week doesn’t change. Shoot it, clean it, take it to a gunsmith, buy a case of ammo for it. None of that gets touched.

If you’re trying to buy one new, that’s where the wall goes up. Come July 1, 2026, you can’t walk into a California shop and buy a new affected Glock-pattern pistol off the rack, unless a court has stepped in first.

Carry a Glock on your CCW? The one on your hip is fine. The squeeze is on the next gun. A brand-new permit holder, or somebody who wants to swap to a different carry pistol a few years down the road, loses easy access to the platform half the instructors in this state train on.

Dealers eat the risk and the paperwork. They have to know which guns are affected, move what they can before the deadline, and watch a real chunk of their handgun business get walled off. The penalties land on them, not on Sacramento.

Cops are exempt. Sworn officers and certain agencies can still get these pistols, so duty carry rolls right along. The Senate analysis even pointed out that the exemption list left off some agencies whose officers carry Glocks, which tells you how clean the line-drawing really was.

Glock and the other makers get a choice. Redesign for California, or sit out new dealer sales in the third-biggest gun market in the country.

The used market stays open. Person-to-person transfers through a dealer are an exception, so private sales keep happening. Just expect the price tags to climb as the new-gun supply dries up. Off-roster Glocks already trade at a stiff premium out here. This pours gas on that.

And that brings us to hunters, the part you might be tempted to scroll past.

The State’s Case

Give California’s side a real hearing, because it isn’t nothing.

Switches are ugly business. A little illegal part, some of them printed on a cheap 3D printer, can turn a pistol into something that dumps a magazine in a couple of seconds. That’s not a hypothetical. It has shown up in shooting after shooting, with real people dead. Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel, who carried the bill, was blunt about his goal. He wants this law to force Glock into changing the design so the switch has nothing to grab. He has said the company has known about the weak point for years and could save lives by fixing it.

The pitch is prevention. If this is the platform criminals keep exploiting, lean on the company to redesign the platform. And for the families who have buried somebody killed by a converted Glock, none of this is a policy abstraction. A mother in Sacramento lost her son when a gunman opened up with a switched pistol in a downtown nightclub, eleven rounds in a few seconds, and she has spent her grief at the capitol pushing for exactly this kind of law. Pretending that loss isn’t part of the engine here would be dishonest.

The Other Side

Now the opposition, and their argument is almost insultingly simple.

The switch is already illegal. Making one, selling one, owning one, all of it was already a felony before AB 1127 added a single comma. So the law doesn’t criminalize anything new about the dangerous part. What it restricts is the boring part, the everyday pistol that millions of people who’ve never broken a law in their lives happen to own.

From there it snowballs. You’re punishing a common, legal firearm for what some criminal might do to it. You’re squeezing ordinary buyers and the dealers who serve them, while the guy who actually wants a switched pistol is going to find one on the street no matter what the roster says. And you’re setting a precedent with teeth: a gun can be restricted not for what it is, but for what somebody could illegally turn it into.

That last point is the one worth losing sleep over, and not because of Glocks. Once “this gun could theoretically be modified into something illegal” is enough to justify banning its sale, that reasoning doesn’t stay parked on one pistol. It can be aimed at the next gun, and the one after that.

A common, legal gun, restricted not for what it is but for what a criminal might turn it into. That’s the precedent, and precedents get reused.

The gun-rights crowd figures the Constitution is on its side, too. The Supreme Court has said arms in common use by regular people for legal reasons get strong protection, and that handguns in particular can’t be banned. A Glock is about as “common use” as a firearm gets in America. That’s the backbone of the legal challenge. It’s an advocacy position, and I’m flagging it as one, but it’s built on actual Supreme Court rulings, not wishful thinking.

Why Hunters and Outdoorsmen Should Care

Nobody’s jump-shooting mallards with a 9mm. A Glock isn’t a duck gun, an elk gun, or an upland gun, and I’m not going to pretend it is. So why should a guy who lives for the teal opener care about a handgun law out of Sacramento?

Because this was never really about one pistol. It’s about who gets to decide which legal guns you’re allowed to buy, in the biggest and most copied gun market in the country.

Start with plain access. Hunters live and die by a healthy, legal market for the guns and gear we use. A law that bans a common firearm over a crime that hasn’t even happened yet is not a principle that knows how to stay in its lane. Today the trigger is a cruciform bar. The logic is the part that travels.

Then there’s the sidearm question, which is a lot more real for sportsmen than the duck-gun line lets on. Plenty of us carry a handgun in the field. Bears and hogs, two-legged trouble at a dark trailhead, or just the basic fact of being armed where you live and hunt. Glock-pattern pistols are a default backcountry and carry choice, and for good reason. Choke off that option through the front door and you shrink what’s practical for anybody who actually packs a sidearm into the marsh or up the mountain.

There’s your local shop, too. Pile legal risk and red tape onto handgun sales and you’re leaning on the same FFL who stocks your nontox loads, your slugs, your glass, and your shotguns. A gun store bleeding margin on a third of its business is not a gun store that’s good for any of us.

And here’s the one that ought to hit home for every sportsman, because it’s not abstract at all. The whole conservation-funding machine in this country runs in large part on Pittman-Robertson, the excise tax on firearms, ammunition, and gear that quietly bankrolls habitat, wildlife management, and the access we all hunt on. The Congressional Sportsmen’s Foundation has been waving the flag about this exact thing. Kneecap firearm sales in a giant market like California and you drive a wedge straight into the money that pays for ducks, deer, and dirt. Fewer legal guns sold can mean fewer conservation dollars in the ground. That’s your wildlife areas, your boat ramps, your habitat projects, all of it downstream.

Last one, and it’s the soft kind that ends up mattering more than people admit. Hunting and lawful gun ownership grew up in the same house. Same roots, same critics, same fate. Once the culture decides common firearms are guilty until proven innocent, hunting is never far behind in that line.

You don’t have to own a Glock, like Glocks, or care one bit about Glocks to see the trap. A rule that lets the state wall off a legal gun over what someone might illegally do to it does not stop at Glocks. It has a long reach. Sooner or later it reaches the guns in your safe too.

Key Takeaways

The Five Things to Remember

  • It’s law, and it’s real. Signed October 10, 2025. The dealer-sale ban starts July 1, 2026.
  • It’s a sales ban, not a possession ban. Keep the Glock you already own. Private transfers through a dealer are still allowed.
  • It targets a part, not a brand. The trigger is the cruciform trigger bar, but the practical effect, by California’s own admission, is killing Glock sales in the state.
  • The fight leveled up. Private groups sued, then dropped it during talks. Now the DOJ is threatening a federal lawsuit, with a June 30 deadline for California to answer.
  • The precedent is the point. Restricting a common, legal gun over a hypothetical illegal modification is a template, and templates get reused.

The Legal Fight

The courtroom story comes in two acts, and act two is breaking right now.

Act one was the private lawsuit. Three days after Newsom signed, on October 13, 2025, a coalition of gun-rights heavyweights sued in federal court in San Diego. Jaymes v. Bonta put the NRA, the Firearms Policy Coalition, the Second Amendment Foundation, the San Diego retailer Poway Weapons and Gear, and a couple of individual gun owners on the same complaint. Their argument was the common-use one: Glock-pattern handguns are everywhere and legal, the Constitution protects common arms, and you can’t ban the sale of them.

It never reached a verdict. The two sides started talking, the judge paused the case on March 27, 2026, and then the plaintiffs themselves asked the court to toss it, which the judge did on April 13, 2026. A voluntary dismissal like that usually leaves the door cracked to refile, so it closed the round without closing the fight.

Worth knowing the backdrop here. California’s broader handgun roster, the list that decides which new pistols a dealer can sell at all, is already getting hammered in separate cases like Boland v. Bonta and Renna v. Bonta. In Boland, a federal judge actually struck down the roster’s feature mandates as unconstitutional, and then that ruling got stayed while the state appeals, so the roster is still standing for now. AB 1127 basically bolted a fresh restriction onto a system that was already in court.

Act two is the federal government, and this is the live wire. On June 24, 2026, Harmeet Dhillon, who runs the DOJ’s Civil Rights Division, sent Newsom and Attorney General Rob Bonta a formal notice of suit. She gave California until 5 p.m. Eastern on June 30 to say whether it wants to negotiate. If the state stays quiet, the letter says, the United States may just file its complaint with no further warning.

Definition

“Pattern or practice” (34 U.S.C. § 12601)

A federal civil-rights tool normally aimed at police departments accused of systemic misconduct. By framing California’s firearm enforcement this way, the DOJ is treating the state’s gun laws as a civil-rights violation against lawful gun owners, which is an unusually aggressive posture.

And the federal posture is not gentle. It goes after both AB 1127 and the handgun roster, and it frames California’s enforcement as a “pattern or practice” of misconduct. The demands reportedly run all the way to making California stop enforcing the laws, admit they’re unconstitutional, sign a court-enforceable agreement never to pass anything like them again, and preserve every related record. As of this writing, Bonta hasn’t said a word in public.

So the people lined up against this law have changed. Round one was advocacy groups with good lawyers. Round two, if it comes, is the United States of America.

What to Watch Next

  • The June 30 deadline. Whether California negotiates, ignores the DOJ, or gets sued is the single biggest near-term domino.
  • State dealer guidance. Watch for the California DOJ to hand FFLs compliance instructions as July 1 closes in. The fine print on inventory and exceptions matters enormously to anybody behind a counter.
  • Glock’s move. There’s been chatter about a possible California-compliant redesign, sometimes floated as a “V” series, but Glock hasn’t publicly committed to a clear plan and the details are thin. If the company does redesign and re-certify, the law has a built-in path to put modified models back on the roster, with a testing window running into early 2027.
  • Roster cases. Movement in Boland or Renna could reshape what’s even sellable in California, AB 1127 or not.
  • What dealers do with their stock. How shops handle remaining affected inventory before and after the deadline will drive both availability and price.
  • The private-transfer reading. Expect heavy use of the dealer-facilitated private-sale exception, and watch how it actually gets applied.
  • New lawsuits. A dismissed case can come back, and a federal suit would open a brand-new front.
  • Copycats. Lawmakers in Maryland, Connecticut, and New York have already run with similar measures. If California’s survives, more states pile on.

Final Takeaway

Let me be square about what this fight is, because the spin runs both directions.

It is not a fight over whether switches are dangerous. They are. Full stop. A converter turns a handgun into something no private citizen has any business firing, it’s already illegal six ways from Sunday, and nobody honest is arguing otherwise.

The fight is over a different and much bigger question. Can the government restrict common, legal pistols, owned by millions of people who’ve done nothing wrong, because some criminal might illegally modify them? California said yes. The gun-rights groups said no. And now the Department of Justice is saying no with the full weight of the federal government behind it.

July 1, 2026 was supposed to be the day this law settled in for good. It’s shaping up to be the day the real fight starts.

California phasing out UPFs in school meals

By Jeff Gelski

LOS ANGELES — California Governor Gavin Newsom on Oct. 8 signed Assembly Bill No. 1264 into a state law called the “Real Foods, Healthy Kids Act.” The law will define “ultra-processed foods” and “ultra-processed foods of concern” and phase them out of public schools for grades kindergarten through 12th grade over a 10-year period.

“California has never waited for Washington or anyone else to lead on kids’ health,” Newsom said at a signing ceremony in Los Angeles. “We’ve been out front for years, removing harmful additives and improving school nutrition. This first-in-the-nation law builds on that work to make sure every California student has access to healthy, delicious meals that help them thrive.”

Jesse Gabriel, a member of the California assembly, introduced the bill. It passed by a vote of 40-0 on Sept. 11 in the California state senate and by a vote of 79-1 on Sept. 12 in the California state assembly.

The 10-year timeline

Gavin Newsom firmó una ley que impacta en las comidas de todas las escuelas de California

La nueva legislación tiene como fin mejorar la salud alimentaria de los niños en los establecimientos educativos del Estado Dorado

  • 10 de octubre de 2025
  • 06:00

LA NACION

Gavin Newsom promulgó la norma AB 1264, conocida como “Ley de Comida Real, Niños Saludables”. Esta normativa firmada por el gobernador busca eliminar de manera progresiva los alimentos ultraprocesados de los menús en las escuelas de California durante la próxima década.

AB 1264: qué dice la “Ley de Comida Real, Niños Saludables” sobre los alimentos escolares en California

El gobernador republicano aprobó esta legislación impulsada con apoyo bipartidista, que establece una estrategia gradual para reducir y eliminar los alimentos ultraprocesados en los almuerzos escolares. El objetivo es garantizar que los estudiantes consuman productos más saludables que favorezcan su bienestar físico y su rendimiento académico.

La iniciativa introduce un marco regulatorio que prioriza los productos agrícolas frescos y los alimentos integrales en lugar de aquellos con aditivos artificiales o altos niveles de sodio, azúcar y grasas saturadas. La norma define dos pasos principales a seguir:

  • Definición de alimento ultraprocesado (UPF, por sus siglas en inglés): cualquier comida o bebida que contiene una sustancia definida por la Administración de Alimentos y Medicamentos (FDA, por sus siglas en inglés), como agentes tensioactivos, estabilizadores, colorantes, saborizantes, etc., y que además tiene altos niveles de grasa saturada (10% o más de las calorías totales), sodio (ratio sodio-calorías de 1:1 o mayor) o azúcares añadidos (10% o más de las calorías totales).
  • Mandato regulatorio: requiere que Departamento de Salud Pública del Estado (DPH, por sus siglas en inglés) adopte regulaciones, a más tardar el 1° de junio de 2028, para definir dos categorías clave: alimentos escolares restringidos y alimentos ultraprocesados de preocupación.

Obligaciones de la nueva ley sobre los alimentos en las escuelas de California

Seguido de la definición de los alimentos ultraprocesados y las regulaciones que deberá establecer DPH, también impone obligaciones a los vendedores de alimentos en las escuelas. Estos deben reportar información específica al DPH anualmente, desde febrero de 2028 hasta febrero de 2032.

Estos informes debe incluir la cantidad total de cada producto vendido, el nombre del mismo, la categoría a la que pertenece, el listado de ingredientes, los datos nutricionales y si se trata de un alimento ultraprocesado, restringido o de preocupación.

Por otro lado, la legislación impone requisitos adicionales a las escuelas públicas, lo que podría constituir un “programa local con mandato estatal”. En ese caso, si la Comisión de Mandatos Estatales determina que la ley contiene costos obligatorios, el estado debe proporcionar un reembolso.

Newsom celebró la ley “pionera en el país” que impacta en la alimentación en las escuelas de California

Gavin Newsom presentó la medida junto al asambleísta Jesse Gabriel, principal promotor del proyecto. Durante la conferencia de prensa, el mandatario demócrata destacó que la AB 1264 “es pionera en el país” y que busca que los niños de California “tengan acceso a comidas saludables y deliciosas que fortalezcan su desarrollo”.

Además, subrayó que el Estado Dorado “no esperará a Washington D. C. ni a otras jurisdicciones para cuidar la salud infantil”. En esa misma línea, completó: “California ha estado al frente de las políticas de nutrición escolar durante años, eliminando aditivos dañinos y promoviendo una alimentación más sana”, afirmó.

Por su parte, Gabriel celebró la aprobación de la norma: “Con esta ley, California da un paso histórico para proteger a nuestros niños de los efectos negativos de los alimentos ultraprocesados y de los aditivos químicos presentes en sus comidas diarias”.

California Enacts Law Defining Ultra-Processed Foods, Will Ban UPFs in Schools

By Bailee Henderson

October 9, 2025

California Governor Gavin Newsom has signed into law Assembly Bill (AB) 1264, also known as the Real Food, Healthy Kids Act. This first-of-its kind U.S. legislation establishes a legal definition for ultra-processed foods (UPFs), and tasks the state Department of Public Health with identifying and phasing out the “most harmful” UPFs from California schools.

Specifically, the act establishes the first-ever statutory definition of UPFs and directs California’s Department of Public Health, in cooperation with leading experts from the University of California, to identify and phase out UPFs of concern from schools by 2035.

The Real Food, Healthy Kids Act defines ultra-processed foods as those “high in” saturated fat, added sugar (or contains a non-sugar sweetener), or sodium, and contains one or more of certain additives, including artificial dyes, flavors, sweeteners, emulsifiers, and thickening agents. Raw agricultural products, minimally processed foods, and pasteurized milk are exempt from the definition of UPFs.

State scientists will determine whether a product should be phased out of schools based on certain factors, including:

  • Whether the product includes additives that are banned, restricted, or subject to warnings in other jurisdictions
  • Whether, based upon scientific research, the product or ingredients in the product are linked to cancer, cardiovascular disease, metabolic disease, developmental harms, reproductive harms, obesity, type 2 diabetes, or other health harms
  • Whether the product or ingredients in the product contribute to food addiction
  • Whether the food meets the U.S. Food and Drug Administration’s (FDA’s) definition for “healthy”
  • Whether the food is a UPF due to a “common natural additive.”

AB 1264 was originally introduced by Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel, who also championed two precedent-setting, now-enacted additives bans, the California Food Safety Act and California School Food Safety Act. Additionally, in January, Governor Newsom issued an executive order that mandates California agencies to explore the safety of UPFs, food dyes, and "generally recognized as safe" (GRAS) ingredients, and recommend actions to mitigate the adverse health effects.

Since the passage of the California Food Safety Act in 2023, a wave of state-level food additives regulations have been introduced or passed (most recently, in Louisiana), and the “Make America Healthy Again” (MAHA) movement has piggybacked on this momentum.

Despite the elevation of MAHA to the White House by U.S. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. (RFK Jr.), Assemblymember Gabriel cites federal inaction regarding the regulation of harmful foods and food ingredients as the impetus for the Real Food, Healthy Kids Act.

AB 1264 was co-sponsored by Consumer Reports, the Environmental Working Group, and Eat Real.

KEYWORDS: additives California colorant legislation MAHA ultra-processed foods

Bailee Henderson is the Director of Content Strategy for Food Safety Magazine. In the day-to-day, she covers industry-relevant current events, regulatory affairs, and scientific developments. She also produces the Food Safety Five Newsreel, edits the twice-weekly Food Safety Digest newsletter, and manages the brand's social media channels. Notably, Bailee's coverage for Food Safety Magazine has been featured in national televised news segments including CBS Sunday Morning and MSNBC's Rachel Maddow Show. She can be reached at hendersonb@bnpmedia.com.

California’s ultra-processed food ban could reshape school meals and national policy

By Elizabeth Crawford

As California Gov. Gavin Newsom on Wednesday signed landmark legislation to define and phase out ultra-processed foods from public school meals in the state, he and other local legislators taunted the Trump administration and federal legislators for failing to lead on food safety and nutrition.

“California has never waited for Washington or anyone else to lead on kids’ health – we’ve been out front for years, removing harmful additives and improving school nutrition,” Newsom said after signing into law the state’s bipartisan Assembly Bill 1264.

The law requires the California Department of Public Health to work with the University of California to identify “the most harmful UPFs” by June 1, 2028, after which schools would have one year to begin phasing out the “UPFs of concern.” Beginning in July 2032, vendors will no longer be allowed to offer restricted UPFs of concern to schools. Schools have an additional three years before they are formally prohibited from offering these foods.

The bill is the latest in a series of laws Newsom has signed in recent years to ban ingredients local legislators consider “dangerous.” These include the California Food Safety Act, signed in October 2023, that prohibited the sale, production or distribution in California of products including brominated vegetable oil, potassium bromate, propylparaben and Red Dye 3. A year later, Newsom signed legislation banning common dyes from food served in the state’s public schools.

Those laws became templates for other states to pursue similar restrictions – and could signal a similar path for the current law at the state level or within HHS Secretary Robert F Kennedy’s broader Make America Healthy Again movement.

“California has long been a bellwether state for public health protections,” notes the Environmental Working Group. “Now similar food actions are sweeping the country, with food chemical bills introduced, debated and in some cases enacted in states from Arizona to Vermont, including Utah, Virgina and West Virginia.”

Copycat legislation and rhetoric by Kennedy and MAHA proponents could create headaches for food manufacturers trying to navigate a patchwork of state legislation or uncertainty around the Trump administration’s preferred approach of strongarming industry into voluntary action versus a formal rulemaking with comment period.

Against this backdrop, CPG companies can protect their business by auditing ingredient lists, exploring clean reformulation paths and engaging with school buyers, experts previously advised.

UPFs latest flashpoint in increasing partisan political debate about food safety

Newsom’s signing of AB 1264 comes at a time when ultra-processed food and nutrition have become flashpoints for the Trump administration, federal legislators and regulators who are mired in political gridlock.

FDA and USDA recently requested information to formally define UPFs – setting an original deadline for comments of Sept. 23. Late last month they extended the deadline to Oct. 23, but the next steps could be further delayed depending on how long the current government shutdown extends.

These delays became fodder for political jostling by California legislators.

“While Washington, DC, is paralyzed by inaction, California is once again leading the nation with a bipartisan, commonsense, science-based approached,” said Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel, D-Encino, who introduced AB 1264.

On the social media platform X, Newsom taunted, “DC politicians can talk all day about ‘Making America Healthy Again,’ but we’ve been walking the walk on boosting nutrition and removing toxic additives and dyes for decades.”

Public trust in food safety and science is eroding

The increased politicization of food safety and nutrition science has alarmed some industry leaders and public health advocates who say they worry public trust in leadership is eroding.

A 2024 survey by the International Food Information Council found only two in five American strongly trust food, nutrition and diet science.

This mirrors results from Gallup’s longstanding annual Consumption Habits poll that found last Fall only 57% of US adults say that have a “great deal” or “fair amount” of confidence in the government to keep the food supply safe – a dramatic drop of 11 percentage points from the poll’s initial assessment in 2019.

“We don’t love our kids any less than they do in Europe, or Asia, or Latin America,” Gabriel said at a bill signing event. “So why would we offer them less protection from harmful products linked to cancer, cardiovascular disease and reproductive harm?”

s02375:
New California laws: From Diwali to refrigerators

SACRAMENTO, Calif. - California's governor is busy signing bills into laws, from banning police masks to creating Diwali as a state holiday, from California State University admissions to making sure landlords provide basic appliances.

Here is a look at some of the new legislation:

Ban police masks

SB 627, signed by Governor Newsom, prohibits law enforcement officers from wearing face coverings while on duty and requires them to display their name and badge number to ensure transparency and accountability.

Gov. Gavin Newsom signed a set of bills meant to check the Trump administration’s aggressive immigration crackdown in California, including a first-in-the nation measure to ban officers from wearing masks and others that limit their access to schools and hospitals, CalMatters reported.

AB 49 prohibits schools from allowing immigration enforcement officers on campus without a warrant.
SB 627 widely prohibits federal and local law enforcement officers from wearing face masks while conducting their duties.
SB 805 requires that law enforcement officers identify themselves while conducting their duties, with some exceptions.
SB 81 prohibits immigration enforcement from entering restricted areas of a health facility without a judicial warrant or court order.
SB 98 requires schools and higher education institutions to send community notifications when immigration enforcement is on campus, and prohibits immigration enforcement from entering certain areas without a judicial warrant or court order.

Diwali state holiday

People light earthen lamps on the banks of Saryu River during a cultural programme, on the eve of Diwali festival, on November 11, 2023, Ayodhya, India. (Photo by Ritesh Shukla/Getty Images)

Diwali, the vibrant festival of lights celebrated in Hinduism and other religions, will become an official state holiday in California next year.

The new law, AB 268, was sponsored by Democratic state Assemblymembers Ash Kalra, who represents part of San Jose, and Darshana Patel, who represents San Diego. Starting in 2026, public schools and community colleges will be able to close on Diwali, and state employees can choose to take the day off with pay.

Last year, Pennsylvania became the first state and this year Connecticut became the second state to officially recognize Diwali as a state holiday, according Kalra's office. New York requires public schools in the city of New York to be closed on Diwali as a school holiday. Other states are also considering Diwali holiday recognitions.

Kalra is the first Indian American to serve in the California State Legislature.

Admit qualified high school graduates to CSU

Qualified high school graduates will automatically be admitted to the California State University system in the 2026-27 school year without having to apply, because SB 640 was signed into law.

The author was Sen. Christopher Cabaldon.

Ultra-processed foods banned

California leaders are hoping to see most ultraprocessed foods banned from school-provided meals by 2035.

California Governor Gavin Newsom signed AB 1264 into law, which bans the most "harmful" ultra-processed foods from school lunches by 2035.

Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel (D-San Fernando Valley) authored the bill, making California the first state in the nation to ban certain foods from public schools.

Antisemitism prevention coordinator

AB 715 establishes a new Office of Civil Rights and a first-in-the-nation statewide Antisemitism Prevention Coordinator in an effort to rein in antisemitism in schools.

The Antisemitism Prevention Coordinator will be appointed by Newsom and confirmed by the state Senate, tasked with tracking and reporting antisemitism in California schools, as well as training and advising local educational agencies on how to address antisemitism.

The bill was authored by Democratic Assemblymembers Rick Chavez Zbur of Los Angeles and Dawn Addis of San Luis Obispo.

Outdoor dining options

AB 592, written by Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel (D-Encino), enables open-kitchen restaurants to utilize California’s climate by permitting windows, folding doors, or non-fixed storefronts — which gives restaurant owners greater flexibility in providing outside premises.

Fridges in apartments

AB 628 requires apartments to come with a refrigerator and stove, as well as basic appliances that many reasonable renters expect would already be required. The mandate applies to all leases that are signed, amended or renewed on or after Jan. 1, 2026.

It was authored by Assemblymemember Tina McKinnor (D-Inglewood).

Return cars for refund

FILE-Vehicles for sale at a Ford dealership in Colma, California. (David Paul Morris/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Consumers who buy or lease a new or used car from a California dealer will now have a first-in-the-nation right to return a used car for a refund within three days of purchase and improved pricing transparency.

SB 766, authored by Sen. Ben Allen (D-Santa Monica) is similar to a regulation adopted by the Federal Trade Commission early last year under President Joe Biden.

The law also gives consumers the right to find out the full price of any vehicle upon request and bans outright junk products and services, like "free oil changes" for an electric car, according to UC Berkeley's Center for Consumer Law.

s02377:
An ACIP surprise

Driving the Day

COVID SHOT CHANGE — The CDC and its panel of expert advisers quietly expanded access to Covid-19 vaccination during pregnancy, undoing an earlier recommendation from HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. to stop recommending that pregnant women get the shots.

The CDC’s Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices voted in September to recommend that adults can choose to get the Covid shot after consulting with their providers, also known as shared clinical decision-making. The panel didn’t specifically vote on whether the shot should be administered during pregnancy, yet the vote appears to encompass pregnant women, according to an update this month on the CDC website that reflects the new guidance.

That development surprised some, including legal experts.

“Covid-19 vaccine in pregnancy had been discussed initially — ACIP recommended them — then the secretary took that back,” said Dorit Reiss, a vaccine law expert at the University of California’s law school in San Francisco.“Under these circumstances, if they were going to change the decision about pregnancy, I would have expected them to address it expressly, since it was changed expressly [by Kennedy].”

It’s unclear whether all 12 panel members, handpicked by Kennedy, were aware that the move would undo his decision. Much of the panel’s two-day September meeting in Atlanta was marked by confusion as recently appointed members struggled with the procedures. ACIP Chair Martin Kulldorff did not immediately respond to a request for comment, nor did a spokesperson for HHS.

Why it matters: The new guidance for adults means that pharmacies can administer the vaccine to pregnant women, and almost all insurers must cover the shots with no cost-sharing — guaranteeing expanded access for people who want to be vaccinated.

Vaccinating children under 6 months against Covid-19 isn’t recommended, so many providers see vaccination during pregnancy as a key tool for protecting vulnerable infants from the infection.

The panel’s Covid recommendation contradicts what many public health experts had expected from the September meeting. Kennedy fired all the panel’s members in June, and some new members have argued that Covid vaccines aren’t safe, spurring concerns that the panel would vote to drastically narrow access to the shots.

WELCOME TO THURSDAY PULSE. Speaker Mike Johnson will hold a call with House Republicans today at 11:30 a.m., during which he’s expected to fill GOP members in on the current state of play around the shutdown. Send your tips, scoops and feedback to khooper@politico.com and sgardner@politico.com, and follow along @kelhoops and @sophie_gardnerj.

AROUND THE AGENCIES

TYLENOL CONFUSION — Most people are uncertain about whether they believe the claim that Tylenol causes autism, according to a KFF poll published today.

Last month, President Donald Trump told women not to take the common pain reliever during pregnancy, linking it to an increased risk of autism, though most prominent voices in the public health establishment say there is no proven causal link between the two.

The public is unsure what to believe. Most adults say the claim is either “probably true” or “probably false,” with only 4 percent saying they believe the claim was “definitely true” and 35 percent saying it was “definitely false.” Nearly 80 percent of adults reported having heard the claim.

Republicans were much more likely to say the claim was probably or definitely true, at 57 percent, while 86 percent of Democrats said the claim was probably or definitely false.

CDC trust: Trust in the CDC’s vaccine guidance has reached its lowest level since the beginning of the COVID-19 pandemic, KFF reports. Half of the public reported trusting the CDC “a great deal” or “fair amount” to provide reliable information about vaccines.

Kennedy support: Most people are critical of Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s performance as health secretary, according to KFF.

Around 4 in 10 adults say they “strongly” or “somewhat” approve of the way Kennedy is handling his job as HHS secretary, compared with 59 percent who say they either “somewhat” or “strongly” disapprove of his job performance.

The public was similarly critical of Kennedy’s actions on vaccines, with 37 percent of adults saying they approve of his handling of vaccine policy compared with 62 percent who disapprove.

Poll details: The nationwide KFF Health Tracking Poll was conducted September 23-2 online and by phone, with a sample of 1,334 U.S. adults.

IN THE STATES

IS GAVIN NEWSOM ‘MAHA’? California Gov. Gavin Newsom signed legislation to phase out ultraprocessed foods from California schools— drawing attention for the plan’s parallels to HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s Make America Healthy Again movement to combat chronic diseases, POLITICO’s Nicole Norman reports.

Why it matters: The policy marked a rare moment of bipartisanship in the legislature, drawing support not only from Democrats but from Republicans who saw it as an advancement of the MAHA initiative.

The bill creates the nation’s first statutory definition of ultraprocessed, initially a sticking point for the bill as it moved through the legislature. Democratic Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel said he took more than 50 amendments from lawmakers and agricultural interests who were concerned the definition would ban foods that aren’t necessarily unhealthy, like shredded cheese.

Key context: The move comes as Kennedy and the federal government appear to be working toward their own definition of ultraprocessed. In September, the MAHA Commission recommended a slew of strategies to President Donald Trump meant to address “America’s childhood chronic disease epidemic.” Among them was a recommendation to have the USDA, HHS and the FDA continue efforts to develop a government-wide definition of ultraprocessed foods “to support future research and policy activity.”

In Congress

FIGHTING WORDS — Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and Senate HELP Chair Bill Cassidy finally agree on something: a push to reconsider the American Medical Association’s role in determining how doctors are paid, POLITICO’s Simon J. Levien reports.

The Louisiana Republican has harshly criticized Kennedy for firing the CDC director, replacing members of a vaccine advisory panel and reconsidering government guidance on Covid and hepatitis B shots. But the two are aligned in questioning the key role the nation’s leading physicians’ society, the AMA, plays in setting the rates doctors are paid.

In an Oct. 6 letter to AMA President Bobby Mukkamala, Cassidy attacked the AMA for its coding system, which doctors use to bill Medicare, Medicaid and private insurers for their services. Cassidy said he suspected the AMA is driving up health costs by charging fees to the doctors, hospitals, health plans and health IT vendors that must license its codes.

Kennedy has reportedly weighed a plan to reduce the AMA’s role. Besides the group’s sway over the codes — which Congress endorsed in the 1996 Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act — an AMA panel recommends reimbursement rates for medical procedures to Medicare, the insurance program for seniors, which are often adopted.

The AMA declined to comment on Cassidy’s criticism.

Names in the News

Debra Lubar, former chief operating officer at the CDC, is joining the Milbank Memorial Fund — a New York–based foundation that supports health policy research — as its president on December 1.

WHAT WE'RE READING

POLITICO’s Juliann Ventura reports on several states joining a bipartisan effort formed earlier this year to focus on implementing and enforcing privacy laws nationwide.

The Washington Post’s Craig Whitlock, Lisa Rein and Nate Jones report on the persistent issue of veterans defrauding the VA’s disability program.

캘리포니아, 학교 급식서 ‘초가공식품 퇴출’ 첫 주 됐다

뉴섬 주지사, 2035년까지 학교 급식서 초가공식품 단계적 제거 법안 서명

2025년 10월 09일 0

개빈 뉴섬 캘리포니아 주지사가 8일, 초가공식품 (ultra-processed foods, UPFs)을 법적으로 정의하고 이를 공립학교 급식에서 점진적으로 퇴출시키는 전국 최초의 법안에 서명했다.

‘진짜 음식, 건강한 아이들 법(Real Food, Healthy Kids Act)’으로 알려진 주 하원법안 1264호는 캘리포니아 보건국에 초가공식품(UPFs) 중 학생 건강에 가장 큰 위험을 초래하는 식품을 식별하고, 2035년까지 이를 학교 급식에서 제거하도록 지시한다.

이 법안을 발의한 제시 가브리엘 의원은 “공립학교가 유해한 화학 첨가물이 가득한 초가공식품을 학생들에게 제공해서는 안 된다”며, “이번 입법을 통해 민주당과 공화당이 함께 아동의 건강과 안전을 최우선으로 삼고 있으며, 과학에 기반한 초당적 접근으로 다시 한번 전국을 선도하게 되어 자랑스럽다”고 밝혔다.

이 법에 따르면, 학교는 늦어도 2029년 7월 1일까지 제한 대상 식품과 우려되는 초가공식품을 단계적으로 급식에서 제외해야 하며, 2032년 7월 1일부터는 공급업체가 이들 식품을 학교에 제공하는 것이 금지된다.

‘초가공식품(ultra-processed foods, UPFs)’은 단순히 가공된 음식이 아니라, 공장에서 인공적인 성분과 첨가물로 구성된 식품을 말합니다. 주로 원재료의 형태가 거의 남지 않을 정도로 가공된 음식

새 법률에 따라, 주정부 과학자들은 캘리포니아 대학교 소속 전문가들과 협력해 아래와 같은 기준을 바탕으로 식품이 ‘우려되는 초가공식품’ 또는 ‘제한 대상 학교 식품’에 해당하는지 판단하게 된다.

가브리엘 의원은 그동안 캘리포니아 주민들을 위한 식품 건강 개선을 목표로 여러 입법을 추진해 왔다.

2023년에는 ‘스키틀즈 금지법’(AB 418)으로 불린 법안을 발의해 브로민화 식물성 기름, 적색 색소 3번(Red Dye No. 3) 등 특정 유해 성분을 포함한 식품의 유통을 금지했으며, AB 2316 법안을 통해 학교 급식에서 특정 합성 색소 사용도 금지시켰다.

많은 학부모들은 이번 법안에 환영 입장을 밝히면서도 학생들의 급식의 질 상승도 함께 기대한다고 밝혔다.

California trở thành tiểu bang đầu tiên loại bỏ thực phẩm siêu chế biến khỏi bữa ăn học đường

October 8, 2025

0

1149


Luật mới, được Thống đốc Gavin Newsom ký hôm thứ Tư, đặt ra thời hạn 10 năm để hoàn tất quá trình thay đổi này.

Một đạo luật mới sẽ khiến California trở thành tiểu bang đầu tiên của Hoa Kỳ loại bỏ dần một số loại thực phẩm siêu chế biến ra khỏi bữa ăn học đường.

Thống đốc Gavin Newsom đã ký đạo luật hôm thứ Tư, cấm các trường công lập phục vụ học sinh những loại thực phẩm được mô tả là “thực phẩm siêu chế biến đáng lo ngại” trong bữa sáng hoặc bữa trưa. Chính sách này đặt ra thời hạn 10 năm để hoàn toàn loại bỏ những món ăn đó.

Luật định nghĩa nhóm thực phẩm này là những sản phẩm có bằng chứng khoa học cho thấy gây hại cho sức khỏe, và giao cho Sở Y tế Công cộng bang California xác định cụ thể các loại thực phẩm nằm trong danh mục này trước tháng 6 năm 2028.

“Hiện nay có một nhận thức ngày càng rõ ràng, đặc biệt là trong giới cha mẹ trẻ như tôi, rằng những gì chúng ta cho con ăn không chỉ ảnh hưởng đến sức khỏe thể chất mà còn liên quan sâu sắc đến sức khỏe tinh thần và cảm xúc của trẻ,” Dân biểu tiểu bang Jesse Gabriel, người bảo trợ dự luật, chia sẻ qua điện thoại. “Trong cơ quan lập pháp có rất nhiều phụ huynh như tôi, và dù họ là Dân chủ hay Cộng hòa, bảo thủ hay cấp tiến, tất cả cha mẹ đều muốn điều tốt nhất cho con cái mình.”

Dự luật được thông qua hồi tháng 9 với sự ủng hộ lưỡng đảng.
“Tôi nghĩ đây là một phong trào có thể gắn kết tất cả chúng ta, bất kể khác biệt chính trị,” Thống đốc Newsom nói trong lễ ký kết tại Trường Trung học Belvedere ở Los Angeles.

Tác động và định nghĩa

Trung bình, trẻ em và thanh thiếu niên tại Hoa Kỳ nhận gần 62% lượng calo từ thực phẩm siêu chế biến — thuật ngữ chỉ các sản phẩm chứa rất ít thành phần tự nhiên. Tiêu thụ nhiều loại thực phẩm này đã được liên kết với nguy cơ ung thư, bệnh tim mạch và tiểu đường loại 2.

California hiện tạo ra định nghĩa riêng cho “thực phẩm siêu chế biến”: đó là các sản phẩm chứa ít nhất một loại phụ gia (như chất ổn định, làm đặc, tạo màu hoặc chất tạo ngọt nhân tạo), cộng với hàm lượng cao chất béo bão hòa, natri hoặc đường bổ sung.

Luật cũng xác định riêng khái niệm “thực phẩm siêu chế biến đáng lo ngại” — đây là nhóm sản phẩm bị cấm phục vụ trong trường học.
Để xác định danh mục này, Sở Y tế tiểu bang sẽ đánh giá mức độ gây nghiện, bằng chứng khoa học về rủi ro sức khỏe, và các lệnh cấm hoặc cảnh báo hiện hành ở các bang hay quốc gia khác.

Các trường sẽ bắt đầu loại bỏ nhóm thực phẩm này từ năm 2029 và phải hoàn tất vào năm 2035.

Hiệu quả kinh tế và mở rộng chính sách

Theo Dân biểu Gabriel, nhiều học khu ở California đã áp dụng mô hình bữa ăn lành mạnh và kết quả cho thấy “chi phí không tăng mà thậm chí tiết kiệm được tiền.”

Trong những năm gần đây, Gabriel cũng là người đề xuất luật cấm phẩm màu nhân tạo trong bữa ăn học đường và cấm một số phụ gia hóa học trong thực phẩm bán trên thị trường bang.

Tháng 1 vừa qua, Thống đốc Newsom ban hành sắc lệnh hành pháp yêu cầu các cơ quan tiểu bang siết chặt kiểm soát thực phẩm siêu chế biến và phẩm màu nhân tạo.

Phong trào này diễn ra song song với nỗ lực trên toàn quốc nhằm nâng cao giá trị dinh dưỡng của bữa ăn học đường. Kể từ khi nhậm chức tháng 2, Bộ trưởng Y tế và Dịch vụ Nhân sinh Robert F. Kennedy Jr. đã khuyến khích các bang ban hành luật hạn chế thực phẩm siêu chế biến và phẩm màu nhân tạo trong trường học.

Tháng 3, Thống đốc Patrick Morrisey của West Virginia ký luật cấm bảy loại phẩm màu nhân tạo trong bữa ăn học đường — và ông cho biết động lực đến từ chính Kennedy. Đến tháng 8, Thống đốc Greg Abbott của Texas, cùng Kennedy tham dự, ký ban hành luật cấm phục vụ bữa ăn miễn phí hoặc giảm giá có chứa phụ gia nhất định.

Tuy nhiên, Gabriel khẳng định nỗ lực của California không bắt nguồn từ phong trào “Make America Healthy Again” của Kennedy:
“Chúng tôi đã bắt đầu công việc bảo vệ sức khỏe trẻ em ở California từ trước khi người ta biết đến phong trào đó,” ông nói.

Trong lễ ký kết, Newsom nhấn mạnh California tiếp tục dẫn đầu cả nước:
“Khi chúng tôi bắt đầu nói về việc cấm kẹo Skittles, chẳng ai hiểu và thậm chí nhiều người còn phản đối. Giờ thì các bang khác — kể cả những bang bảo thủ như Louisiana — lại đang chạy đua để làm điều tương tự. Tôi thấy điều đó thật thú vị và đáng mừng.”

Nguồn NBC News

纽森州长签署全美首项法案 禁止学校餐食使用“超加工食品” 加州再次走在全国前列 以立法守护儿童健康、提升学校营养标准

    【洛杉矶讯】

    加州州长加文·纽森（Gavin Newsom） 本周三（8日）正式签署 AB 1264 法案，这项由州众议员 杰西·加布里埃尔（Jesse Gabriel） 提出的跨党派立法，将成为全美首个禁止学校餐食中使用“超加工食品”（Ultra-Processed Foods, UPF）的法律。

    该法案首次在美国法律中定义了“超加工食品”，并要求加州学校逐步淘汰被认为对儿童健康构成风险的食品，确保学生获得更健康、更有营养的餐食。

    纽森表示，“加州从不等待华盛顿或他人来引领儿童健康——多年来我们一直走在前面，移除有害添加物、提升校园营养标准。这项全美首创的法律将进一步确保每位加州学生都能吃到健康、美味、有助成长的餐食。”

    加州“第一夫人” 詹妮弗·西贝尔·纽森（Jennifer Siebel Newsom）表示，这项法律对于保障学生健康至关重要：“对许多孩子来说，学校餐是他们一天中最重要、甚至是唯一的一餐。通过移除最令人担忧的超加工食品，我们帮助孩子保持专注、健康与活力。当华盛顿仍在辩论如何‘让美国重新健康’，他们不妨看看加州已经在做什么。”

    法案作者加布里埃尔议员表示，这项立法是加州在食品安全和儿童健康领域迈出的历史性一步：“随着纽森州长签署 AB 1264，加州再一次以科学与常识为基础，以两党合作的方式引领全国。我们正在确保孩子们吃到真正的食物，而不是充满化学添加剂的加工品。”

    延续加州在健康校园饮食上的全国领导地位

    AB 1264 延续了加州多年来在学校营养与食品安全上的政策创新。

    • 2023 年，纽森签署 AB 418，禁止州内销售含红色染料 3 号、溴化植物油等与癌症及儿童行为障碍相关的化学添加物。

    • 2024 年，又通过 AB 2316，禁止学校销售或供应含有合成食用色素的食品。

    • 同年，加州还扩大了食品援助项目覆盖面，并通过 “农场到校园计划”（Farm to School） 提升本地健康食材在校园餐中的比例。

    此外，纽森州长在 2025 年 1 月 发布行政命令，要求州政府制定减少超加工食品危害的政策建议，而 AB 1264 正与该行政命令相呼应。

    全民校餐与健康食品计划

    加州是全美首个实施 “全民校餐计划”（Universal Meals Program） 的州，为所有学前班至 12 年级学生提供每日两餐免费校餐，无论家庭收入如何。

    在“第一夫人”詹妮弗的推动下，“农场到校园计划” 确保这些校餐不仅免费，还要使用本地农产品、营养均衡且美味可口。

    2025 年夏季，超过 400 万名加州儿童 通过 “SUN Bucks” 食品补助计划 获得了每人 120 美元的食品补助，用于暑期期间的健康饮食。

    加州还在 2023 年 成为首个将拜登总统新版学校营养标准（减少糖和盐摄入）写入州法的州，并建立应对机制，以防未来联邦政府放宽相关标准。

    为什么这项法案至关重要

    根据美国疾病控制与预防中心（CDC） 2025 年 7 月发布的报告，全美 12 至 19 岁青少年中有32.7% 处于糖尿病前期。

    同时，国立卫生研究院（NIH） 与 CDC 研究均表明，健康饮食能显著降低心脏病、中风、糖尿病及其他慢性病的风险。

    在纽森领导下，加州还保持了全国最严格的校园饮食标准，包括：

    • 全面禁止销售含糖汽水（适用于 K-12 所有年级）；

    • 禁止任何年级提供含咖啡因饮品；

    • 要求学校餐品在菜单出现当日或次日销售，并严格控制热量、脂肪与反式脂肪含量——高于联邦标准。

    加州模式：以儿童健康为先

    随着 AB 1264 的签署，加州再次确立其在全国公共健康政策中的领导地位。

    这项法案不仅是食品安全的里程碑，更象征着加州对儿童健康、教育公平与社会责任的持续承诺。

    纽森强调，“加州再次向全国展示：真正把孩子放在首位是什么样子。”

Text of the ProQuest PDF (3 pages)

California enacts nation’s first law to define and ban ultraprocessed foods

By Sandee LaMotte

(CNN) — California made history Wednesday by enacting the first law in the United States to define and ultimately ban unhealthy ultraprocessed foods, or UPFs, from what’s projected to be over 1 billion meals served to California schoolchildren in the 2025-26 school year.

By signing the “Real Food, Healthy Kids Act” into law, California Gov. Gavin Newsom has taken control of a growing movement to reform the nation’s food supply. The state legislature passed the bill in mid-September.

On average, children in the United States get nearly two-thirds of their calories from ultraprocessed foods packed full of additives and high-calorie sugars, salt and fat, according to a recent CDC report.

Not only does the California legislation define ultraprocessed food — a task which most of the world has yet to accomplish — it requires public health officials and scientists to decide which UPFs are most harmful to human health. Any “ultraprocessed food of concern” would then be phased out of the school food supply.

California’s decisive action is a sharp contrast to the “Make American Healthy Again,” or MAHA, movement spearheaded by US Health and Human Services director Robert F. Kennedy, Jr.

“While folks in DC are commissioning reports and debating hypotheticals, California is leading with decisive action,” Jesse Gabriel, the Democratic California Assemblymember who introduced the bill, said in a press conference.

“Or to put it more bluntly, here in California, we are actually doing the work to protect our kids health, and we’ve been doing it since well before anyone had ever heard of the MAHA movement,” Gabriel added.

The MAHA Commission promised decisive action on ultraprocessed food by August of this year. However, the final report, released in September, only promised the government would “continue efforts” to define ultraprocessed foods. “Unfortunately, the final MAHA report is all promises and has no teeth,” Barry Popkin, the W.R. Kenan, Jr. Distinguished Professor at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill’s Gillings School of Global Public Health told CNN at the time. “In my opinion, it shows the food, agricultural, and pharmaceutical industries got to the White House and won the day,” Popkin said.

A strong lobbying effort That scenario could have happened in California as well, said Bernadette Del Chiaro, senior vice president for California at the Environmental Working Group, or EWG, a health advocacy organization based in Washington, DC, that cosponsored the bill.

“There was very serious opposition. Industry always kicks and screams and fights like bloody hell to keep these bills from becoming law,” Del Chiaro told CNN. “Just the number of committees we had to go through to get the bill passed illustrates how much lobbying was going on.”

The final vote, however, told it all: Out of 120 California assemblymembers and senators from both the Republican and Democratic parties, only one voted no — a Republican from San Diego.

“We had broad bipartisan support because ultimately, this is coming from the grassroots up — from politicians hearing about these issues in their community and wanting to do something about it,” Del Chiaro said. “We’re in this moment where Americans are waking up to the fact that we have chemicals in everything — our food, our water and our air — and we need to do something about it.”

CNN reached out to the Consumer Brands Association, which represents major food manufacturers, but did not hear back before publication.

The best and worst ultraprocessed foods The “Real Food, Healthy Kids Act” specifically defines an ultraprocessed food as one that may contain such ingredients as nonnutritive sweeteners; high amounts of saturated fat, sodium and added sugar; additives such as emulsifiers, stabilizers and thickeners; flavor enhancers; a host of food dyes; and more.

The California law provides guidance on how much of an ingredient like sugar or salt can be in a food in order to be served to elementary and middle-school children, with a slightly different standard for high schoolers.

But not all ultraprocessed foods will be phased out of the state’s school supply, Gabriel told CNN.

“We can’t eliminate all ultraprocessed foods — we need them, we need the shelf stability, the safety, the convenience,” he said. “But the foods with the most harmful additives, foods that are linked to food addiction or cancer or diabetes or fatty liver disease, that’s the group of ultraprocessed foods we will phase out of our schools.”

An ultraprocessed food can also be banned for containing additives that have been banned, restricted or required to carry a warning by other local, state, federal or international jurisdictions, according to the law. (The European Union has taken action on various food dyes and other additives.)

Another red flag: Has the ultraprocessed food been modified to include high levels of sugar, salt or fat? (That’s a key way manufacturers design ultraprocessed foods to meet the “bliss point” human taste buds yearn for.)

It won’t happen overnight

Eliminating ultraprocessed foods from the California school food supply is not going to be a quick process. In earlier iterations of the bill, regulators were required to take some actions in 2026. In the final law, the first regulation — requiring food vendors to report all ultraprocessed foods they will supply — is due on or before February 1, 2028. All ultraprocessed food of concern must be identified and out of schools by July 1, 2035.

There’s also a concern that California’s efforts could be derailed by a federal government controlled by Republicans. “We are constantly concerned that Congress will fight to preempt our authority with some kind of watered down, weak federal effort,” Del Chiaro said. “There’s certainly members of Congress that are threatening that, right? “But we had broad bipartisan support, and I would certainly hope that, politicians at the federal level see that we’re all on the same team. We’re on Team Public Health and Team Kids and I hope they will continue to let states be the laboratories of democracy that we are.”

It defines such foods as those that pose the greatest risks to consumers based on scientific evidence of adverse health outcomes, and it directs the state Public Health Department to determine which particular products meet the definition by June 2028.

The Legislature passed the bill in September, with bipartisan support.

“It’s a movement that should unite all of us, regardless of political stripes,” Newsom said at a signing ceremony at Belvedere Middle School in Los Angeles.

On average, children and adolescents in the United States consume nearly 62% of their calories from ultraprocessed foods — a term that often broadly refers to foods with few whole ingredients. High consumption of such foods has been linked to cancer, heart disease and Type 2 diabetes, among other negative health outcomes.

There is no single standardized definition of ultraprocessed food, so California’s new law establishes its own: It considers foods and beverages “ultraprocessed” if they contain one or more additives (such as stabilizers, thickeners, colorings or nonnutritive sweeteners), plus high levels of saturated fat, sodium or added sugar.

The law creates a separate definition for “ultraprocessed food of concern,” and those products are the target of the new ban.

To determine which items fall into that category, the law directs the state health department to evaluate foods' addictive potential, scientific evidence of their health risks and existing bans, restrictions or warning labels in other states or countries.

Schools are required to start phasing out these ultraprocessed foods by 2029 and to fully do so by 2035.

Gabriel added that California has being protecting public health since "well before the MAHA movement," which has also targeted ultraprocessed foods.

After a series of amendments over the summer, a coalition of agricultural groups moved to a neutral position, while two prominent fruit organizations actively backed the bill. Yet cattle, dairy, egg, poultry and wheat producers remained opposed, along with the California Farm Bureau and the Consumer Brands Association.

The California Grocers Association, American Beverage Association and other trade groups have also warned of potential compliance challenges for school food vendors and manufacturers, arguing schools need more funding and time to adapt menus and supply chains.

Implementation will roll out over the next decade, giving school districts and suppliers time to prepare for the changes.

The measure’s broad scope and long timeline leave room for debate over cost, practicality and science. As implementation begins, lawmakers and regulators will face pressure from both health advocates and food producers to strike a balance between public health goals and agricultural realities.

State law to ban some ultraprocessed foods from school meals

Daniel Miller

It’s a little after 9:30 a.m. on a recent weekday, and hair-netted workers at the Alhambra Unified School District’s central production kitchen are boxing up the last of 350 handmade sushi rolls for the city’s three high schools.

The spicy tuna rolls, redolent of cooked fish blended with sriracha and mayonnaise, are a popular lunch offering among students.

“It’s one of our signature items that you can never take away,” said Dwayne Dionne, Alhambra Unified’s culinary specialist.

Alhambra Unified has sold the sushi for about 25 years. At one point, the district switched from white to brown rice — a healthier whole grain. Yet, it’s the kind of meal that will be scrutinized under a new state law: the Real Food, Healthy Kids Act.

The law, which Gov. Gavin Newsom signed on Wednesday, provides a first-ever statutory definition of ultraprocessed foods in the U.S. and will ban some that are “of concern” in California schools starting in 2035.

Under the legislation, which is expected to touch off a major overhaul of school cafeteria meals, the state’s Department of Public Health will identify ultraprocessed foods “of concern” and “restricted school foods” — another prohibited category — by 2028. A year later, schools are required to begin phasing them out.

“There’s this really great opportunity to help a ton of people in a pretty straightforward way,” said Assemblyman Jesse Gabriel (D-Encino), author of the legislation. “I’m still learning about all this. ... I [was] going to the grocery store trying to do right by my kids, but had no idea that we might be feeding them things that could be harmful.”

For years, scientific studies have shown that ultraprocessed food can lead to significant health issues among children, increasing the risk of obesity and asthma. Ashley Gearhardt, a professor of psychology at the University of Michigan, said that children are particularly vulnerable to “high-risk” ultraprocessed foods that deliver “really unnatural levels of rewarding ingredients like refined carbohydrates and added fats, and ... they’re being amplified with all these colors, preservatives and flavor enhancers.”

Dwayne Dionne, Alhambra Unified’s culinary specialist, at the district’s central production kitchen.

(Carlin Stiehl / Los Angeles Times)

Such ingredients can trigger in children “compulsive, addictive [behavior] that you see so often with these sorts of products,” said Gearhardt, an expert on food addiction who testified in support of the bill.

The legislation will not ban all ultraprocessed foods from schools — far from it.

Consider Alhambra Unified’s sriracha-laced spicy tuna roll. Sriracha could be regarded as an ultraprocessed food — owing in part to the presence of xanthan gum, a thickening agent — but it is not expected to be classified one under the new law’s definition of the category. The sushi, therefore, is unlikely to be deemed an ultraprocessed food “of concern” or appear on the “restricted” list, experts said.

That would be welcome news for Patty Zaragoza, a food service worker at Alhambra Unified’s central kitchen. After boxing up the last of the 350 sushi rolls, she said she never tires of them.

“Oh no, I love it!” she said.

The path to law

For Gabriel, who was first elected in 2018, the Real Food, Healthy Kids Act marks the third food-related law he has spearheaded.

In 2023, Gabriel authored the California Food Safety Act, which prohibits several food additives — including red dye No. 3 — that are commonly found in soda, candy and cereal. A year later, the assemblyman authored the California School Food Safety Act, which gained widespread attention because it bans from schools Flamin’ Hot Cheetos and other products that include certain synthetic food dyes.

Gabriel said that his extended foray into food safety was an unexpected turn — but one that is personal. He has three children in elementary school. “A lot of the ways that I look at the world are through the lens of a dad,” he said.

A turning point: Gabriel learned that the ill effects of certain synthetic food dyes can be amplified in children who have attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder.

ADHD “was something I struggled with as a kid,” he said, “and one of my sons is working through” it.

Since Gabriel began authoring food-related legislation, the rise of the controversial Make America Healthy Again movement has spotlighted issues related to dyes and other additives, and their possible links to a variety of health issues. But he said that the new law emanates out of “sound science,” adding, “We were doing a lot of this work before anybody had ever heard of MAHA.”

In a statement, Newsom said that “California has never waited for Washington or anyone else to lead on kids’ health.”

“We’ve been out front for years, removing harmful additives and improving school nutrition,” he said. “This first-in-the-nation law builds on that work to make sure every California student has access to healthy, delicious meals that help them thrive.”

Carol Chan portions out beef and bean chili at the Alhambra Unified central production kitchen.

(Carlin Stiehl / Los Angeles Times)

Gabriel’s bill garnered strong bipartisan support. But it was opposed by groups including the California Farm Bureau. Christopher Reardon, vice president of policy advocacy for the bureau, said in a statement that it “supports efforts to improve public health,” but has questions about how the law will be implemented.

The Farm Bureau, he said, “will continue working with its agricultural coalition to advocate for science-based food classification standards and ensure that legislation supports farmers in adapting to changes.”

Inside the ban

So what will be banned?

It’s complicated.

First, to be considered ultraprocessed, food must contain one of several nonnatural substances spanning eight categories, among them emulsifiers, stabilizers, flavor enhancers and flavoring agents. Then, it must have high amounts of saturated fat, sodium or added sugar, or contain certain kinds of nonnutritive sweeteners.

Amanda Tejada loads a tray of chicken salad to be stored in the freezer at the Alhambra Unified central production kitchen.

(Carlin Stiehl / Los Angeles Times)

There are several carve-outs. For example, a food that would be considered ultraprocessed only because of the inclusion of salt or certain natural seasonings cannot be categorized as one. And other items cannot be considered ultraprocessed, including raw agricultural commodities.

Gabriel said he worked with the food and beverage industries to exempt certain items that made sense, such as minimally processed prepared foods, which include canned fruit and vegetables. There were talks, he said, with representatives of the dairy industry, the protein industry, and some that don’t even serve food in schools — such as makers of alcohol.

“For a lot of them, it was about, ‘As you define ultraprocessed foods, how are you doing that? How is that going to impact our product?’” he said.

It isn’t yet clear what foods will be deemed ultraprocessed foods “of concern,” or which will be classified as “restricted.” The state’s Department of Public Health will create these lists of foods by 2028, so that schools can prepare for the ban to take effect.

The department must weigh a variety of factors, among them whether the products include a warning label in another jurisdiction about “adverse health consequences,” and whether they contain a substance that, based “on reputable peer-reviewed scientific evidence,” is linked to “health harms or adverse health consequences” such as cancer and cardiovascular disease.

“That’s an inquiry that ought to be undertaken by California state scientists, not by legislators,” said Scott Faber, senior vice president of government affairs at the nonprofit Environmental Working Group, who testified in support of the legislation.

Andrew Vasquez prepares black bean and corn relish at Alhambra Unified’s central production kitchen.

(Carlin Stiehl / Los Angeles Times)

The law will put the onus on vendors, prohibiting them from selling the banned items to California school districts starting in 2032. But it isn’t yet clear how districts will respond to it.

Los Angeles Unified, the largest school meal provider in the state, declined to make its director of food services available for an interview.

William Fong, Alhambra Unified’s director of food and nutrition services, pointed out that his district already complies with U.S. Department of Agriculture standards for school food. Adhering to a new standard won’t be too difficult, he said, even if changes are required.

“There’s always a way we can substitute ... items in a recipe,” Fong said. “And we have time.”

Gabriel believes that vendors supplying food to school districts will comply with the law because California is a lucrative market for them. It could be as simple as swapping out an ingredient or two in a pepperoni pizza or corn dog.

And, he noted, about a billion meals will be served in California schools this year.

해당 법안은 학교는 학생의 건강을 해치거나 학습 능력을 저해할 수 있는 음식을 제공해서는 안 된다는 상식적 원칙에 기반한다.

뉴섬 주지사는 “캘리포니아는 오랫동안 워싱턴이나 다른 주를 기다리지 않고 아이들의 건강을 위해 앞장서 왔다”며 “이번 초가공식품 규제법은 모든 학생이 건강하고 맛있는 식사를 통해 성장할 수 있도록 보장하는 또 하나의 역사적 진전”이라고 밝혔다.

<캘리포니아에서 초가공식품을 학교 급식에서 단계적으로 퇴출하는 AB 1264 법안에 서명한 개빈 뉴섬 주지사(왼쪽)가 이 안을 발의한 제시 가브리엘 주하원의원과 함께 '진짜 음식을 아이들에게'에 대한 기자회견을 하고 있다. 출처 캘리포니아 주지사실>

법안을 발의한 가브리엘 의원은 “워싱턴이 무기력한 동안 캘리포니아는 초당적으로, 과학에 기반한 상식적인 접근으로 또다시 미국을 이끌고 있다”며 “이번 조치는 아이들이 유해한 화학첨가물이 아닌 ‘진짜 음식’을 먹을 수 있도록 하는 중요한 발걸음”이라고 강조했다.

AB 1264 법안은 뉴섬 주지사가 올해 초 서명한 행정명령과도 일치한다. 해당 명령은 초가공식품 및 건강에 해로운 식품 성분의 위험을 제한하기 위한 구체적 조치를 마련하도록 주 기관에 지시한 바 있다.

뉴섬 주지사는 이미 2023년과 2024년에 각각 AB 418, AB 2316 법안에 서명해 레드다이 3(red dye 3), 브로민화 식물성 오일(brominated vegetable oil) 등 발암 가능성, 면역체계 손상, 신경행동장애를 유발할 수 있는 화학첨가물 4종을 주 내 판매 금지 목록에 포함시켰다고 주지사실은 전했다.

또한 학교에서 이러한 첨가물이 들어간 식품을 판매하거나 제공하는 것을 금지했다고 덧붙였다.

캘리포니아는 전국 최초로 모든 TK~12(유치원~고등학교) 학생들에게 무료 급식을 제공하는 ‘유니버설 밀 프로그램(Universal Meals Program)’을 시행 중이며, 지역 농산물을 활용한 건강한 급식을 보급하고 있다.

주정부는 또, 2024년 식품 지원 프로그램 확대 법안을 통과시켜 저소득층 아동에게 식품 지원금(SUN Bucks)을 제공했다. 지난 여름, 400만 명 이상의 아동이 EBT 카드를 통해 1인당 120달러의 식품 보조금을 받았다.

보도자료에 따르면 뉴섬 주지사 재임 이후 캘리포니아는 전국에서 가장 엄격한 학생 건강 보호 기준을 유지하고 있고, 소다 음료는 K-12 전 학년에서 금지됐다. 카페인 음료 또한 제한된다. 학교는 모든 주식류 메뉴가 칼로리, 지방, 트랜스지방 기준을 충족해야만 판매할 수 있도록 의무화했다고 밝혔다.

한편, 연방 질병통제예방센터(CDC)에 따르면 2025년 기준 미국 청소년(12~19세)의 32.7%가 당뇨 전단계로 보고됐다. 전문가들은 건강한 식습관이 심혈관질환, 뇌졸중, 당뇨병 등 만성질환의 위험을 크게 낮춘다고 설명했다.

뉴섬 주지사는 이번 법 제정으로 캘리포니아는 학교 급식의 건강 기준을 한층 강화하며, 초가공식품의 유해성으로부터 학생들을 보호하는 선도적인 모델로 자리 잡게 됐다고 강조했다.

They were driven, in their endeavors, by stories from the state's own children suffering the scourge of antisemitism and discrimination—"When we hear what these kids and families have faced, we know we have to act," said Assemblymember Dawn Addis, whose sentiments were echoed in a statement. Acknowledging this collective effort, Governor Newsom stated, "Today, California is sending a strong and unambiguous message — hate has no place in our schools and will not be tolerated."

The introduction of AB 715 and SB 48 not only promises to combat bigotry but also weaves into the rich tapestry of California's ongoing efforts to defend its students against the rising tide of intolerance by championing inclusive education and robust hate crime prevention; these bills are kindred with previous legislative endeavors such as the Commission on the State of Hate, California vs. Hate reporting hotline, and the Governor’s Council on Holocaust and Genocide Education, they reaffirm the state's enduring commitment, as stated in the same announcement.
