<h2 class="wp-block-heading" id="3f1b6544-10a7-41dc-a3b3-95a0d6fcee1b">What is Red No. 3?</h2>
<p>Red No. 3 — <a data-id="32a8dced-1091-4577-be82-49f0cd00501f" href="https://www.fda.gov/industry/color-additives/fdc-red-no-3#:~:text=FD%26C%20Red%20No.%203%2C%20also,and%20icings%2C%20and%20ingested%20drugs." rel="noopener" target="_blank">also known as FD&C Red No. 3, erythrosine or Red 3</a> — is a synthetic dye that is <a data-id="32a8dced-1091-4577-be82-49f0cd00501f" href="https://wayback.archive-it.org/org-1137/20170406211659/https:/www.fda.gov/downloads/AdvisoryCommittees/CommitteesMeetingMaterials/FoodAdvisoryCommittee/UCM248549.pdf" rel="noopener" target="_blank">made from petroleum</a> and adds a “bright, cherry-red color” to the products it is added to.  </p>
<p>In 1990, the FDA banned Red No. 3 in cosmetics, but no law barred the synthetic dye from being added to numerous types of foods and drinks in the decades that followed.</p>
<div class="wp-block-ziff-davis-exco-video is-injected" data-exco-autoplay="0" data-exco-playlist-id="698e783ea04b8c612553f0cf" data-exco-sticky="1" data-exco-suppress-ads="0" data-exco-video-duration="0" data-exco-video-id="" data-exco-video-poster="" data-exco-video-src="" data-exco-video-title="" id="exco-video-block-698e783ea04b8c612553f0cf-3070398-4">
<p class="exco-video__eyebrow">More from CNET</p>
<div class="exco-video-player" id="exco-playlist-698e783ea04b8c612553f0cf-3070398-4">
</div>
</div>
<p>The FDA cited the <a data-id="7fc2c927-271c-40be-bac9-8f070762ea5e" href="https://www.fda.gov/about-fda/changes-science-law-and-regulatory-authorities/part-iii-drugs-and-foods-under-1938-act-and-its-amendments" rel="noopener" target="_blank">Delaney Clause</a> as its reasoning behind the ban, which “prohibits FDA authorization of a food additive or color additive if it has been found to induce cancer in humans or animals.”</p>
<p>Although studies did show a link to cancer in laboratory rats, a link between the dye and cancer in humans has not been found. </p>
<p>“While there are studies noting carcinogenicity in male rats, the FDA noted in their announcement that the hormonal mechanism through which the dye caused cancer in rats is specific to the animal and does not occur in humans,” Bryan Hitchcock, chief science and technology officer of the Institute of Food Technologists, told CNET. </p>
<p>Hitchcock added that the studies used large amounts of the dye, which is more than what the average human would consume when eating the foods that contain it. </p>
<p>“Studies testing Red No. 3 for human safety have done so at amounts well above the average amount of consumption, as noted by various global regulatory bodies,” he says. “The studies referenced by the FDA note that the rats were given roughly <a data-id="7c84214a-4810-4a40-bd31-4fb2f1081590" href="https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2025/01/16/2025-00830/color-additive-petition-from-center-for-science-in-the-public-interest-et-al-request-to-revoke-color" rel="noopener" target="_blank">200 times the likely maximum daily consumption of .25 mg/kg of body weight per day</a>.”</p>
<h2 class="wp-block-heading" id="378286cb-e8e5-435c-a789-10d7c77deff2">Foods that contain Red No. 3</h2>
<p>Here are 9 common types of foods that contain Red No. 3:</p>
<ul class="wp-block-list">
<li>Candy</li>
<li>Cupcakes</li>
<li>Cookies</li>
<li>Frozen desserts</li>
<li>Frostings</li>
<li>Icings</li>
<li>Certain Maraschino cherries</li>
<li>Certain processed meats and meat substitutes</li>
</ul>
<figure class="wp-block-image size-large"><img alt="An artistic close-up photo of red candy or gum spilling out of a package." class="wp-image-4513927" decoding="async" height="683" src="jgimg:9/85fd8be63494a3fc" width="1024"/><figcaption class="wp-element-caption"><p>Red No. 3 has previously been banned in other countries, including Australia. </p><span class="zd-image-credit">Ali Majdfar/Getty Images</span></figcaption></figure>
<p>Specific items that currently have Red No. 3 on their ingredient list are: </p>
<ul class="wp-block-list">
<li>Numerous types of Brach’s candy, including Classic Jelly Beans, Spiced Jelly Beans and Conversation Hearts</li>
<li>MorningStar Farms Plant-Based Bacon Strips</li>
<li>Good Humor Strawberry Shortcake Frozen Dessert Bars</li>
<li>Pez candy</li>
</ul>
<p>According to a <a data-id="939c43e0-c670-45d6-af94-22cc18e0361f" href="https://www.drugs.com/inactive/fd-c-red-no-3-247.html" rel="noopener" target="_blank">list compiled by Drugs.com</a>, some drugs that have Red No. 3 include: </p>
<ul class="wp-block-list">
<li>Acetaminophen</li>
<li>Doxycycline Monohydrate</li>
<li>Gabapentin</li>
<li>Vyvanse</li>
</ul>
<p>The <a data-id="cfc4b02b-60a3-42a0-9b54-725a7b0129bb" href="https://www.ewg.org/foodscores/ingredients/19151-RED3/search/" rel="noopener" target="_blank">Environmental Working Group has compiled a searchable database</a> of food products that use the now-banned dye. As of April 29, 2025, the site had collected 3,225 products that list Red No. 3 as an ingredient. </p>
<h2 class="wp-block-heading" id="a45973c5-05b0-4398-8b7e-765061cc8c85">When do companies need to remove Red No. 3 from products? </h2>
<p>Despite the ban, don’t expect to see the Red No. 3 ingredient disappear from ingredient lists too quickly. According to the FDA, companies have a couple of years to remove it from their products.</p>
<p>“Manufacturers who use FD&C Red No. 3 in food and ingested drugs will have until January 15, 2027, or January 18, 2028, respectively, to reformulate their products,” the <a data-id="e3300e2e-d5c5-4651-8b46-7013c44990a6" href="https://www.fda.gov/food/hfp-constituent-updates/fda-revoke-authorization-use-red-no-3-food-and-ingested-drugs" rel="noopener" target="_blank">FDA statement</a> reads. </p>
<h2 class="wp-block-heading" id="eb403974-895e-49fb-93c1-a0a39eb9d8cb">What will replace Red No. 3?</h2>
<figure class="wp-block-image size-large"><img alt="beets in a bowl on a gray countertop" class="wp-image-4508965" decoding="async" height="683" src="jgimg:9/06fe99e7370965cd" width="1024"/><figcaption class="wp-element-caption"><p>Red Dye No. 3 will soon be replaced by food coloring made from beets and other natural ingredients.</p><span class="zd-image-credit">istetiana/Getty Images</span></figcaption></figure>
<p><a data-id="b80e381c-bb0e-4f45-bac5-d0177cc33ffc" href="https://ddwcolor.com/about-givaudan-sense-colour/" rel="noopener" target="_blank">Givaudan Sense Colour</a>, a manufacturing company that creates natural food and drink colorings, highlighted <a data-id="b80e381c-bb0e-4f45-bac5-d0177cc33ffc" href="https://learn.ddwcolor.com/replacements-for-red-3/" rel="noopener" target="_blank">three possible alternatives to Red No. 3</a> — carmine, which is <a data-id="b80e381c-bb0e-4f45-bac5-d0177cc33ffc" href="https://iawpwellnesscoach.com/what-is-carmine/" rel="noopener" target="_blank">made from bugs</a>; betacyanins, found in beetroots; and anthocyanins, derived from <a data-id="b80e381c-bb0e-4f45-bac5-d0177cc33ffc" href="https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5613902/#:~:text=Anthocyanins%20responsible%20for%20the%20colors,a%20high%20level%20of%20anthocyanins." rel="noopener" target="_blank">fruits and vegetables</a>. </p>
<p>California Assembly member Jesse Gabriel told <a data-id="12380dbd-7586-4649-81e0-a3bdb484c423" href="https://www.nbcnews.com/news/us-news/food-safety-advocates-expect-smooth-transition-away-red-no-3-rcna187802" rel="noopener" target="_blank">NBC News</a> that although synthetic dyes can be cheaper than other alternatives, he does not believe that the Red No. 3 ban will cause prices of the affected products to change.</p>
<p>“We don’t expect the price of any food to increase,” he told the outlet.  </p>
<h2 class="wp-block-heading" id="67fae6df-a017-4fe2-8e2e-2de010d66ce0">New natural food dyes approved by the FDA</h2>
<p>In May of this year, the FDA approved three natural food dye colors. The first is Galdieria extract blue, which is derived from a species of red algae. <a data-id="a257ce87-71a0-483e-806f-e6fdde3334b9" href="https://www.fda.gov/news-events/press-announcements/fda-approves-three-food-colors-natural-sources" rel="noopener" target="_blank">The FDA says</a> this food color has been approved to be added to “nonalcoholic beverages and beverage bases, fruit drinks, fruit smoothies, fruit juices, vegetable juices, dairy-based smoothies, milk shakes and flavored milks, yogurt drinks, milk-based meal replacement and nutritional beverages, breakfast cereal coatings, hard candy, soft candy and chewing gum.” </p>
<p>Butterfly pea flower has also been approved to create blues, purples and greens. This popular natural food dye is already used in sports drinks, teas, alcoholic beverages and more. However, the new approval now allows the dye to be used in “ready-to-eat cereals, crackers, snack mixes, hard pretzels, plain potato chips (restructured or baked), plain corn chips, tortilla chips and multigrain chips.”</p>
<p>Lastly, the mineral, chlorine phosphate, and its white color has been approved for “ready-to-eat chicken products, white candy melts, doughnut sugar and sugar for coated candies,” according to the FDA. </p>
<h2 class="wp-block-heading" id="1e290c6d-b940-4c02-877a-f65690608d99">Will Red No. 40 be banned?</h2>
<p>The FDA has not yet banned <a data-id="d8b3adc2-15a6-4661-a300-30c6c0400e0b" href="https://www.webmd.com/diet/what-is-red-40" rel="noopener" target="_blank">red dye No. 40</a>, but discussions are ongoing. According to a <a data-id="d8b3adc2-15a6-4661-a300-30c6c0400e0b" href="https://www.fda.gov/news-events/press-announcements/hhs-fda-phase-out-petroleum-based-synthetic-dyes-nations-food-supply" rel="noopener" target="_blank">press release from April 22</a>, the FDA plans to eventually phase out all petroleum-based synthetic dyes, which include Red No. 40.</p>
<h2 class="wp-block-heading" id="beaa042e-ee10-4075-bf44-65679a5a190b">Are other syntethic food colorings safe? </h2>
<p>After the Red No. 3 ban, there are now eight approved color additives (but this may change under the current administration). They are FD&C Blue No. 1, FD&C Blue No. 2, FD&C Green No. 3, Orange B, Citrus Red No. 2, FD&C Red No. 40, FD&C Yellow No. 5 and FD&C Yellow No. 6. </p>
<p>Hitchcock says that so far, studies show that there is not a notable risk to consuming these dyes. </p>
<p>“While science tells us that there is little to no risk in consuming other synthetic dyes, it is important that we continue to monitor and evaluate food ingredient safety,” he says. “It is paramount that we continue to invest in more scientific research around the health of our foods to ensure safety and provide peace of mind for consumers.”</p>
<p>According to the FDA, the above dyes do not pose the same possible risks as Red No. 3, which is why they are still available for use in the US. But, some studies show possible links between certain dyes and potential health conditions. For example, some studies have linked Red 40 to hyperactivity, according to the <a data-id="4acb77d5-7f33-4e87-908f-4d8126b0c4a9" href="https://health.clevelandclinic.org/red-dye-40" rel="noopener" target="_blank">Cleveland Clinic</a>, but further studies are still needed to determine a direct link between the dye and the condition. </p>
<p>When asked about the safety of other food dyes, Hitchcock highlighted the need for transparency from the FDA, which he says the agency has been addressing. </p>
<p>“We believe there needs to be a clear framework for post-market review for food additive safety,” Hitchcock says. “The FDA is actively working to address this issue as seen in their <a data-id="cf467ea3-5ccb-41cd-8b4e-585915c9be1f" href="https://www.fda.gov/media/180942/download?attachment" rel="noopener" target="_blank">Development of an Enhanced Systematic Process for the FDA’s Post-Market Assessment of Chemicals in Food</a>. IFT believes that the FDA needs to bring forward a post-market assessment of chemical food safety that is transparent, scientifically grounded, constituent informed and timely.” </p>
<figure class="wp-block-image size-large"><img alt="A set of glass bottles filled with red soda, neatly arranged on a shelf." class="wp-image-4513928" decoding="async" height="768" src="jgimg:9/b5a356e13a01fbab" width="1024"/><figcaption class="wp-element-caption"><p>If a drink looks too red to be natural, it probably is.</p><span class="zd-image-credit">vlad.plus/Getty Images</span></figcaption></figure>
<h2 class="wp-block-heading" id="b06b91ff-5cc2-4d1f-a8fb-379c7b9120ad">Does food coloring have a taste?</h2>
<p>Most foods contain food coloring in such small amounts that you won’t notice a specific taste. However, some food coloring brands, types or certain colors (like red) may taste slightly bitter if a lot is used.</p>
<h2 class="wp-block-heading" id="aad00078-bc15-45b3-97ed-5c8b7a72b9a5">The bottom line on Red No. 3</h2>
<p>Red No. 3 has been fully banned in the US, but will continue to be used in food for the next two years as manufacturers work to change their recipes. However, some manufacturers are making changes much more quickly than that. </p>
<p>In an email to <a data-id="826e6fab-4e83-47f0-bde6-b508027bbb7b" href="https://www.cbsnews.com/news/red-3-fda-ban-food-drug-brands/" rel="noopener" target="_blank">CBS News</a>, Keurig Dr Pepper said that a “new formula” for Yoo-hoo Strawberry Flavored Drink, which is currently made with Red No. 3 to help achieve its color, “will be on shelves before the end of the year.”</p>

California Rank & File Teachers Say "Vote NO on AB 715"

Marcy Winograd

In a desperate maneuver to censor classrooms, the California Legislative Jewish Caucus (LJC) aims to amend an old bill that once rewritten is sure to instill fear in the hearts of school board members and teachers when students dare to whisper the words “Free Palestine.”

Taking a page out of Trump’s playbook, State Senator Wiener (D-SF), State Assembly members Jesse Gabriel (D-SFV), Rick Chavez-Zbur (D-Santa Monica), Dawn Addis (D-Morro Bay) and the chairs of the state’s diversity (Black, Latino, AAPI) caucuses are introducing AB 715 to ramp up the Uniform Complaint Procedures in the state education code to punish teachers, school board members and teacher trainers accused of antisemitism for teaching about Israel’s genocide in Gaza. 

The proposed legislation, according to press reports, would also establish a state antisemitism czar to police school discussion of Israel and Palestine. News of the bill comes on Mother’s Day, a few days after California’s Jewish anti-Zionist educators submitted a letter to the Assembly Education Committee in opposition to any anti-Palestine bill that would vilify teachers for discussing the horror students are witnessing on their cell phones. 

Jesse Gabriel, Scott Wiener, and Donald Trump

Jewish Educators Addressing Actual Antisemitism (JEAAAN) wrote:

“...we are concerned about our ability, and especially our BIPOC colleagues’ ability to teach without falsely being labeled “antisemites”, getting unjustly censored, attacked, doxxed, and potentially even losing careers and livelihoods under these false claims of antisemitism, which are instead designed to protect Israel’s human rights crimes and violations.”

With a last-minute submission of a newly amended AB 715, the lawmakers may hope to skip public scrutiny and wipe the slate clean of letters in opposition to Palestinian censorship. Chairs of the California diversity caucuses: Senator Akilah Weber Pierson, (D-San Diego) Black Caucus; Senator Lena Gonzalez (D-Long Beach) Latino Caucus; Assemblymember Mike Fong (D-Alhambra) AAPI Caucus, have, according to the LJC, all signed on to AB 715 as "principal co-authors," which begs the question why these caucus chairs would do the bidding of the California Legislative Jewish Caucus. This is the same caucus that once posted an Israeli flag on its state web portal, spent months lobbying unsuccessfully to establish an Attorney General’s list of Israel boycotters and now promotes the Anti-Defamation League’s contemporary antisemitism curriculum that conflates antisemitism with anti-Zionism.

RootsAction, a social justice organization, was first out of the gate with a one-click message to state legislators. The message implied the diversity caucus chairs might want to please Wiener and Gabriel, the LJC co-chairs who also chair the budget committees in the assembly and state senate and can influence whether Ethnic Studies receives funding.

The RootsAction alert reads, “Fully funding ethnic studies is essential, but this rumored backroom deal is terrible for teachers, students, and all Californians.”

Al Muratsuchi (D-Torrance), chair of the Assembly Education Committee and a candidate for State Superintendent of Instruction, is expected to curry favor with the LJC by waiving notice requirements to conduct a hearing on the newly amended bill on Wednesday, May 14th.

Muratsuchi constituents Melanie Cohen and Reggie Wong are urging the Chair of the Assembly Education Committee to vote no in committee and on the floor on AB 715. Cohen, however, is not hopeful. “Muratsuchi always toes the middle of the road line from the state Democratic Party.” Said Wong, “Muratsuchi should be focusing on the white supremacists in his district, not false definitions of antisemitism to target teachers and public education.”

A newly amended AB 715 comes in the face of widespread opposition from teacher unions–CTA, UTLA, CFT– to Zbur’s previous bill, AB 1468, that would have limited classroom Ethnic Studies lessons to “domestic” issues and discouraged conversation about the causes of ethnic marginalization. Ethnic Studies scholars called the bill racist in its attempt to dumb down curriculum. One of AB 1468’s coauthors, Senator Josh Becker (D-Menlo Park), was recorded on a Jewish Public Affairs Committee (JPAC) webinar on AB 1468 asserting “There was no Palestine” before the UN created Israel.

Facing mounting opposition, Zbur and the Legislative Jewish Caucus decided, without admitting defeat, to assign AB 1468 to the waste bin, and amend Zbur’s fossilized attorney bill first introduced in February, 2024.

If the amended AB 715 passes out of committee with at least five of a possible eight votes, the bill could hit the floor of the assembly as soon as Thursday, May15th, before assembly members and staff have time to read and evaluate the proposed legislation. Critics of the LJC suspect the lawmakers will continue to amend AB 715 to rely on the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance (IHRA) definition and examples of antisemitism in leveling accusations against teachers. Seven of the eleven IHRA examples center Israel, with one example of so-called antisemitism reading, “Denying the Jewish people their right to self-determination, such as, by claiming that the existence of a State of Israel is a racist endeavor.”

In opposition to AB 715, Jewish Voice for Peace (JVP)-Action acknowledges that antisemitism –bigotry and persecution of Jews –is a problem but notes antisemitism largely stems from white supremacy, similar to other forms of racism and discrimination.

The JVP-Action statement reads, “At a time when MAGA white supremacists and nationalists are sowing confusion and promoting antisemitism, Islamophobia, and racism, misstating what antisemitism is harms all of our work for justice and endangers our communities. Opposition to the political movement of Zionism and/or the policies of the state of Israel is no different from criticism of any other political ideology or policies of any other nation-state.”

The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive.

The Trump factor in the state budget

By ERIC HE, BLAKE JONES and DUSTIN GARDINER

THE BUZZ: ‘TRUMP SLUMP’ — Gov. Gavin Newsom and other California Democrats have been quick to blame this year’s anticipated budget woes on the blanket tariffs President Donald Trump has imposed and his administration’s funding cuts to safety net programs.

Newsom has taken to calling the broader economic damage a “Trump slump.” Senate Pro Tem Mike McGuire wished “good luck to anyone trying to predict what President Trump will have done to our federal budget and economy by September.” And a spokesperson for Assembly Speaker Robert Rivas said lawmakers could be forced to rejigger their budget in the fall given “the chaotic and punitive budget realities coming from Washington.”

“The whole ballgame is in Washington, D.C.,” Assembly Budget Chair Jesse Gabriel said.

Newsom presumably will keep up with the verbal assaults later this week when he is expected to announce that the state’s budget has plunged from roughly balanced into a deficit of at least $10 billion.

Along with offering the chance to toss a few more barbs at the president — a pastime of sorts for Newsom — blaming the Trump administration’s stop-and-go trade policy for battering California’s budget offers a convenient way for the governor to insulate himself and the Democratic Party from political blowback over an 11-figure shortfall.

And it’s not just a talking point.

The nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office, which critiques Newsom’s budget proposals every year, noted that Trump administration’s actions on tariffs and elsewhere have already pummeled consumer sentiment and narrowed the path for California’s economy to grow. Also concerning is the drop in stock prices since Trump launched his tariff campaign, since market declines have an outsized impact on state revenues because California’s tax structure is heavily reliant on capital gains.

“Things have been pushed and pushed in the wrong direction, principally,” Department of Finance spokesperson H.D. Palmer said, “by the effects that the tariffs are having.”

California has been flush with cash of late, pulling in $4.4 billion more this fiscal year than Finance projected when it unveiled a small surplus in January. But spending has increased as well, fueled in part by a Medi-Cal budget ballooning from growing caseloads of older Californians and immigrants living in the country illegally, among other demands.

Unlike in January, Finance will incorporate the impact of tariffs into its estimates of future revenue — meaning the state will plan on having less money to cover the increasing costs.

Republican state Sen. Roger Niello, the vice chair of the Senate Budget Committee who never misses a chance to accuse Democrats of over-spending, acknowledged that tariffs — which he opposes — may hurt the state’s revenues and that “there are certainly issues at the federal level that are having an effect.” But he said Newsom is “always overly optimistic” in his budget projections, pointing to the Medi-Cal shortfall and a minimum wage increase for health care workers that took effect last year.

“Frankly, just those two items add up to about $10 billion,” Niello said. “So we have built into the budget some of our very own problems.”

Casting the blame for the budget deficit on Trump is all well and good, but Jeff Freitas, president of the California Federation of Teachers, said how Newsom addresses the shortfall is on him. Freitas wants the governor to raise taxes on the wealthy to backfill federal cuts, and reverse an 8 percent slash to both the University of California and California State University systems that he proposed in January.

“If you want to be the shadow president and be opposed to what’s happening at the national level, you can’t hit your university system,” Freitas said.

John Affeldt, managing attorney at the public interest law firm Public Advocates, sounded a similar note. He said that while Newsom has “a lot of maneuverability” to “point the finger elsewhere” for the state’s upcoming budget woes, “The question is, given these external factors that have been imposed on him, what is he going to do with it? California Lawmaker Seeks to Ban Glock Handgun Rather Than Going After Criminals – California Globe

A California bill to ban the sale of handguns that can be converted from semi-automatic to automatic is scheduled to be heard soon in the crucial Assembly Appropriations Committee.

Assembly Bill 1127, authored by Assemblyman Jesse Gabriel (D-Encino), would specifically prohibit a licensed firearms dealer to sell, offer for sale, exchange, give, transfer, or deliver any semiautomatic machinegun-convertible pistol. The bill would define “machinegun-convertible pistol” as any semiautomatic pistol with a cruciform trigger bar that can be readily converted by hand or with common household tools into a machinegun by the installation or attachment of a pistol converter, or any device or instrument that, when installed in or attached to the rear of the slide of a semiautomatic pistol, replaces the backplate and interferes with the trigger mechanism and thereby enables the pistol to shoot automatically more than one shot by a single function of the trigger. 

AB 1127 would also make a violation of these provisions punishable by a fine, a 2nd violation punishable by a fine that may result in a suspension or revocation of the dealer’s license and removal from certain centralized lists maintained by the Department of Justice, and a 3rd violation punishable as a misdemeanor that shall result in the revocation of the dealer’s license and removal from certain centralized lists.

Assemblyman Gabriel wrote the bill to help reduce the number of mass shootings and shooting incidents. Specifically, he noted that some handguns, like Glocks, could be easily converted to fully automatic usage, thus necessitating the increased ban on handguns.

“AB 1127 is a common-sense bill to hold the firearm industry accountable for their failure to prevent conversion of their guns to dangerous automatic weapons,” said Assemblyman Gabriel. “The firearm industry has known for decades about a vulnerability in some designs rendering them readily convertible into automatic weapons. This bill is focused on the industry’s lack of action to prevent conversion and will ensure we are doing everything we possibly can to protect our communities from mass shootings.”

Gun control groups, who are in support of the bill, further pointed out that Glocks and similar weapons altered to fire automatically have been used in many high profile shootings, including the 2022 K Street shooting in Sacramento.

“No novice should be able to convert their pistol into a DIY machine gun with just a 3D printer and a screwdriver within minutes,” added Everytown for Gun Safety senior firearms analyst Greg Lickenbrock. “Modified pistols equipped with Glock switches are exceptionally deadly weapons that have become a weapon of choice for criminals and are increasingly turning up at crime scenes in California and across the country. Glock and other copycat companies must take action to ensure their pistols are not so easily susceptible to these devices.” 

However, opponents of AB 1127 have said that the bill would only take away weapons that have conversely saved lives through civilian and police use, as well as chipping away at the Second Amendment by removing more types of guns that can legally be sold in California. Others also pointed out that focus should be on going after criminals themselves rather than gun owners and dealers.

“Once again ASM Gabriel leads a cast of anti Second Amendment advocates in banning the most popular handgun in the country for personal protection,” said California Rifle and Pistol Association (CRPA) Legislative Director Rick Travis to the Globe Wednesday. “In the name of public safety ASM Gabriel seeks to ban the very firearm that has saved thousands of lives by seeking to ban something that is already a felony in the status quo. Don’t be fooled, he is seeking to ban one firearm at a time to dismantle our constitutional rights. When will we ever see ASM Gabriel go after the criminals instead of law abiding citizens?”

“What the state of California needs to do is they need to focus on the criminal element, increasing the punishments for the misuse of any firearms or modifying any gun into a configuration,” added Gun Owners of California President Sam Paredes. ”The bill will only criminalize lawful gun dealers and owners. It is a ban, because anyone else in the future who wants to purchase a Glock will not be allowed to do so without committing an egregious crime.”

While opposition has been strong, lawmakers, so far, have been deciding on the issue strictly across party lines, ignoring the potential second amendment lawsuits that the passage of AB 1127 could bring. Both of the Assembly Committee votes last month proved to be highly polarized, with the Assembly Judiciary Committee vote coming to a 9-2 vote with one abstention, split between Republicans and Democrats.

However, as the bill moves up this month, there may be some roadblocks ahead. The more finicky Senate could pose a challenge to the bill, as could growing worry that courts could stop AB 1127 once it is law because of it being unconstitutional. Other firearms bills by Assemblyman Gabriel are currently stuck in the courts over constitutionality issues.

“You may recall Asm. Gabriel as the author of the 11% excise tax that CRPA is challenging in court as you read this,” said the CRPA earlier this month. “Clearly, he’s undaunted by the fact that his bills don’t pass constitutional muster.”

AB 1127 is currently scheduled to be heard next in the Assembly Appropriations Committee later this month.

A new bill has been proposed to ban all ultra-processed foods from schools, and Mendez Middle School in Santa Ana is already ahead of the legislation.

“If we’re going to invest in anything as a society, it should be children’s health, and there’s no better way to do that than through food,” said Goddard.

Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel proposed the new bill to reduce all ultra-processed foods from California schools by 2032.

“Our public schools should not be serving students ultra-processed food products filled with chemical additives that can harm their physical and mental health,” said Gabriel on his website. “Democrats and Republicans are joining forces to prioritize the health and safety of our children and we are proud to be leading the nation with a bipartisan, science-based approach.”

According to the Environmental Working Group, ultra-processed foods have been linked to health problems like cancer, cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes, a variety of metabolic disorders, reproductive issues, and have been shown to cause neurobehavioral harm.

California bill would ban one of nation’s most popular handguns

Lauren Keenan Lauren Keenan was an anchor and reporter for Straight Arrow News.

California lawmakers will have a hearing Wednesday, May 7, on a recently introduced a bill that would ban certain machine gun-convertible pistols in the state. While gun rights advocates are calling the legislation the “Glock ban bill” because Glock manufactures popular pistols that can be converted into an automatic weapon using an attachment, gun control advocates are lauding the move as a necessary step to prevent mass shootings.

California’s Assembly Bill 1127, introduced by Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel, would prohibit a licensed firearms seller from dealing in any semiautomatic pistol that is easily “converted by hand or with common household tools” into a machine gun.

After being amended, the bill awaits another hearing in the Assembly Appropriations Committee scheduled for Wednesday.

Gabriel introduced the bill three years after six people were killed and another 12 were wounded during a Sacramento shooting in which more than 100 rounds were fired from Glocks equipped with switch technology.

How does a Glock switch work?

Glock switch technology turns semi-automatic pistols into fully automatic firearms. It’s already against federal law to own a machine gun without prior approval from, and registration with, the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives.

However, even with federal permission, California bans fully-automatic firearms. California law also states that the sale of pistol switches is illegal. The bill does not apply to law enforcement officers, military members or current owners of the weapons.

Support from gun control groups

In a press release, gun control advocacy group Everytown for Gun Safety lauded the legislation, saying that Glock has long been aware that its firearms can be turned into illegal machine guns “with just a screwdriver and a $25 switch,” but “refused” to address the issue.

“With this new measure,” Everytown for Gun Safety writes, “California lawmakers are telling Glock and its copycats, loudly and clearly, that if they fail to take reasonable steps to fix this problem to prevent these illegal conversions, they will be forced to stop selling their firearms in California.”

Opposition from gun rights advocates

Meanwhile, the National Association for Gun Rights opposes the measure, and accused California of “pushing rapidly towards a total ban of Glock pistols.”

“The most popular firearm in the country. If you think there is a line they will not cross, think again,” the group posted on X.

Gun Owners of California President Sam Paredes told KXTV that should the bill become law, gun rights groups will immediately file legal challenges.

Glock has not yet responded to the proposed legislation.

Is Newsom ready to take California’s budget rules to the ballot?

By EMILY SCHULTHEIS and WILL MCCARTHY

BUDGET BALLOT MOMENTUM? — A year ago, after his political operation polled voters on whether they supported amending the state constitution to loosen budgeting constraints, Gov. Gavin Newsom declared that “we’ve got work to do” to convince them those changes are necessary.

Newsom may find his on-again-off-again nemesis Donald Trump is doing the work for him. The federal-level economic turmoil caused by Trump’s multifront trade war will likely lead the governor to update his budget proposal later this month to show a projected shortfall. That could give a boost to a pair of potential constitutional amendments that Newsom and other supporters say would give the state new tools to weather financial storms.

“There’s been more energy and momentum around thinking about some structural changes that could help to address those challenges,” said Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel, who chairs the Budget Committee.

The first proposal, making its way through the Legislature with Democratic sponsors as ACA 1, would allow state officials to allocate more money to the state’s rainy-day fund in years when the state has a budget surplus, while lifting the so-called Gann limit on government spending.

As part of the small-government drive that inspired the passage of Proposition 13 in 1978, voters the next year approved Proposition 4, which caps spending in perpetuity at then-current levels (while adjusting for inflation and population). If revenue exceeds that spending level, half of the extra funds must be returned to taxpayers and the other half put toward education. In 2014, voters approved Prop 2, which set the maximum amount that can be allocated to the rainy-day fund as 10 percent of the general fund proceeds of taxes.

Newsom and other Democrats have argued that raising the rainy-day fund cap and amending the Gann limit will help cushion California from the massive fluctuations in revenue that result from the state’s progressive tax laws. (As revisions of previous constitutional amendments, these budget- and revenue-related questions need to be resolved at the ballot box.)

“It’s very suboptimal, from a public policy perspective and from a budgetary perspective, to have these wild swings in revenue,” said Gabriel.

Others are looking to bolster the state’s finances by focusing on revenue. Backers of an existing tax on high earners, established by 2012’s Proposition 30 and extended by 2016’s Prop 55, are considering putting it before voters for another extension in 2026. The tax is set to expire in 2030, meaning its supporters are deciding whether to pull the trigger this year or hold off for a (potentially) more favorable electorate in 2028.

“Proponents seeking additional revenue face an incredibly high bar in 2026 to demonstrate need, efficacy and that their measures won’t hit voters’ wallets,” veteran ballot-measure consultant Ned Wigglesworth told Playbook. “A ballot measure’s impact on family finances is always a concern for voters, but the current anxiety and stress around cost of living and economic issues make this cycle more fraught.”

The Assembly Budget Committee is set to hear proposals related to the rainy-day fund in a hearing on Wednesday, which could give an early indication as to lawmakers’ interest in pushing the issue to the ballot. Trump’s trade policy and the attendant market convulsions are making it hard for anyone to anticipate where the economy is likely to be next November.

“Part of the challenge for everybody,” said Gabriel, “is that it feels like things can change in Washington four times before noon.”

Welcome to Ballot Measure Weekly, a special edition of Playbook PM focused on California’s lively realm of ballot measure campaigns. Drop us a line at eschultheis@politico.com and wmccarthy@politico.com, or find us on X — @emilyrs and @wrmccart.

A highly subjective ranking of the ballot measures — past and future, certain and possible — getting our attention this week.

1. Measure A (San Jose): Officials in this Bay Area city will find out how much patience voters have to face their third school funding-related measure in six months. Measure A would extend an existing parcel tax to bring in $5 million per year for academic programs and teacher-retention efforts, although tomorrow’s mail-only special election could cost nearly half that to administer.

2. Affordable housing bond (2026?): The Assembly’s Appropriations Committee last week sent Buffy Wicks’ proposed $10 billion affordable housing bond to the suspense file. That leaves AB 736’s fate for this session to be decided later this month alongside those of other pricey proposals.

3. Voter ID (Shasta County, 2026?): Backers of a proposed charter amendment to reshape voting procedures in this remote northern county, including requiring voter ID and announcing election results on Election Day, have begun gathering signatures after county officials unsuccessfully sought to disqualify it earlier this spring.

4. Homelessness funding (2026?): Assemblymember Corey Jackson’s proposed constitutional amendment to require five percent of the state’s general fund be spent on homelessness and affordable housing programs was referred to the Appropriations Committee, where its high cost will come under scrutiny.

5. Measure E (Ross Valley School District, Marin County): A local anti-tax group called the Coalition of Sensible Taxpayers is hoping tomorrow to defeat a 52-cent per-square foot parcel tax that would raise an estimated $7.8 million annually for teacher pay and educational programs. The district claims it has the lowest starting salaries in all of Marin County and is losing teachers to better-paying jobs in neighboring districts.

6. Measure M (California Pines, Modoc County): The 300-odd residents of the largest subdivision in California vote tomorrow on whether to triple their parcel-tax bill for fire response (from $25 to $75). We’re still hoping for last-minute campaign ads from Erik Estrada.

7. Measure N (California Pines, Modoc County): A companion measure on tomorrow’s special-election ballot, to increase the subdivision’s parcel tax for power and wastewater systems from $66 to $116, gives us one more chance to link to the Erik Estrada ads.

Ohio voters will weigh in tomorrow on a constitutional amendment to issue $2.5 billion in bonds for local infrastructure projects … Lawmakers in Tennessee certified a measure for the November 2026 ballot that would remove the right to pre-trial bail for those accused of committing certain felonies …

A group backing a 2026 constitutional amendment effort to expand Medicaid in Florida is suing the state over a law Gov. Ron DeSantis recently signed that tightens the signature-gathering requirements to qualify citizen-led measures for the ballot … Missouri’s senate is considering a constitutional amendment that would undo many of the abortion protections voters enacted at the ballot last fall, arguing that the measure passed because it was misleading …

And Elon Musk won his first vote by a Kim Jong Il-like margin, as an unincorporated part of Cameron County, Texas, that is home to SpaceX’s launch facilities, approved a proposal to incorporate as the town of Starbase with 97.25 percent of the vote. You can read Will’s dispatch from the newly incorporated Muskville for POLITICO Magazine here.

Spotlighting the legislative wrangling over bills that could lead to 2026 ballot measures.

BONDS AWAY (AB 48): The state borrowed $10 billion to fund K-12 school construction and upgrades with last November’s Prop 2. Assemblymember David Alvarez wants to do something similar for public colleges and universities, with one major difference: His AB 48 would also include provisions for building student housing.

In a hearing of the Assembly Housing and Community Development Committee, Alvarez argued it’s a crucial need in a state where many college kids lack stable housing and some are proposing that students be allowed to sleep in their cars. The bill passed the committee by a vote of 9-1, but even some of those who support the proposal’s aims asked for more specificity about the bond’s total cost and how that would be allocated.

Assemblymember Ash Kalra asked “how much of it will go to actual housing versus other kinds of infrastructure needs,” noting that California’s public universities have “almost unlimited” needs for infrastructure investments. Alvarez said he is speaking with University of California and California State University officials about their needs and balancing those with how much bond borrowing the state can afford to take on.

AB 48 heads to the Appropriations Committee next.

CANNABIS ALIGNED: An effort to overhaul California’s decade-old laws regulating marijuana sales appear to be dead for 2026.

“We’re going to extend our timeline,” Nina Parks, a veteran industry consultant who had organized the coalition of small business owners, said last week. “Trying to push it for next year was very ambitious.”

Her group, Cannabis Aligned, had intended to ask voters to repeal and replace Proposition 64, a 2016 initiative that legalized recreational marijuana in the state for the first time while imposing taxes on retail sales and cultivation. Parks spent months leading Zoom-based strategy sessions with business owners that she promoted with can-do Instagram posts, but never filed paperwork with the secretary of state.

The growing coalition reached a consensus that it should delay its deliberations, according to Parks, to let key regulatory issues play out in the coming months before reassessing its path to the ballot. On July 1, the tax rate for cannabis will rise from 15 percent to 19 percent, raising prices in a way that drives buyers toward the illegal market. In Los Angeles, industry groups are pushing the city council to pass a “cannabis equity and market stabilization act” that would shut down illegal shops and provide retroactive tax credits to businesses.

Parks believes those developments could further incentivize legal cannabis businesses to fund a campaign to cut taxes and streamline regulations via the ballot. While she says the coalition plans to continue with regular coalition meetings and viability polling, it is likely that Cannabis Aligned will file an initiative in the coming months.

“This was to get the industry excited and galvanized again,” Parks said. “The realistic timeline is 2028.”

Cannabis Aligned is survived by other groups that hope to see California voters change the way marijuana is bought and sold, including a veterans’ group known as Weed for Warriors.

DIETARY ACRYLAMIDE: Proposition 65 may be California’s most-ubiquitous ballot measure, thanks to the labels the 1986 initiative placed on everyday products warning of potential carcinogens. But the presence of one chemical should no longer trigger warnings, a federal court ruled last week.

Acrylamide is a chemical used in drinking water treatment, and can also form naturally in certain foods — including potatoes and grains — during the cooking process. It was added to the list of approximately 900 chemicals covered by Prop 65 after studies showed it produced cancer in laboratory mice.

The California Chamber of Commerce first filed suit against the state in 2019, arguing it violated the First Amendment to require that businesses disseminate “false or misleading speech” about a chemical never clearly linked to cancer in human beings. (The FDA says “it’s not clear exactly what risk” it poses, although the agency recommends trying to reduce exposure.)

A federal district court granted a preliminary injunction for Prop 65 warnings on acrylamide in 2021, but the nonprofit Council for Education and Research on Toxics quickly appealed the decision. The Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals upheld the injunction in 2022, and a judge made it permanent on Friday after concluding that the warnings were “misleading and controversial.” (The state has given no indication about whether it intends to appeal.)

CalChamber President and CEO Jennifer Barrera said in a statement that the ruling “not only protects businesses from enforcement actions based on these warnings, but also upholds the principle that government-mandated disclosures must be factually accurate and not misleading.”

… GROVER BEACH: The former mayor of an upper-middle-class beach community believes its government is rife with corruption. The best way to fix it, according to her, is to have more Grover Beach officials owe their jobs to voters than to politicians.

Next year, the approximately 12,000 residents of this Central Coast city will likely be asked to convert the jobs of city clerk and city attorney from appointed positions, chosen by city council, to elected offices. The measures’ top booster argues that the current arrangement — which prioritizes having government staff aligned with small-town leadership — has created something of a deep state that opposes the will of voters.

“I’m not a conspiracy theorist, I never have been,” said Debbie Peterson, a self-described lifelong Democrat who resigned from office in 2019 to (quite literally) write the book on her city’s corruption. “It has just been going on so long that people don’t see it.”

Last year, Peterson led an effort to recall two council members and her mayoral successor due to their support of a water project that she believed was evidence of their corruption and disconnect with voters. Only one of her recall petitions actually led to a vote — the council member, Daniel Rushing, was ultimately recalled — but Peterson clashed with the city clerk during the process.

Soon after, Peterson began another petition drive, this time to turn the clerk’s office into an elected post. Just last month, she decided to broaden her ambitions, drafting a parallel initiative that would make the city attorney position elected, too.

The current mayor, Kassi Dee, says both of the ballot measures are unnecessary and will prove costly for a city that usually hires its attorney on a contract basis and would pay more to fill an elected position in an ongoing way.

Besides, she argues, her predecessor’s allegations just promote conflict between staff and city council. Dee says she has never observed any corruption within city government, let alone of the kind that would require revising the charter.

California Now Looking to Ban Most Popular Handgun Model on Planet

By Tom Knighton | 12:30 PM | May 03, 2025

When I decided I needed a new carry gun, there were a number of factors I considered. My CZ-75B is a fantastic firearm, but it's heavy and there aren't options for things like lights and such. Plus, magazines aren't exactly plentiful.

I went with a Glock 19 because it met my criteria at the time, and I'm pleased with it. It's nothing fancy, but I know that anywhere I look for a holster, a light, or aftermarket upgrades, I'll probably be able to get it because the guns are just so damn common. A company would have to be stupid not to offer something for that firearm.

Despite these firearms being so common, though, California is looking to ban them.

GLOCK, one of the most popular gun manufacturers, faces a rocky future in California as the state legislature considers banning guns that could be easily converted to machine guns

Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel authored AB 1127 to help eliminate gun violence and mass shootings, which would ban the sale of semiautomatic pistols that could be easily converted with an attachment to a fully automatic weapon.

"AB 1127 is a common-sense bill to hold the firearm industry accountable for their failure to prevent conversion of their guns to dangerous automatic weapons. The firearm industry has known for decades about a vulnerability in some designs rendering them readily convertible into automatic weapons. This bill is focused on the industry’s lack of action to prevent conversion and will ensure we are doing everything we possibly can to protect our communities from mass shootings," Assemblymember Gabriel said in a statement to ABC10.

The effort comes after the converted weapons were used in several mass shootings, including the 2022 Sacramento K Street shooting.

It is already federally illegal to own machine guns and the sale of pistol switches is already prohibited in California. Still, advocates say they can be easily brought into the state or made illegally through processes like 3-D printing.

“Ultimately, we need the manufacturers of these easily convertible pistols to act responsibly and change their design, and they shouldn’t be allowed to sell in California until they do so,” said Krystal Lopilato, the director for public policy for Everytown for Gun Safety, at a committee hearing.

The devices used to convert these guns are illegal at the federal level. Putting one on your gun is illegal at the federal level.

Despite this, full-auto switches keep showing up at crime scenes, particularly in places like California.

If gun control worked, this would be a non-issue. It doesn't, though, and so now they want Glock to change a time-tested, proven design or be prohibited in the Golden State.

This is a big issue because while I might disagree with the phrase, the courts have long held that you cannot ban guns "in common use." I fail to see how Glocks won't fall into that category. I'm sure the Ninth Circuit can figure a way, of course, but damned if I can.

Sure, this is a brand, not a category, so maybe that's the approach they'll take.

However, while it's clear they understand that some of these switches come in from out of state, it's ridiculous that they don't understand that Glocks will just come in illegally from out of state. Glock won't be selling them to the bad guys through California gun stores, but I hate to break it to them, they're not doing that now. These are generally stolen guns.

So this will do nothing except to punish Glock and would-be Glock buyers for something Glock never did.

I swear, I can't imagine why anyone would move to California.

Tom Knighton is a Navy veteran, a former newspaperman, a novelist, and a blogger and lifetime shooter. He lives with his family in Southwest Georgia. He also puts out a daily newsletter of non-Second Amendment stories at https://tomknighton.substack.com/ and on YouTube.

Switch technology, a small device allowing a semiautomatic pistol to fire automatically, is also called a “Glock switch.”

Under the bill, law enforcement and military personnel would be exempt from the ban and could still purchase the pistols.

LOSE-LOSE: A freshman Democrat today threw gasoline on an already smoldering sex-trafficking dumpster fire — forcing Assembly Speaker Robert Rivas to very publicly put it out on the body’s floor.

After Maggy Krell couldn’t get her Public Safety Committee colleagues on board with a proposal to add 16- and 17-year-olds to a child solicitation law, the state lawmaker joined with Republicans to take the provision to the Assembly floor and force the entire body to consider it.

Her move — defying Rivas and Public Safety Chair Nick Schultz — sent Democrats into crisis-management mode and handed GOP lawmakers the chance to assert the moral high ground (and gather plenty of campaign ad fodder) while slamming Dems as lacking character.

“It’s our chance to choose the kids of California, to save them,” said Assemblymember David Tangipa, a Fresno Republican.

After a leadership huddle that lasted more than an hour, Rivas responded by taking Krell’s name off the bill, giving it to Schultz and moderate Sacramento Democrat Stephanie Nguyen. Democratic leaders also added language stating their “intent” to draft the “strongest laws to protect 16- and 17-year-old victims.”

Lawmakers approved the changes on a mostly party-line vote, and the bill now heads to the Assembly Appropriations Committee for further amendments.

But Democrats made their legislative moves from a defensive crouch, once again pressured into explaining that, yes, they are against trafficking and, yes, there are existing laws to protect minors approached for sex. Those who object to including older teens in the soliciting law have expressed hesitations about enacting harsh penalties in a blanket manner, especially as the state moves in a conservative direction on crime.

Schultz told reporters his concern is that Krell’s proposal would treat “an 18-year-old exactly the same as a 50-year-old trafficker of children.”

“I’m not saying that one should have a consequence and the other should not,” he said. “But it’s imperative that the law be just and that we account for differences in circumstance for each case.”

Krell — a former prosecutor who’s dedicated much of her professional life to fighting sex trafficking — said she was fine with the bill getting taken away from her, as long as it takes older teens into consideration. She ended up voting against the amendments.

“I don’t care whether my name is on the bill, but I would happily support it if it includes protections for 16- and 17-year-olds, if it treats them as victims, because they truly are,” Krell said on the floor. “If it recognizes the fights that survivors have led for decades for the basic understanding that if you’re 17 years old on a street corner, and an old man comes up and purchases you for sex, that’s rape.”

Following the floor session, Rivas and Schultz blamed Krell for the blowup, saying they offered her the choice of shelving her bill for a year or accepting the older teen carveout. When Krell took the latter option, they said, the two of them believed she had accepted a deal — and then went on to shred it.

Now, the leaders’ plan is to craft what they see as a more nuanced piece of legislation. Rivas said he had not spoken to Gov. Gavin Newsom about the situation. The governor’s office earlier in the week issued a statement supporting Krell’s efforts.

When asked whether Krell will face consequences for her legislative maneuvering, Rivas dodged the question.

“I respect all of our colleagues,” he said, “and we’re all very passionate about the work we have to do.”

Nicole Nixon

**MAHA MEETS CALIFORNIA CRUNCHY**

It’s not a new type of fusion sushi roll — instead, call it a recipe for bipartisanship.

Two years after California began taking on synthetic food dyes and additives, **Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.** this week announced the **FDA** would phase out several of the same dyes beginning next year. Republican lawmakers from Utah and West Virginia attended his press event to tout similar new laws.

The controversial HHS head has angered many with his belief — against evidence — that autism is linked to vaccines and recent plans to create an “autism registry.”

But vaccine skepticism has simmered in both conservative and left-leaning parenthood circles for a while, and food dyes are another area of common ground the leader of the “**Make America Healthy Again**” movement has found with holistic lefties who seek more natural foods and products for their children.

The movement has hadstrong roots in California for years. And while many liberal L.A. and Marin County moms were early practitioners of “crunchy” (or its less-rigid relative, “scrunchie”) parenthood, conservative women have begun to embrace a similar “tradwife” lifestyle — growing their own food, raising backyard chickens and baking homemade Oreos.

**Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel,** D-San Fernando Valley, put synthetic additive bans on the legislative map two years ago with a “Skittles law” that bans Red Dye No. 3 and three other food preservatives by 2027. A follow-up law targets a number of dyes in foods at schools.

Since then, more than 20 states have introduced legislation to do the same.

Large food and candy makers are resisting the change, pointing out that even as the FDA moved to ban Red Dye No. 3 in January, it acknowledged a lack of scientific evidence that it causes harm in humans.

“We are thrilled to see Washington, D.C. following California’s lead and phasing out harmful chemicals,” Gabriel said in an interview, adding that it’s “encouraging” to see how quickly the issue spread. (The L.A.-area lawmaker, it should be noted, did not self-identify as “crunchy,” but said his family is “being more mindful about what is in the products we’re buying.”)

This year, he’s back with a bill to have regulators study the harms of “ultraprocessed foods” and begin phasing them out of schools. **Gov. Gavin Newsom** issued a similar order in January.

Getting synthetic dyes out of foods “is something that really resonates very broadly with folks across the political spectrum,” Gabriel said. “That’s what politics should be — finding areas where we agree and working together to protect our kids.”

**FINALLY FOURTH**

California nudged past Japan to (unofficially) become the world’s fourth largest economy, a distinction Newsomwas quick to celebrate Wednesday evening.

California’s total gross domestic product in 2024 was $4.1 trillion, while Japan’s was $4.02 trillion, according to data from the **International Monetary Fund** and the **Bureau of Economic Analysis**.

The state won’t be included on IMF’s rankings, but the updated numbers mean California remains the largest sub-national economy in the world.

Only the United States, China and Germany had larger GDP totals last year than California.

The Golden State’s outsized economy — driven by tech, entertainment, healthcare and agriculture industries — has always been a point of pride for Newsom, who often refers to California as a “nation-state.”

The milestone is one Newsom has been waiting for. He briefly — and prematurely — began referring to the state as “fourth-largest” after a 2022 **Bloomberg** columnist wrote that the state was “poised to overtake Germany,” which didn’t quite happen.

It also comes at a precarious time for the global economy due to **President Donald Trump’s** imposed tariffs and retaliation from countries including China.

“The global economic system that has operated for the last 80 years is being reset,” IMF Chief Economist **Pierre-Olivier Gourinchas** warned this week.

Newsom acknowledged as much himself yesterday and teased a bleaker picture for his revised budget proposal, which is due in mid-May.

“The projections have significantly changed since January as it relates to our economic outlook,” he said. “All of a sudden, with all the uncertainty with these tariffs and uncertainty with this new administration, that volatility is putting tremendous strain on our general fund.”
