‘California 49’: The Golden State’s most influential public officials in 2025

Brett Stover and Emily Hamann

SACRAMENTO — The legislative session is in full swing and speculation abounds about next year’s gubernatorial race to replace term-limited Gov. Gavin Newsom, all against the backdrop of a bleak budget outlook and a new administration in the White House poised to antagonize California’s Democratic supermajority.

With that in mind, welcome to the inaugural “California 49.” Brought to you by CapitolTrack/*State Affairs*, the 2025 list is modeled after the “Power 50” — a yearly feature at our sister outlets; but notably, the Golden State version highlights powerful elected officials and those who hold sway in their respective legislative or judicial office.

The 49 is an attempt at ranking the state’s most influential leaders in politics and policy. *State Affairs* will publish a new version of these rankings each year, and we want your feedback to refine each subsequent edition. So if you don’t agree with someone who’s on the list, not on the list or too high or low, let us know! Without further ado, the California 49:

**1. Gavin Newsom**

Newsom’s dominance in California politics is without question. Not surprising. Backed by major revenue growth, the Democratic governor has overseen a massive expansion in state spending, creating or expanding programs for housing, early childhood education, health care and climate change. But now, a murkier economic and fiscal outlook for the state has put some of those lofty goals in jeopardy. With just 20 months left for Newsom atop the state’s political pyramid, it’s time for him to cement his legacy — and set up his future, including a long-rumored leap into the 2028 presidential race.

**2. Robert Rivas**

The rise to the top in Sacramento has been swift for the Democratic Assembly speaker. It took Rivas just a few years to win enough support to supplant then-Speaker Anthony Rendon, though the change was one marked by a shift more in management style than in ideology. Rivas, who grew up in rural San Benito County, commands his caucus with a tighter grip than his predecessor. He has also become even more media-shy in recent months, drawing the ire of the Capitol Press Corps. The 2026 election — with a new governor and a likely favorable environment for Democrats nationwide — will provide an opportunity for Rivas to increase his influence.

**3. Mike McGuire**

The Democratic Senate president pro tempore is now in his second full year leading the upper house of the Legislature after taking over from the formidable Toni Atkins in a somewhat more peaceful transition than the power struggle that elevated his counterpart in the Assembly around the same time. As presiding officer of the chamber, McGuire, who was born and raised in Sonoma County, has brought his trademark boundless energy and positive attitude to the Senate’s top spot, although he has a small window to get things done before he is term-limited out of the Legislature at the end of next year. The Democrat is already eyeing a run for insurance commissioner as his potential next move.

**4. Nancy Pelosi**

On the national level, few politicians are as closely associated with California as the former Democratic House speaker, who has represented San Francisco in the U.S. House of Representatives for nearly four decades. When she ascended to the role of speaker of the House in 2007, she made history as not only the first woman but also the first Californian to hold the position. And although her formal leadership in the House is over, she remains an influential, albeit polarizing, figure and powerful fundraiser in Democratic politics — nationwide. Major questions remain about her future, however, as the 85-year-old powerhouse dodges questions about retirement and faces a challenge from the left for her House seat in 2026.

**5. Rob Bonta**

After nearly a decade in the Assembly, Bonta was appointed attorney general by Gov. Gavin Newsom to replace Xavier Becerra and won reelection shortly thereafter. But President Donald Trump’s victory in November has elevated Bonta’s profile, particularly on the national stage. He’s filed at least 13 lawsuits against the president’s administration in just three months — along with countless other statements — building up his “resistance” bona fides. It’s early, but Bonta’s ability to lead other blue states as they fight federal actions could help his political future — much like a similar approach helped the next entry on this list.

**6. Adam Schiff**

Becoming a prominent anti-Trump voice can pay dividends in a state like California. Just ask Democratic U.S. Sen. Adam Schiff, who became an overnight sensation in Trump’s first term, first by pushing for investigations into collusion between the president and Russia and later by serving as lead manager in Trump’s first impeachment trial. That popularity translated into a pocketbook boost last year, when Schiff’s financial advantage in the state’s most expensive Senate race allowed him to prop up Republican candidate Steve Garvey and box out fellow #resistance favorite Katie Porter, earning an easy victory and completing his journey from California senator in the late 1990s to U.S. senator. Schiff also served for several years as co-chair of the bipartisan Congressional Caucus for the Freedom of the Press, cementing his position internationally as a stalwart for press freedom and democracy.

**7. Alex Padilla**

Long before Trump took office, Democratic U.S. Sen. Alex Padilla stood out as one of the fiercest advocates in the Senate for immigration rights — even breaking with fellow Democrats over policies he saw as harmful to immigrants. He seems almost uniquely suited to the job. It was California’s 1994 anti-immigrant initiative, Proposition 187, that got Padilla, whose parents are immigrants from Mexico, involved in politics. Now that he’s in Congress and chairs the Senate Judiciary Subcommittee on Immigration, Citizenship and Border Safety, Padilla could emerge as one of the loudest voices opposing Trump’s immigration policies.

**8. Karen Bass**

The Los Angeles mayor faces significant challenges in her first term leading the nation’s second-largest city, including a nearly $1 billion budget deficit and devastating L.A. wildfires that have sparked criticism of her handling. The rough few months in local leadership comes after a long career in state and national politics, during which time she made history as the first Black woman to lead the Assembly, was so well-regarded by congressional Democrats that she was once pushed to challenge then-U.S. House Speaker Nancy Pelosi for the speakership (Bass declined) and was under consideration to be Joe Biden’s running mate in 2020.

**9. Buffy Wicks**

As chair of the Assembly Appropriations Committee, Wicks, a Democrat, wields considerable power in carrying out the committee’s business of deciding which bills make it to the Assembly floor and which ones do not. Hundreds of bills die every year through the committee’s suspense file process without coming up for a public discussion or vote. It’s Wicks’ second year leading the powerful committee after being appointed by Assembly Speaker Robert Rivas in late 2023.

**10. Anna Caballero**

Caballero’s position as chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee makes her one of the most powerful members of her chamber. Caballero, a Democrat, wields significant influence over which bills move ahead during the committee’s suspense file process. Senate President Mike McGuire appointed her to the coveted position after he took over leadership of the House at the beginning of last year.

**11. Scott Wiener**

Wiener’s appointment as chair of the Budget and Fiscal Review Committee gives him significant influence over the state budget — a job that becomes much harder during years, such as this one, that require tough choices on state spending. But the San Francisco senator is no stranger to controversy; he routinely introduces some of the most far-reaching and attention-grabbing bills each session, tackling topics like housing, tech and AI, climate change and LGBTQ+ rights, and he has been one of the Legislature’s loudest and most ardent critics of the Trump administration. Although the Democrat can stay in his seat through 2028, he already has his sights set on higher office and has been quietly organizing for years to take Nancy Pelosi’s House seat once she decides to retire.

**12. Jesse Gabriel**

The Encino assemblyman is serving his second year as chair of the Assembly Budget Committee — putting the Democrat at the head of one of the most powerful committees in the Legislature. Outside of his work on the panel, he’s passed significant legislation addressing gun violence prevention, banning food additives, regulating social media companies and protecting reproductive health care. He is also co-chair of the California Legislative Jewish Caucus.

**13. Eleni Kounalakis**

The lieutenant governor has a strong résumé with a background in business and deep connections within the Democratic Party — former President Barack Obama appointed her U.S. Ambassador to Hungary in 2010. Also, former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton and former Sen. Barbara Boxer backed Kounalakis’ bid for governor. Everything was shaping up nearly perfectly for Kounalakis until Harris lost the presidency last fall. Now we’ll have to wait and see whether Kounalakis will pivot to an alternative next step, which could be a run for state treasurer, according to some media reports.

**14. Fiona Ma**

After time in the Assembly — including a term as speaker pro tempore — and on the Board of Equalization, Ma broke through statewide in 2018, taking over as state treasurer. It’s an under-the-radar role, but one that could help Ma climb another rung up the ladder of California leadership. She has also exited a lengthy legal battle resulting from a former staffer accusing Ma of sexual harassment. The staffer dropped her lawsuit last year and the state settled for $350,000, but Ma has always denied any wrongdoing. Now Ma’s sights are set on another statewide office, though she’s eschewing the frenzied gubernatorial race for a run for lieutenant governor in 2026.

**15. Tony Thurmond**

The state superintendent of public instruction hopes his two terms as the state’s top educational leader will help kickstart a long-shot bid for governor. After two terms in the Assembly, he was backed in 2018 by the California Teachers Association and the California Federation of Teachers; the race became a sort of referendum on charter schools as his opponent, Marshall Tuck, was a vocal charter advocate. Thurmond was criticized for hiring a “superintendent of equity” who lived and worked in Philadelphia. Will the long odds pay off for Thurmond, or will he be looking to regroup after next year’s primary?

**16. Donald Trump**

California has long been a preferred punching bag for the president: The state is a “paradise lost,” it’s “out of control,” governed by “Gavin Newscum.” Trump has already threatened to withhold federal aid in the aftermath of the January wildfires and recently targeted California’s climate policies with an executive order. But those clashes carry benefits for Democrats, too: Conflict with the president, or at least the appearance of it, can be a major boost. Although Trump has gained ground in California — his vote share increased to above 38% last November from below 32% in 2016 — many Republicans still avoid associating with the president’s policies.

**17. Cecilia Aguiar-Curry**

Just a few months into Speaker Robert Rivas’ reign, he remade his leadership team, replacing a close ally, Assemblyman Isaac Bryan, as head of the majority party in the Assembly. Aguiar-Curry is also chair of the Legislative Women’s Caucus, which reached a high-water mark last year when a record 59 women — one lawmaker shy of half the Legislature — were elected in November.

**18. Lena Gonzalez**

The Senate majority leader is in the midst of her second session as the Senate’s second-in-command. In addition to her time in Democratic leadership and work on environmental policy, Gonzalez also serves as chair of the 35-member Latino Legislative Caucus, which is backing her bill to bar ICE agents from entering schools without a warrant. Now, can she use her growing influence to finally get enough lawmakers on board with her biggest goal: forcing CalPERS to divest from fossil fuel companies?

**19. Maxine Waters**

Whether it was during the Clinton administration, when she was rebuked for repeatedly interrupting a fellow U.S. representative criticizing her on the House floor, or it was a few weeks ago, when she suggested Trump should be “tried for treason,” Waters has never shied away from speaking her mind during her long tenure in Congress. She has wielded considerable power during her three decades representing South Los Angeles, including her current appointment as ranking member of the House Financial Services Committee.

**20. Patricia Guerrero**

Within a year, Guerrero became the first Latina to serve on California’s highest court before moving into the chief justice spot. And that’s no small feat in a state where courts don’t reflect the diverse population. Since 2023, though, it hasn’t been smooth sailing for the third branch. Guerrero had to oversee nearly $100 million in cuts last year, causing court closures and furloughs. That money is back in Gov. Gavin Newsom’s budget this year and Guerrero wants to get to work addressing a slate of challenges, including an increasingly congested justice system.

**21. Ricardo Lara**

The state’s insurance commissioner has been in the hot seat recently, as lawmakers and consumers alike look to him to stabilize the FAIR Plan in the wake of the Los Angeles wildfires — the costliest natural disaster in state history. Even before the fires, he had the daunting task of regulating an insurance market in crisis. And although the job was once a stepping stone for ambitious politicians, Lara has faced criticism since he’s been at it, including claims he is too friendly with insurance companies and questions about his meeting and travel activities. His next move after he is termed out in 2026 remains unclear.

**22. Shirley Weber**

When Gavin Newsom promoted Alex Padilla to U.S. senator in 2021, the governor also picked Weber from the Legislature to become California’s first Black secretary of state. (Her daughter, Sen. Akilah Weber Pierson, was elected to replace her in the Assembly in 2021.) Weber’s time as the state’s top election official is a departure from her past work in education, both for decades as a professor and later as an advocate for school reforms during her decadelong tenure as a Democratic in the Assembly.

**23. Malia Cohen**

After serving for most of the 2010s on the San Francisco Board of Supervisors, Cohen broke onto the state scene first in 2018 as a member of the State Board of Equalization and then in 2022 by winning her first statewide race for controller. But her ties to the top of this list go back even further — Cohen worked as a field organizer and later as an aide for Gavin Newsom during his campaign for and first term as mayor of San Francisco. Two years ago, she was floated as a candidate to replace the late Sen. Dianne Feinstein. The future is bright for Cohen, but her next move is unclear: another term as controller or perhaps a run for another statewide office like treasurer?

**24. Mike Thompson**

Thompson is one of California’s longest-serving lawmakers in the U.S. House of Representatives, having first taken his seat in the chamber in 1999. He sits on the powerful Ways and Means Committee, serves as the ranking member on the Subcommittee on Tax and is the senior member of the Health Subcommittee. Over the years, he has secured major funding relevant to his district in Wine Country and the state as a whole, including wildfire mitigation, agriculture disaster relief and roads, public transit, broadband and other infrastructure projects. He’s also a co-founder of the Congressional Wine Caucus and a member of the Blue Dog Democrats.

**25. Pete Aguilar**

As the old guard of California’s congressional Democratic leadership enters its career twilight, Aguilar is angling to step up and mentor the next generation. As chair of the House Democratic Caucus, the San Bernardino lawmaker is the third-highest-ranking Democrat in the U.S. House of Representatives and the highest-ranking from California. During the last election, he raised more than $30 million for caucus members and launched an ambitious campaign to flip five California House seats for Democrats. He was partially successful — three of the five seats went to Democrats in November — and he has pledged to continue working to flip the House in 2026.

**26. Doris Matsui**

Although she may not be the most outspoken member of California’s congressional delegation, Matsui has worked behind the scenes over the last 20 years to become one of the state’s most effective lawmakers. Her district includes Sacramento, which, in addition to being home to the state capitol, is one of the most vulnerable cities in the country for flood risk, and Matsui has secured billions of federal dollars for levee improvements and other flooding infrastructure. She also sits on the Energy and Commerce Committee, including serving as ranking member of the Subcommittee on Communications and Technology, and authored the CHIPS for America Act, which invested $52 billion in domestic semiconductor research and manufacturing.

**27. Josh Lowenthal**

As Assembly speaker pro tempore, Lowenthal runs floor sessions when Assembly Speaker Robert Rivas isn’t available. It’s a new leadership role for the Long Beach Democrat, who started his second term at the beginning of this year. Lowenthal comes from a family dynasty of politicians — his mother is former Assemblywoman Bonnie Lowenthal and his father is former Rep. Alan Lowenthal; however, he resisted following in his parents’ footsteps until he was approaching his 50s and ran a number of businesses, including local restaurants, and worked as a teacher before going into politics.

**28. Mary H. Murguia**

Murguia, age 64, was appointed to the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals by Obama in 2010. The chief circuit judge became the first woman of color to lead a U.S. circuit court when she became chief judge of the appellate court, the largest in the country, in 2021.

**29. Barbara Lee**

The freshly elected Democratic mayor of Oakland hasn’t officially taken office yet — that will come in a few weeks — but she already looms large in Oakland politics, having represented the East Bay city in the U.S. House of Representatives for more than two decades, where she served as a trailblazer and staunch progressive icon. But the hard-won election victory comes just a year after she was boxed out of the U.S. Senate race, and now she has just a few short months to enact her vision for the city and address its serious budget deficit before she’ll have to start defending her seat in the 2026 election.

**30. Ami Bera**

Bera, a medical doctor, gained prominence during the COVID-19 pandemic and still serves on the Select Subcommittee on the Coronavirus Pandemic. He’s also on the U.S. House Committee on Foreign Affairs, where he sits as ranking member of the Subcommittee on the Indo-Pacific and on the Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence.

**31. Ro Khanna**

Khanna isn’t the easiest politician to briefly sum up, but one word that comes to mind — not in a pejorative sense — is idiosyncratic. The U.S. representative is a progressive capitalist; pro-labor but backed by big tech and venture capital; an Obama alum and Bernie Sanders supporter praised by Trump loyalist Steve Bannon. Now, Khanna is taking the show on the road, hosting town halls in central California and even in Ohio, where he took aim at U.S. vice president and fellow self-described populist JD Vance at an event last week. Where these paths will take Khanna is an open question, but there’s no doubt he’s taking the road less traveled.

**32. Tom Umberg**

Now in his third stint in the Legislature, Umberg is nearing the tail end of a career that’s spanned four decades in and out of the Capitol. It also took the Democratic mainstay to Washington during the Clinton administration. As chair of the Senate Judiciary Committee, the former prosecutor and retired colonel takes a no-nonsense approach, and he’s not afraid to stand up to members of his own party when necessary — and he’s always been one of the most productive lawmakers in terms of bills passed.

**33. John Laird**

During his first term in the Senate, Laird, a Democrat, had a whopping 59 of his bills signed into law, focusing on environmental issues, climate change, health care and other issues. And he remains a prolific lawmaker today, with 34 of his bills passing into law in the last session — a 77% success rate. He also chairs the influential Budget Subcommittee on Education, and co-chairs the joint legislative audit and rules committees. His current position in the Senate is the latest in a long career in public service that included serving as secretary of the California Natural Resources Agency under Gov. Jerry Brown.

**34. Mia Bonta**

Bonta replaced her husband, Rob, in the California Assembly after his ascension to the attorney general’s office in 2021 and has quickly become a force within the Assembly. The progressive Democrat rose further when she became chair of the Health Committee in late 2023, a position she still holds. Bonta’s role is one that will only gain prominence as Medi-Cal and other health care programs fall under the shadow of budget cuts.

**35. Gail Pellerin**

A longtime elections official in Santa Cruz County, Pellerin got elected to the Assembly in 2022 and immediately got to work, steering seven bills through the Legislature in her first year alone. Her work rate has continued, propelling the Democratic lawmaker into a position as one of Sacramento’s leaders on election issues — she became chair of the Assembly Elections Committee less than a year into her first term.

**36. Marc Berman**

When it comes to authoring bills, Berman is one of the Legislature’s most prolific and successful lawmakers. Last session, 40 of the bills authored by the Democrat made it into law, on topics including education, elections and artificial intelligence. He also has a high success rate when it comes to getting his bills across the finish line — just 17 of the bills he introduced last session failed to be enacted. During his first eight years in office, he has sent a total of 99 bills to the governor’s desk — where all but six of them were signed. Berman, who’s from Palo Alto, also chairs the Assembly Business and Professions Committee.

**37. Kevin McCarty**

Although he no longer works at the Capitol, McCarty has not gone far — just a few blocks away to the mayor’s office at the Sacramento City Hall. After 10 years in the Assembly, McCarty gave up his seat last year to run for mayor of the capital city, his hometown, in a tight, competitive race that he won by just 1% of the vote.

**38. James Gallagher**

As Assembly minority leader, Gallagher holds the designation of being the most powerful Republican in the Statehouse — however much power that entails in the deeply blue Legislature. The Sutter County lawmaker has led the 19-member caucus since 2022 and has consistently been one of the most outspoken critics of Democrats’ control over the state, especially of Gov. Gavin Newsom, and the state’s environmental policies.

**39. Brian Jones**

Leading the smallest of the four major caucuses — just 10 members make up the Senate GOP this session — isn’t the most glamorous job at the Capitol. But Senate Minority Leader Jones doesn’t shy away from the tough task of leading the superminority party, picking when to work across the aisle and when to pick more vocal fights, like his push this year to limit California’s sanctuary state law.

**40. Daniel Lurie**

The San Francisco mayor just hit 100 days in office after successfully ousting former Mayor London Breed and taking charge of California’s most densely populated city. The early returns have been positive, at least on the morale side of things, but murkier waters lie ahead as Lurie faces a major budget deficit and the expectation of following through on lofty campaign promises — he’s already backed off a vow to build 1,500 shelter beds in his first six months. Can the “vibe shift” continue, or will some of SF’s persistent problems prove too troublesome for Lurie?

**41. Nathan Hochman**

The Los Angeles County district attorney now sits at the head of the busiest DA  office in the country, after soundly winning the race to become Los Angeles County’s top prosecutor in November. Hochman unseated the incumbent — progressive prosecutor George Gascón — by a more-than 20-point margin, which has largely been attributed to backlash from voters against criminal justice reforms and a rise in crime. Although he previously ran for state attorney general as a Republican, Hochman ran in the DA race with an independent, “hard middle” approach, and pledged to reject mass incarceration while also undoing the “extreme pro-criminal, decarceration policies” of his predecessor.

**42. Bill Essayli**

Essayli, interim U.S. attorney for the Central District of California, wouldn’t have been on this list if it had been written a month ago. But Trump has elevated the fiery former assemblyman to lead the largest judicial district in the nation — and like Attorney General Rob Bonta’s status as a thorn in the president’s side can boost his profile, so can Essayli’s opportunities to investigate Democratic leaders in southern California and Los Angeles. He’s already announced a wide-reaching probe into alleged “fraud, waste, abuse and corruption” within programs that receive federal homelessness funding. Don’t be surprised to see Essayli become — or, well, continue to be — one of the state’s most outspoken Republicans.

**43. Dolly M. Gee**

Gee, 65, has been serving on the bench of the U.S. District Court for the Central District of California for 15 years. Originally an Obama appointee, she became chief judge of the nation’s largest district court last spring. Her notable rulings include a finding against the U.S. Justice Department during Trump’s first term, when she appointed an independent monitor to oversee migrant child detention facilities at the border over concerns that detained children weren’t being held in safe or sanitary conditions.

**44. Richard Seeborg**

Seeborg, who will turn 69 in November, is nearing the end of his time as the top judge on the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California. His time on the bench since 2010 has been busy, ruling on a variety of issues including the pipeline of tech-related cases that originate from the Bay Area.

**45. Troy L. Nunley**

Nunley, who will turn 61 this year, became chief judge of the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of California last year after first being appointed to the federal bench by Obama in 2013. In the role, he oversees the largest geographical district of the four California district courts that includes Sacramento.

**46. Cynthia Bashant**

Now in her second decade on the federal bench, Bashant was first appointed to the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of California by Obama. She became the chief judge of the judicial district in January, a position the 65-year-old Bashant is eligible to hold for another five years.

**47. Patricia Lock Dawson**

Lock Dawson was reelected last fall to a second term leading Riverside, the Inland Empire’s largest city. But she’s on this list because she was also chosen to lead the “Big City Mayors,” the coalition that represents California’s 13 largest cities — a small group of local leaders who represent more than a quarter of the state’s population. She succeeds San Diego Mayor Todd Gloria in leading a group that’s lobbied for increased state funding for homelessness and housing in the past. The group could look to flex its muscle again amid future budget fights.

**48. Celeste Rodriguez**

One of a handful of mayors who joined the legislative ranks this session, Assistant Assembly Speaker Pro Tempore Rodriguez stands out. Speaker Robert Rivas backed her election bid last year and immediately appointed her to his leadership team following her victory. What’s next is uncertain, but that’s an auspicious start to Rodriguez’s time at the Capitol.

**49. Avelino Valencia**

The Anaheim assemblyman chairs the Banking and Finance Committee. He also has a knack for introducing successful bills — last year, nearly 75% of the bills he introduced were signed by the governor. The two-termer is also eyeing a move up in 2026 —he’s already announced that he plans to run for Tom Umberg’s Senate seat after he is termed-out at the next election.

California advances a ban on ultraprocessed foods and drinks in school meals

04/23/25 7:07 AM By Brad Hooker No Comments

The Legislature is mulling a proposal to phase out by 2032 “harmful” ultraprocessed foods from about a billion school meals served each year in California. The measure would make the state the first governmental body in the U.S. to ban the ingredients.

Casting a shadow over the forward momentum of the bill, food and agriculture associations warn the well-intentioned legislation stands to increase costs for schools and reduce choices.

Assembly Bill 1264 rides on the success of a 2023 state ban on food additives and a ban last year on dyes in school meals. The Southern California liberal behind the legislation, Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel, D-Encino, has formed an uncanny alliance with Republicans over the food bans, echoing many of the claims of the Trump administration.

“These products are often filled with harmful additives and specifically engineered to interfere with our brain signals in ways that can contribute to food addiction,” said Gabriel during a recent committee hearing on the bill. “The science is clear. Consumption of ultraprocessed foods is a leading driver of poor health outcomes and rising healthcare costs.”

Gabriel’s justification for the ban is that 73% of U.S. adults in the U.S. are overweight or obese and 38% of children are prediabetic, with diet-related diseases the nation’s leading cause of death. He blamed ultraprocessed foods for health issues ranging from cancer to cardiovascular disease and neurobehavioral issues.

“Our public schools should not be serving students products that can harm their physical or mental health or interfere with their ability to learn,” said Gabriel.

From LA to MAHA

His bill would define the specific ingredients in state code and direct state agencies to partner with University of California food and nutrition researchers to determine the specific foods to ban. The endeavor would consider additives that are linked to health harms; contribute to food addiction; contain excessive fat, sugar or salt; or are already restricted or require warning labels in other jurisdictions.

Asm. Jesse Gabriel, D-Encino (Gabriel office photo)

At a time when Governor Gavin Newsom and California’s other Democratic leaders are attempting to find common ground with President Donald Trump on critical issues like water infrastructure and wildfire recovery, Gabriel is confident his bipartisan bill will face little resistance this legislative session. He noted that his measure on school meals inspired the FDA to ban two of the chemicals on his list and more than 20 other states to introduce similar versions of the legislation.

FDA Commissioner Martin Makary and Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. have been outspoken about food dyes and the potential links to chronic health conditions. On Tuesday FDA announced plans to phase out all petroleum-based dyes from the nation’s food supply.

The "Make America Healthy Again" movement and Kennedy’s previous advocacy roles also have ties to the same interest groups behind Gabriel’s bills.

Several food and nutrition groups support AB 1264. On that list as well is Kat Taylor, a billionaire hedge fund manager and Newsom campaign donor who has played an insider role with developing nutrition and farm-to-school programs within the California Department of Food and Agriculture.

Among those interest groups, the national nonprofit Eat Real has developed a certification program that seeks to verify K-12 schools are providing healthy meals by adhering to 34 performance indicators, including metrics for sustainable farming practices. CEO Nora LaTorre says the organization is on track to reach a million children in 20 states nationwide, with about a third of those students in California.

“Our work proves that not only is it possible for schools to feed our kids nutritious, local and minimally processed meals, but our kids prefer it and they need it,” said LaTorre, testifying in support of AB 1264. “Kids eat more than a bathtub of added sugar per year. Our food system is failing our kids.”

Eat Real has partnered with the Fresno Unified School District, the state’s third largest, to transition more than 100 schools to healthier foods. Half of the produce in the school meals is now locally sourced, and some schools have incorporated regenerative beef and chicken products, according to LaTorre.

Ashley Gearhardt, a University of Michigan psychology professor, issued a dire warning to the lawmakers if they do not back Gabriel’s bill.

“If we truly care about children's health, we must treat ultraprocessed food like the public health threat that it is,” said Gearhardt. “This means removing it from schools and putting real nourishing food first.”

She argued unhealthy foods hijack the brain’s reward system in a downward cycle that is “great for corporate profits but devastating for public health.” She equated it to cigarette companies manipulating consumers and claimed the same companies then purchased major food manufacturers in the 1970s and 80s.

“They used the same tactics in our food supply,” said Gearhardt. “They added flavor chemicals from cigarettes to sugary drinks for children. They designed foods to hit bliss points and maximize craving, and they aggressively marketed these products to kids.”

Bans run up against California's affordability crisis

Opponents agreed with the overall intent of the bill and lauded the goal of improving student nutrition as commendable but held strong reservations about enacting a sweeping ban. Representing the Consumer Brands Association and a coalition of California agricultural associations, lobbyist Dennis Albiani explained the challenge with implementing AB 1264.

Dennis Albiani, Consumer Brands Association (photo: Brad Hooker, Agri-Pulse)

The Biden administration, he said, attempted to define ultraprocessed foods through the Dietary Guidelines Advisory Committee but found it to be virtually impossible. The ambiguity of Gabriel's definition could target bread, dairy and locally grown canned fruits or vegetables. The bill also “places a scarlet letter” on what Gabriel views as the particularly harmful ultraprocessed foods and pushes an overly ambitious six-month timeline to perform a thorough scientific review and draft the potentially complex regulations. That review process, Albiani argued, would override the existing oversight programs at FDA as well as the California Department of Public Health, which inspired Gabriel’s previous legislation through its review of synthetic dyes.

The bill “paints a broad brush” that encompasses companies considered to be healthier than their traditional counterparts, added Jimmy Fremgen, policy director at Food Solutions Action, a charity nonprofit advocating for alternative protein products.

Both Albiani and Fremgen are pressing for amendments to narrow the scope of AB 1264, which has precedent with the lawmaker. Gabriel’s 2023 push for a food ban garnered his legislation the moniker of a “Skittles ban” for prohibiting several common ingredients, before the lawmaker agreed to remove titanium dioxide, the most controversial ingredient on his blacklist. He has also worked with school districts to minimize their costs for implementing the bills, concerns that drove Asm. Leticia Castillo, R-Corona, to hold back from voting on AB 1264.

Before voting in favor of the measure, Asm. Mia Bonta, D-Oakland, raised concerns about asking schools to make the transition before the vendors and infrastructure are in place, likening the potential unintended consequences to the California Air Board’s ban on diesel truck engines through its Advanced Clean Fleets Rule.

Gabriel defended his measure as simply substituting one brand of applesauce with another, for example, and not a ban on chocolate milk, as opponents portrayed it. He believed alternatives should be readily available, since companies have already reformulated those products for other countries.

“This is about products out there on the market that include some of the most dangerous chemicals, many of which are outlawed in other countries,” said Gabriel. “They cannot be placed in foods in the EU. They cannot be put in foods in Latin America. They cannot be put in foods in South Korea.”

Arizona Passes Law Banning Sale of Some ‘Ultra-Processed Foods’ in Schools

By Bailee Henderson

April 15, 2025

On April 14, 2025, Arizona Governor Katie Hobbs signed into law House Bill 2164, named the Arizona Healthy Schools Act, banning “ultra-processed foods” containing certain additives and dyes from being served in public schools, including foods served in school meals and foods sold in vending machines or by third-party vendors. Schools will be expected to comply with the legislation by the 2026–2027 school year.

“Ultra-processed foods” as defined by the legislation are any food or beverage containing:

  1. Potassium bromate
  2. Propylparaben
  3. Titanium dioxide
  4. Brominated vegetable oil (BVO)
  5. Yellow dye 5
  6. Yellow dye 6
  7. Blue dye 1
  8. Blue dye 2
  9. Green dye 3
  10. Red dye 3
  11. Red dye 40.

It is worth noting that red dye 3 and BVO are no longer permitted for use in foods at the federal level, as their authorizations were revoked by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) in January 2025 and July 2024, respectively.

The Arizona Healthy Schools Act was sponsored by state Representative Leo Biasiucci (R-5), who credited U.S. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s “Make American Healthy Again” (MAHA) agenda as impetus for the bill, saying, “This is a public health issue. We now have overwhelming evidence that these chemicals [targeted in the bill] can contribute to everything from hyperactivity to increased cancer risk—yet they remain in school meals.”

California was the first U.S. state to buck federal food additives regulation and enact its own bans of many of the same chemicals listed in the Arizona Healthy Schools Act, with the passage of the California Food Safety Act and California School Food Safety Act in October 2023 and August 2024, respectively. The sponsor of both pieces of legislation, California Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel (D-46), cited as the reasoning behind his bills the same toxicity concerns as voiced by Arizona Rep. Biasiucci. For example, the California Environmental Protection Agency published a report that the artificial colorants banned by the California School Food Safety Act can cause hyperactivity and other neurobehavioral effects in children. Some of the other non-colorant additives prohibited in Arizona and California’s bills have been banned in the EU and other nations due to possible carcinogenicity and hormone disruption.

Since the passage of the California Food Safety Act and California School Food Safety Act, public concern over the safety of food additives has grown, fueled by and reflected in the MAHA movement. Other states have introduced their own bills similar to those passed in Arizona and California; for example, West Virginia passed its own legislation prohibiting certain colorants from school foods in March 2025. A similar bill is also being considered in Texas. Additionally, California Assemblymember Gabriel also recently introduced another bill to define and identify “ultra-processed foods” so that they can be phased out of state public schools.

Bailee Henderson is the Director of Content Strategy for Food Safety Magazine. In the day-to-day, she covers industry-relevant current events, regulatory affairs, and scientific developments. She also produces the Food Safety Five Newsreel, edits the twice-weekly Food Safety Digest newsletter, and manages the brand's social media channels. Notably, Bailee's coverage for Food Safety Magazine has been featured in national televised news segments including CBS Sunday Morning and MSNBC's Rachel Maddow Show. She can be reached at hendersonb@bnpmedia.com.

Source: Sierra Nevada Conservancy

Governor Gavin Newsom has affixed his signature to a piece of legislation that earmarks an additional $170 million for forest and vegetation management projects to bolster California's defenses against the ever-looming threat of wildfires. The funding is specifically aimed at ramping up the state's preparedness before the peak of fire season arrives, according to details released in a press release from the Governor's office.

Assembly Bill 100 was introduced by Assemblymember Gabriel, which carries not just the $170 million boost but also an additional $10 million dedicated to wildfire response and resilience. Governor Newsom remarked, "With this latest round of funding, we're continuing to increase the speed and size of forest and vegetation management essential to protecting communities. We are leaving no stone unturned – including cutting red tape – in our mission to ensure our neighborhoods are protected from destructive wildfires." These funds are to be distributed among numerous conservancies, including the Sierra Nevada Conservancy and the Santa Monica Mountains Conservancy, to name a few. Each of these conservancies is set to receive millions to aid in various management activities.

Furthermore, Governor Newsom has also signed an executive order to quickly put into effect the projects financed under AB 100. This move follows a previous emergency proclamation, which was intended to cut through bureaucratic delays by waiving certain regulations. These steps signify a furtherance of the state's multi-year strategy to fortify its approach to wildfire management and resilience building.

Backed by a substantial budget, California has been relentlessly working to implement the Governor's Wildfire and Forest Resilience Action Plan, which delineates 99 key actions — all of which are either completed or in progress. The aim has been to notably accelerate the pace of fuel reduction, prescribed fire, and overall forest health. Moreover, California initiated a strategic plan to increase the use of prescribed burning, recognizing its vital role in forging both forest and community resilience. "More forest management and prescribed burns than ever before," stated the release, as the state works to nearly double prescribed fire activity from 2021 to 2023.

The tracking of wildfire prevention is also taking a step forward with the introduction of new dashboards, making California's efforts in this area more transparent and accessible to the public. These efforts trace back to one of Governor Newsom's first acts in office in 2019, when he declared a state of emergency in response to wildfires and facilitated the exemption of crucial wildfire and forest management projects from lengthy environmental law processes.

A podcast from the Ethnic Studies Council at the University of California.

The Lower Frequencies

Episode 1: Policing Ethnic Studies: The Legislative Jewish Caucus and AB 1468

The Lower Frequencies, Episode 1

Policing Ethnic Studies: The Legislative Jewish Caucus and AB 1468

The inaugural episode of The Lower Frequencies features guest Marcy Winograd and members of the UC Ethnic Studies Council discussing AB 1468, a bill authored and introduced by the California Legislative Jewish Caucus, without any consultation of ethnic studies experts, that would impose a massive and costly set of rules policing the ways in which ethnic studies can be taught by K-12 teachers in the state.

Gov. Newsom signs $170 million wildfire resiliency bill

Ian Bradley

Published April 14, 2025 4:00 PM PDT

Gov. Gavin Newsom speaks about California wildfire preparedness at Grass Valley Interagency Air Attack Base in Nevada Co., June 29, 2023.

OAKLAND, Calif. - With California's wildfire season fast approaching, Gov. Gavin Newsom on Monday signed a bill to allocate over $170 million toward wildfire resiliency.

Newsom signed Assembly Bill 100, sponsored by Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel (D-46), which accelerates funding to conservancies for forest and vegetation management across the state. The bill also puts $10 million toward wildfire response and resiliency.

"With this latest round of funding, we're continuing to increase the speed and size of forest and vegetation management essential to protecting communities," Newsom said in a press release. "We are leaving no stone unturned — including cutting red tape — in our mission to ensure our neighborhoods are protected from destructive wildfires."

The bill implements the "early action" 2025 budget package to address items necessary for adoption this fiscal year.

Fair share

By the numbers:

The conservancies receiving funding include:

- $30,904,000 to the Sierra Nevada Conservancy
- $23,524,000 to the California Tahoe Conservancy
- $31,349,000 to the Santa Monica Mountains Conservancy
- $30,904,000 to the State Coastal Conservancy
- $30,904,000 to the San Gabriel and Lower Los Angeles Rivers and Mountains Conservancy
- $23,524,000 to the San Diego River Conservancy

Cutting tape

Dig deeper:

Gov. Newsom also signed an executive order to guarantee that the projects funded by AB 100 benefit are streamlined and exempt from "bureaucratic red tape" that can delay efforts to mitigate wildfire risks.

Newsom has for years worked to increase forest management and wildfire resilience, including several executive orders to improve community hardening and wildfire mitigation strategies statewide.

Fighting back

Why you should care:

Of the 20 most destructive fires in California's history, 15 have occurred in the last decade, including two that swept through Los Angeles earlier this year, the Eaton and Palisades fires.

California is investing $2.5 billion to implement Newsom's Wildfire and Forest Resilience Action Plan, which was adopted in 2021. The plan calls for more fuel reduction and prescribed burns. All of the key actions outlined in the plan are underway or have already been implemented. That plan comes in addition to the $200 million invested annually through the 2028-2029 fiscal year for healthy forest and fire prevention programs.

West Valley Food Pantry Opens New Facility

  • by VNG
  • April 11, 2025April 11, 2025

Supervisor Lindsey Horvath called it “faith in action” and Councilman Bob Blumenfield said it would change lives.

They were both present along with other elected officials, community leaders, religious representatives and residents to celebrate the grand opening of the West Valley Food Pantry’s new facility.

Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel said that it wasn’t just that they provided services – but how they did it, praising Executive Director Debbie Decker’s sense of purpose, dynamism and dedication.

Decker said that they do not just dispense food to those in need, but also diapers, hygiene products, pet food, school supplies and referrals to community services, housing help and more.

The new 7,000-square-foot building consolidates all West Valley Food Pantry operations under one roof, improving service efficiency and accessibility for the thousands it serves in the valley.

Decker explained that those they see include not just homeless, but seniors, families in need and now victims of the recent fires. “We offer everyone companionship and a listening ear, and respect where they are in life and try to help,” she said at the opening.

The number they served in 2024 is staggering – 97,000 people who needed a bag of groceries, a helping hand, a referral or a service from Decker, her team or the more than 200 volunteers that show up to help distribute 900,000 pounds of food.

To house that much food and supplies was part of the demand for a new building.

The new facility was initially made possible by a $3.5 million appropriation in the state budget in 2021, with additional funding secured in 2023 to further expand the building. Additional funding came from foundations and the generosity of many supporting individuals.

The work of Blumenfield and his staff brought to fruition the completion of the building.

The Reverend John Taylor, Bishop of Los Angeles, said that Decker “turned a spark of imagination into this majestic facility.”

This year marks the 40th anniversary of the pantry, which has grown steadily since its founding – which was basically church members giving out cans of food.

The official founding of the pantry was inspired by Margaret Shively in 1975, who actually saw the groundbreaking of the new building before she passed last year.

Another long-standing supporter of the pantry is the National Charity League of the San Fernando Valley, whose mother-daughter members have volunteered for more than 30 years and donated over $1 million to the organization. So much so that they have a room in the new building dedicated to them.

The West Valley Food Pantry is located on the grounds of Prince of Peace Episcopal Church, 5700 Rudnick Avenue off Shoup Avenue in Woodland Hills.

California Dems get health care heartburn

By LINDSEY HOLDEN

SLASH AND BURN: California Democrats are stressed about funding health care for the state’s poorest residents — a growing crisis made worse by federal cuts that now seem all but certain.

Lawmakers today agreed to provide a $2.8 billion lifeline for Medi-Cal, the state’s version of the federal Medicaid program, which is running out of money because of high enrollment numbers, my colleague Eric He reports for Pro subscribers. Meanwhile, House Republicans approved a budget framework, setting the stage for safety-net program slashing.

Less federal money would intensify a state health care spending problem caused by increased pharmaceutical expenses, greater senior enrollment and an expansion of coverage for undocumented immigrants. With about a month until Gov. Gavin Newsom presents his revised May spending plan, lawmakers are already seeing the writing on the budgetary wall.

Assembly Budget Chair Jesse Gabriel seized on what he views as the unfairness of California residents sending their tax dollars to fund programs in other states.

“It is not right that money from California taxpayers can be taken and spent in other communities,” he said. “Then we’re going to have to be in a position to contemplate really terrible choices for health programs and services that we want to provide for Californians.”

Democrats today also defended their push to provide insurance for undocumented Californians against GOP pushback just before leaving for a weeklong spring recess. Republicans tried to hold their ground.

“All of us support Medi-Cal — it is the most important health care program for the neediest among us,” said Assemblymember Carl DeMaio, a San Diego Republican. “But all of their health coverage has been put at risk because Governor Gavin Newsom and this Legislature decided to grant a gift of public funds to illegal immigrants to cover their health insurance at taxpayer expense.”

An exasperated Gabriel was rubbing his face as soon as he walked onto the floor, later saying he just wanted to go home and see his kids.

But the assemblymember will likely come back from his break to even more financial woes. California could sustain disproportionate damage from President Donald Trump’s tariffs, which have proved to be unpredictable and appear dependent on the president’s whims.

And even if congressional Republicans preserve some federal health care dollars, California leaders will need to substantially rethink the state’s Medi-Cal system.

As Eric reports, Newsom’s administration today acknowledged the cost overruns in an Assembly Budget Committee hearing before the legislative vote.

Erika Li from the Department of Finance called the situation “unsustainable” and said her agency is “looking at ways to curb those costs into the budget year.”

IT’S THURSDAY AFTERNOON. This is California Playbook PM, a POLITICO newsletter that serves as an afternoon temperature check on California politics and a look at what our policy reporters are watching. Got tips or suggestions? Shoot an email to lholden@politico.com.

DEM DISSENTION: A group of Democrats today opposed a resolution from Assemblymember Tri Ta honoring California civil rights hero Sylvia Mendez and called Republicans hypocritical for backing the measure while their party fights DEI initiatives.

Mendez was barred from attending a segregated school in Westminster in the 1940s, and her court case helped pave the way for future civil rights victories.

Ta, an Orange County Republican, previously served as mayor of Westminster. Last year, he authored a bill pushing for California schools to include her case in social studies curriculum.

But Assemblymember Corey Jackson and other Democrats couldn’t stomach Republicans bringing the resolution, asking members to hold off on voting for it. Some said they wanted to honor Mendez, but only with a new resolution.

“It’s time for us to send a message, colleagues,” Jackson said. “It’s time for us to understand that boundaries matter. And it’s time for us to make sure that we do not deem it acceptable to use people who sacrificed on their own — for their people, for their communities — for political points.”

Assemblymember Ash Kalra said GOP members were presenting a “contradiction” by “putting forth the resolution in recognition of a movement that they now want to erase from history.”

Jackson and Assemblymembers Mia Bonta and Alex Lee objected to a voice vote on the resolution, instead asking for a roll call that put members’ decisions on the record.

When the dust had settled, Bonta and Lee were the only lawmakers to register “no” votes, although Jackson and a handful of other Democrats declined to vote.

PALISADES DETENTE: Call it the Redick Accords. JJ Redick, head coach of the Los Angeles Lakers, orchestrated an unusual sight today: Mayor Karen Bass and her once (and possibly future) rival Rick Caruso, smiling side-by-side.

The occasion was the announcement of a new public-private partnership between the city, Caruso’s nonprofit group Steadfast LA and Redick’s own sports-focused initiative to rebuild the Palisades Recreation Center, which was destroyed in January’s historic wildfires.

It was the first time the political foes had been together in public since they faced off on the debate stage during their 2022 mayoral race and the vibes were mostly collegial, with the pair sharing multiple handshakes, a side hug and brief utterances of praise for each other.

After the unveiling of the ambitious rebuilding plans — which would be privately financed on city-owned lands — Bass said her appearance with Caruso, the billionaire developer who has been harshly critical of her leadership, could be summed up by a simple credo: Keeping her “eyes on the prize.”

“The goal is restoring and healing this community. There is nothing to me more important than that, and so I think it is appropriate for us to come together in a public-private partnership. That’s the best way to get things done,” Bass said, praising Caruso’s “outstanding” contribution to the recovery effort.

Caruso, for his part, said that he and Bass are “genuinely friendly” and there’s been no friction in his nonprofit working with the city on recovery efforts. But he still criticized the recovery effort for moving too slowly, regardless of the city hitting certain milestones — such as the clearing of toxic debris and restoring utilities — at a faster rate than what happened in the aftermath of previous major fires.

“Those are failures,” Caruso said of those past recovery efforts. “That would be like if your kid comes home and says, ‘hey Dad, I got a D but everyone else in school got an F.’ Well, that’s nothing to celebrate.” — Melanie Mason

SIX-FIGURE SLAP: The Fair Political Practices Commission quickly and unanimously voted to impose one of its largest penalties ever on a former elected official — ex-Assemblymember Evan Low. It approved the $106,000 fine this morning in response to several campaign finance violations that the enforcement division assistant chief Angela Brereton described as “egregious.” Low had already agreed to the settlement.

Chair Adam Silver recused himself from the 3-0 vote, following a previous promise to abstain from votes on issues regarding the Assembly — where he used to be chief council for the Ethics Committee. — Blake Jones

Major industries that power the nation’s largest economy — from almond growers counting on foreign buyers to Silicon Valley giants reliant on Chinese components — are still trembling from Trump’s shifting trade policies. The economic uncertainty also threatens to tank the stock market, drying up state tax revenue for schools and health care.

“It’s really bad,” said Lenny Mendonca, a former top economic adviser to Newsom. “The United States is the biggest beneficiary of global trade and California’s more dependent on international activity than the country. California Legislature adds funding to Medi-Cal, wildfire recovery efforts through budget changes

Republicans argued against the changes, arguing Medi-Cal expansions that now include undocumented residents have exacerbated the state's monetary problems.

Alan Riquelmy / April 10, 2025

SACRAMENTO, Calif. (CN) — Passions flared Thursday as California’s Democratic legislative supermajority sent a bill to the governor that shifts billions of dollars in “early action” moves to address the Los Angeles wildfires and higher Medi-Cal costs.

Assembly Bill 100, a budget trailer bill, amends this year’s budget act by taking $2.8 billion for the Department of Health Care Services, with another $8.3 billion in federal funds, to address unanticipated Medi-Cal expenses. It also directs the use of dollars set aside earlier this year to offset property tax losses for local governments, as well as response and recovery efforts, stemming from the Palisades and Eaton fires in Los Angeles County.

Senate Republicans opposed the budget trailer bill and offered amendments that would have redirected money to their own priorities. Debating the bill after its Senate passage, their Assembly counterparts also railed against the measure.

“This is an attack on the middle class,” said state Senator Marie Alvarado-Gil, a Jackson Republican, who pushed for an amendment that would have offset proposed cuts to the state’s California State University and University of California systems. “Nothing in this bill addresses affordability.”

State Senator Kelly Seyarto, a Murrieta Republican, had an amendment seeking to allocate money for firefighters. Noting legislation that will maintain Cal Fire staffing levels year-round, Seyarto argued the additional firefighters wouldn’t start until next year. Funding is needed now in preparation for the state’s fire season.

Republicans argued the additional money for Medi-Cal, California’s Medicaid program, stemmed from Democrats expanding it — including the addition of all undocumented people. They said money should instead go to funding priorities like Proposition 36, which voters passed in November and increases penalties for certain theft and drug crimes.

Democrats easily won votes to table the amendments. State Senator John Laird, a Santa Cruz Democrat, noted that cuts to the university systems are proposals for next fiscal year and not in the budget they tweaked on Thursday.

State Senator Lena Gonzalez, a Long Beach Democrat and majority leader, quipped that Republicans previously had opposed funding for the items they now endorsed.

“Now all of a sudden they’re for firefighters,” she added.

The arguments continued moments later in the Assembly, which had to approve changes made by the Senate before the bill could proceed to the governor.

Assemblymember Carl DeMaio, a San Diego Republican, got temporarily mired in a procedural misstep while speaking against the bill and trying to offer an amendment to it. DeMaio wanted to eliminate any Medi-Cal funding for undocumented residents, as well as for the high-speed rail project. However, no amendments could occur at this stage of the legislative process, and Democrats voted down DeMaio’s attempt to overturn Assemblymember and Speaker Pro Tempore Josh Lowenthal’s decision, calling him out of order.

Assembly Democrats pushed back on Republican arguments.

Assemblymember Isaac Bryan, a Los Angeles Democrat, said he grew tired of people not from Los Angeles using the deadly fires earlier this year as a political prop in arguments. California has stepped up its efforts in the wake of President Donald Trump removing funding.

“Libraries have to be DOGE’d as well,” Bryan said, referring to the Department of Government Efficiency.

Governor Gavin Newsom has said that state libraries faced the loss of millions of dollars in grants after Trump closed the agency administering the funds.

Assemblymember Jasmeet Bains, a Delano Democrat and physician, argued that Medi-Cal funding provides access to primary care doctors, opening those doors instead of having people visit a hospital during a later stage of an illness.

“People need to wake up and understand, health care is important,” Bains said.

Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel, an Encino Democrat and author of Assembly Bill 100, said the legislation made modest and targeted investments. He said the Legislature would stand with wildfire victims.

“These are good investments,” he added.

Legislating a better future: UC Student Association takes to the state Capitol On the weekend of March 8, students across the UC system attended UCSA’s annual Student Lobby Conference to lobby politicians for legislation affecting funding, inclusivity, and basic needs at UC.

Abby Offenhauser, Associate Features Editor Apr 7, 2025 “The powers that be should be afraid that you all are here,” Christopher Nellum, executive director of EdTrust-West, an education advocacy organization in California, told 216 University of California students at UC Davis on Saturday, March 8. Nellum addressed the group at the UC Student Association’s annual Student Lobby Conference, where students spent a weekend learning about legislative issues and lobbying techniques, before meeting with politicians at the California state Capitol in Sacramento on Monday. Some students drove for hours to attend the conference, some flew across the state, and most had final exams rapidly approaching. All were there because of their passion for California politics and policy, and by virtue of being UC students, they are all part of the UCSA.

Established in 1971, the UCSA is a student-run, UC-wide organization that advocates for legislation benefiting higher education in California. The organization hosts four conferences every year and encourages all UC students to attend, learn about political organizing, and lobby politicians for bills affecting the UC.

In previous years, the UCSA has helped pass legislation such as Prop 47, SB-967, and AB-218 and contributed to UC-wide divestment from the fossil fuel industry. This time around, the group’s asks were to pass legislative bills which primarily fell under the five campaigns it was promoting this year: Racial Justice Now, which combats racial inequality in education and incarceration; UCweVote, which seeks to increase voter education and turnout on UC campuses; ACQUIRE, which looks to improve holistic student resources for things like health services, academic accommodations, and safety from violence; Students Enacting Environmental Defense, which promotes advocacy for Indigenous-inclusive environmental justice; and Fund the UC, which advocates for high-quality and affordable UC education. Fund the UC is the UCSA’s primary focus this year, given the current statewide budget cuts to higher education.

Throughout their weekend at UC Davis, students heard from panels of California state politicians and other UCSA alumni, participated in workshops, and attended lobbying trainings, all in preparation to lobby politicians on Monday. Nellum, the conference’s opening keynote speaker, addressed the student body on Saturday morning to discuss the profound legislative impacts that student organizers have had throughout history, from the Civil Rights Movement to last year’s nationwide campus protests in support of Palestine. In each case, he emphasized, individuals across campuses and backgrounds worked together to improve the lives of students nationwide.

“Students often understand and exemplify the fact that we know that our fates are tied, and we have seen this time and time again,” Nellum said. “It isn’t good enough [for the UC] to be the leading university in California if they’re not going to do right by their students.”

Judith Gutierrez, director of communications for State Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel, discussed her experience as former president of the UCSA student board in a UC alumni panel on Sunday. Gutierrez shared that, in her political career, she still utilizes the skills she built at the SLCs she participated in as an undergraduate student.

“Right before our lobby day, we were told to research the members we were meeting with, look at their Twitter accounts, everything they care about down to where they went to high school,” she said. “And to this day, now I look for those similarities and things I can connect on with members.”

The conference’s twice-daily workshops informed students on pertinent legislative topics and fostered conversations on justice and advocacy infrastructure on their campuses. Students like Jayla Pete, a second-year UC Irvine student and Indigenous identity commissioner for UC Irvine’s Associated Students, shared how their identities and experiences informed their perspective on state policy decisions. Pete attended the SLC primarily to advocate for SB-4, which aims to establish a Missing and Murdered Indigenous Persons Justice Program in the Department of Justice.

“As an Indigenous student, I feel extremely underrepresented in UCI but also UCSA, and I wanted to have this chance to advocate for my community and bring up these issues,” Pete said. “I feel personally that within UC spaces … Indigenous people and Black people tend to advocate for other communities, but no one ever advocates for them. Really, the only person that can advocate for my community is myself and my community members. That’s why I attended this conference.”

Metzli Perez, a second-year UC Santa Barbara student and statewide policy analyst for the UCSA, spoke about the opportunities these conferences have provided.

“I’m a first-generation student; I’m Latina; I’m low-income,” Perez said. “I would’ve never thought it would be possible for me to come to the Capitol in general, and having the opportunity to do so as a student has been really important to me. My first experience lobbying opened up a bunch of doors for me, and I’ve been able to get more involved on my campus, so it’s been very impactful for me.”

For Rohan Vig, a second-year student at UC Riverside, one of the most beneficial parts of the conference was its emphasis on interpersonal relationships. “Everyone says that networking is everything, but they really emphasized getting to know people,” he said. “I think it was Judith who said this in her presentation; she said, ‘It’s not about who you know, it’s who knows you.’”

Students like Pete, Perez, and Vig left the Capitol on Monday equipped with knowledge and experience that will serve them for the rest of their careers — both in politics and in day-to-day life. Any UC student is welcome to be involved in the UCSA and attend upcoming conferences, such as this summer’s Student Organizing Summit. In helping determine UCSA’s legislative priorities for coming years, attendees have the opportunity to build political knowledge and experience in a supportive and impactful space.

California’s Chief Service Officer Josh Fryday reminded students of the lasting change they can make, at future conferences and at their home campuses.

“I hope your journey doesn’t end on Monday after you leave Sacramento and you say, ‘Alright, I did it, my job’s done.’ That’s not how democracy works,” Fryday said. “My advice is, if you find small ways in your community … you’ll see that you will make a difference and you will change things. … If you serve in your community, you can start the ripple effects that then lead to national change.”

Chair, Assemblymember John Harabedian; Senate President pro Tempore Senator Mike McGuire; senators Bob Archuleta, Megan Dahle, María Elena Durazo, Caroline Menjivar, Sasha Renée Pérez, Eloise Gómez Reyes, Laura Richardson, Susan Rubio and Suzette Martinez Valladares; Speaker Robert Rivas; and Assemblymembers Dawn Addis, Cecilia Aguiar-Curry, Patrick Ahrens, Juan Alanis, Rebecca Bauer-Kahan, Marc Berman, Tasha Boerner, Lisa Calderon, Jessica Caloza, Stan Ellis, Mike Fong, Jesse Gabriel, Robert Garcia, Mike Gipson, Jeff Gonzalez, Mark Gonzalez, Heather Hadwick, Matt Haney, Maggy Krell, Tom Lackey, Alex Lee, Alexandra Macedo, Stephanie Nguyen, Liz Ortega, Blanca Pacheco, Diane Papan, Darshana Patel, Gail Pellerin, Cottie Petrie-Norris, Celeste Rodriguez, Michelle Rodriguez, Chris Rogers, Blanca Rubio, Pilar Schiavo, Nick Schultz, José Luis Solache, Esmeralda Soria, Catherine Stefani, Tri Ta, David Tangipa, Avelino Valencia, and Rick Chavez Zbur.

 The California Armenian Legislative Caucus Foundation serves as a forum for members from the California Senate and Assembly to identify key issues affecting Armenian Americans and develop and empower the Armenian American community throughout California. The Foundation encourages advocacy and participation in cultural, educational, and community efforts in California. Through advocacy, the Foundation strives to ensure that California Armenian American’s voices are heard and given a platform.
